[warm] Where Is the Frog?.

[warm and gentle, drawing out key words] [playful whisper] Let's hide them! said Theo. [soft rustling grass] He tucked the duck and the frog into the tall green grass.
[warm and gentle, drawing out key words] Grandma came out to look, and [pleased] she saw the yellow duck right away. Yellow on green is easy to spot.
[warm and gentle, drawing out key words] [puzzled] But where was the frog? Grandma looked and looked. Green on green is hard to see.
[warm and gentle, drawing out key words] [a child giggling] Theo giggled. [delighted] The frog is green like the grass, he said. It looks just like the grass!

[warm and friendly] The frigid wind made the climbers shiver and pull their hoods tight. Shiver. Hoods. The new word had come to the party with friends, and the friends gave it away. Frigid meant very cold.

[warm and friendly] Two pages later came another stranger. The climbers reached the summit, or the very top of the mountain. This time the clue came right after the word, holding the door open. The little word or was saying: here is what it means.

[warm and friendly] Then came a word with no friends at all. On the ridge, a ptarmigan watched them pass. Nothing around it helped. Was it a rock? A person? Ava finally got off the couch and opened the dictionary. A ptarmigan is a bird whose feathers turn white in winter.

[warm and friendly] Most new words arrive with clues: the words beside them, the sentence before, the picture on the page. Read around the stranger first, and you will guess right more often than not. When the friends stay quiet, the dictionary does the introducing.
[warm] What she did at recess.

[warm and friendly] Jonah's teacher asked the class to describe the new girl, Lina, after her first day. Almost everybody wrote the same thing. She is shy. That was what Lina had said about herself that morning, in a voice so small the back row missed it.
[warm and friendly] One boy wrote that she was tall. The teacher shook her head. Tall is how someone looks, she said. I asked what she is like. A trait is a way of being: brave, honest, kind, shy.

[warm and friendly] Jonah started to write shy, then stopped. At recess he had seen something. A first grader was crying because every swing was taken. Lina got off her swing without a word and gave it to him. Shy people did not do that. Or did they?

[warm and friendly] He wrote it carefully. The where was the playground. The when was recess, under a hot sun with the swing chains creaking. Those two were the setting. And who Lina was did not come from what she said about herself. It came from what she did. She was kind.

[warm and friendly] On Friday, Lina raised her hand and read her poem out loud to the whole class. Her voice shook a little, but she finished. The girl who called herself shy had just been brave. Jonah wrote that down too. Characters can change.

[warm and friendly] That is how characters work in every story. Setting is the where and the when. Characters show who they are by what they say and do, and when the two disagree, believe what they do.
[warm] The day the newspaper came to school.

[warm and friendly] The class was going to make a newspaper. One page, real stories, printed for the whole school, with real bylines. Ms. Reyes handed out red pens and made one rule: every reader must understand every story on the first try.

[warm and friendly] The first job was headlines. A headline is the main idea in a few words. The story about the leaky gym roof had twelve facts in it, from the drip on the free-throw line to the bucket everyone called Gerald. The headline was four words long. Gym Roof Leaks Again.

[warm and friendly] The second job was hard words. The sports report called the fifth grade team unbeatable, and half the class stopped reading. So they took the word apart. Un means not. Able means can be. Unbeatable: cannot be beaten. Once you can see the pieces, a long word opens like a door.

[warm and friendly] Another story said the rain had been torrential. Nobody knew that word either, but the next sentence helped: the gutters overflowed, and the parking lot turned into a lake. Torrential rain is very heavy rain. The words around a stranger usually give it away, so the class left it in.

[warm and friendly] The lunch review was the trickiest. It said the Friday pizza was the best in the world. Fact or opinion? Nobody could check every pizza in the world, so it was an opinion. It stayed in the paper, but now it said whose opinion it was: the writer's.

[warm and friendly] The field trip story had its events in a jumble, like a puzzle dumped on a table. So the writers put them in order and showed the causes. The bus was late because of the rain, so lunch moved indoors, and then the sun came out just in time for the walk home.

[warm and friendly] The best story of all was a profile of Mr. Bell, the custodian. The writer never called him kind. She wrote what he did: he dried the gym floor with his own towels before the big game, and he knew every kid's name by October. Readers could see who he was from what he did.

[warm and friendly] When the page was printed, every reader in the school found the main ideas and opened the long words. They knew what was checked and what was only felt, followed each story in order and met Mr. Bell. That is reading to understand, and the class had learned it by working from the other side of the page.
[warm] Three states in the kitchen.

[warm and friendly] On Saturday morning, Theo dropped an ice cube on a plate and left it on the counter. He poured water into a glass. His mother put the kettle on the stove. Three different things, he thought. Ice, water and steam.

[warm and friendly] When he came back, the ice cube was gone. In its place was a puddle, spreading across the plate. The kettle was whistling, and the kitchen window had gone foggy. Where did the ice go? And where did that fog come from?

[warm and friendly] His mother tapped the plate. The ice cube kept its square shape until it warmed. That is a solid. Then it melted and spread out flat, taking the shape of the plate. That is a liquid. Pour it into a glass and it becomes glass-shaped.

[warm and friendly] The kettle was the next step. Heat the water enough and it boils. It turns into steam, a gas that spreads to fill the whole kitchen. You cannot hold a gas or pour it. It goes wherever there is room.

[warm and friendly] Theo touched the foggy window. It was cold and wet. The steam had cooled on the glass and turned back into tiny drops of water. He filled the ice tray and put it in the freezer. By lunch the water was solid again.

[warm and friendly] Everything around you is a solid, a liquid or a gas. A solid keeps its shape. A liquid takes the shape of its container. A gas fills whatever holds it. Heat moves matter up that list, and cooling brings it back down. Same water, the whole way through.
[warm] Pushes and pulls.

[warm and friendly] The red wagon sat at the bottom of the hill, loaded with three pumpkins for the fall sale at the top. Jamal stood beside it and waited. Nothing happened. Wagons, it turns out, do not move by themselves.

[warm and friendly] He grabbed the handle and pulled, and the wagon rolled, squeaking, up the sidewalk. Then his sister steered it onto the grass to take a shortcut. The wagon slowed and stopped, even though Jamal was still pulling hard. The grass was fighting him. Why?

[warm and friendly] His dad knelt by the wheels. A force is a push or a pull, he said, and nothing starts or stops without one. Jamal's pull was one force. The grass was another. It rubbed against the wheels and slowed them. That rubbing is called friction.
[warm and friendly] So Jamal pulled and his sister pushed from behind. Two forces in the same direction. The wagon crawled up the grass and reached the top, and the pumpkins sold in an hour.

[warm and friendly] At the top, Jamal let go of the empty wagon for one second. It rolled straight back down the hill without anyone touching it. Gravity had pulled it, the same pull that makes a dropped ball fall. At the bottom, the grass rubbed it slower and slower until it stopped.

[warm and friendly] Nothing moves without a force. A push or a pull gets things going, friction slows moving things down, and gravity pulls everything toward the ground. Watch anything roll, slide or fall, and ask which force did that.
[warm] The jar of eggs.

[warm and friendly] Rosa scooped a clump of clear jelly from the pond into a jar on the classroom windowsill. Inside the jelly were hundreds of little black dots. Her brother said they were dirt. She said they were eggs. Nobody could tell.
[warm and friendly] About a week later the dots had wriggled free. They had tails and swam in quick, jerky circles. They were tadpoles. Rosa fed them boiled lettuce and drew them every Friday.

[warm and friendly] After about six weeks, two tiny back legs appeared. A few weeks after that came front legs, and the tails began to shrink. Every time Rosa looked, the thing in the jar was different. Was it even the same animal?

[warm and friendly] It was. Her teacher drew a circle on the board: egg, tadpole, tadpole with legs, frog. Each stage leads to the next. And a grown frog lays eggs, which starts the circle again. That circle is called a life cycle.

[warm and friendly] A bean does it too, her teacher said. Seed, sprout, plant, flower, and the flower makes new seeds. A butterfly goes egg, caterpillar, chrysalis, butterfly. The stages look nothing alike, but each one makes the next.

[warm and friendly] In June, Rosa carried the little frogs back to the pond and let them go at the muddy edge. The next spring she went back to look. Floating by the reeds was a fresh clump of clear jelly, full of black dots.
[warm and friendly] Every living thing goes around its own circle of stages. A frog, a bean, a butterfly and you. The shapes change, but the circle keeps turning.
[warm] Cold in July.

[warm and friendly] Every morning in July, Ava checked the weather station in her Texas backyard. The thermometer read a hundred degrees by noon. The rain gauge had been dry for three weeks. Weather is what the sky is doing today, and today it was baking.

[warm and friendly] Then a letter came from her pen pal, Jack, who lives in the mountains of Australia. He wrote about snow. He had built a snowman in the yard and could not feel his fingers. In July.
[warm and friendly] Ava read it twice. Same month, same planet. How could she be sweating while he wore a scarf? Was the Sun closer to Texas?

[warm and friendly] Her teacher held up a globe and tilted it. The Earth leans. As it travels around the Sun, one half leans toward the light and gets long days and high sun. That is summer. The other half leans away and gets short days and low sun. That is winter.

[warm and friendly] In July, the northern half leans in, and Texas bakes. The southern half leans out, and Australia shivers. In January they swap. The Earth is even a little farther from the Sun in July, which surprised Ava most.
[warm and friendly] The pattern comes back every year, in the same order. Spring warms, summer is hottest, fall cools, winter is coldest. Jack's seasons run the same circle, just half a year apart.

[warm and friendly] Weather is today, and you measure it with tools. Seasons are the pattern, and you can plan for them. They are not about how close the Sun is. They are about which way you are leaning.
[warm] The rubber band.

[warm and friendly] Owen was building a guitar for music class out of a paper cup and a rubber band. He stretched the band over the cup and plucked it. Twang. He plucked it again and, while it was still buzzing, touched it with one finger. It tickled. The sound stopped the moment he touched it.

[warm and friendly] That was strange. Why would a finger stop a sound? He tried again and again. Every time the band shook, there was a sound. Every time he held it still, silence. The sound and the shaking seemed to be the same thing.
[warm and friendly] They were. Sound is a vibration: something shaking fast enough to shake the air. The shaking air travels to your ear, and your ear feels it as sound.

[warm and friendly] Owen plucked harder, and the band shook wider. The sound got louder. He stretched the band tighter, and it shook faster. The sound went higher. He loosened it, and the note dropped low. Bigger shake, louder. Faster shake, higher. Slower shake, lower.

[warm and friendly] Then he put his ear flat on his desk and tapped the far end with a pencil. The tap came through the wood, louder than it came through the air. Sound can travel through air, water or wood. With nothing at all to travel through, like in outer space, there is no sound.

[warm and friendly] Every sound you have ever heard is something vibrating, from a guitar string to a drum skin to your own voice. Put a hand on your throat and hum. That buzz is you, shaking the air.
[warm] The jar.

[warm and friendly] Priya's tomato plants were drooping, and her grandpa said the trouble was in the dirt. Dirt was just dirt, she thought. She scooped some into a jar of water and shook it until the whole thing turned brown. Then she went to bed.

[warm and friendly] In the morning the jar had sorted itself into stripes. Gritty sand lay at the bottom, fine silt above it. The water was still cloudy with clay, and dark bits of old leaves floated near the top. One scoop of dirt had become four things. How?

[warm and friendly] Because soil was never one thing. Most of it is rock, cracked apart over thousands of years by rain, ice and roots, then ground smaller and smaller. The rest is rotted leaves and roots of things that once lived. Heavy sand sank first. Tiny clay took longest to settle.

[warm and friendly] Her grandpa showed her the squeeze test. He wet a handful of each. Clay made a sticky ball that held its shape. Sand fell apart in his fingers. The good garden soil held together a little and crumbled a little. That mix is called loam.

[warm and friendly] Priya's garden bed was mostly clay. Clay packs tight and holds water, so her tomato roots were sitting in a puddle. They dug in rotted leaves from the compost pile, and by summer the plants stood tall.

[warm and friendly] The ground under your feet is a slow recipe of rock and rotted life. Clay holds water, sand drains fast, and loam is the mix that gardens love. A jar of water reads the recipe out.
[warm] The bucket line.

[warm and friendly] At summer camp, Kenji stood at the bottom of a line of kids passing a bucket of water up the hill. He filled it to the brim at the creek. Every hand spilled a little. By the time it reached the top, only a splash sloshed at the bottom.

[warm and friendly] That night the counselor asked a strange question. Why are there so many blades of grass in the meadow and so few hawks above it? The kids guessed hawks were shy, or fast, or hiding. Nobody guessed the bucket.

[warm and friendly] Every food chain starts with the sun. Grass catches sunlight and makes its own food, so grass is a producer. A grasshopper eats the grass, a bird eats the grasshopper, and a hawk eats the bird. Each eater is a consumer, and each one uses up most of the energy it gets, like a spill.
[warm and friendly] By the hawk, only a splash is left. It takes a whole meadow of grass to feed one hawk, which is why the hawk sits at the top of this chain.

[warm and friendly] The next morning Kenji found a rotting log covered in mushrooms. The counselor said those were decomposers. They break down dead things and turn them back into soil, and the soil feeds the grass. The chain was really a circle.
[warm and friendly] Late that summer the creek ran low and the meadow went brown. The grasshoppers thinned out, then the birds, and the hawk flew off to hunt somewhere else.
[warm and friendly] Every link depends on the one below it. Take away the grass, and the whole line goes dry.
[warm] The storm that came to the science fair.

[warm and friendly] The science fair was set up outside on the lawn, which everyone later agreed was a mistake. Table one had an ice cube melting on a plate, a glass of water and a thermos of hot water puffing steam: solid, liquid, gas. Table two had a wagon on a wooden ramp for pushes and pulls.

[warm and friendly] Table three had a jar of tadpoles with tiny back legs, halfway to being frogs. Table four had a rain gauge that had never seen rain. Table five had a jar of garden dirt settled into layers, sand at the bottom, and table six had a poster of a food chain: grass, grasshopper, bird, hawk.

[warm and friendly] Then the sky went dark, and thunder rumbled far off. The principal did not wait. When thunder roars, she called, go indoors! Everyone grabbed a poster and ran for the gym, because thunder means lightning is close enough to be dangerous.

[warm and friendly] They watched the rest through the gym windows. The wind shoved the wagon down its ramp with nobody touching it, and gravity pulled it faster down the slope. It was the best demonstration of a force anyone gave all day. Out on the grass, the rubbing of friction slowed it until it stopped by the flagpole.

[warm and friendly] The rain came down so hard that the gauge filled past its first line in ten minutes. Nobody had ever seen the gauge move that fast. On table one, the ice cube had melted into a puddle, and the thermos had stopped steaming. Rain on the windows ran together into little streams.

[warm and friendly] When the thunder cracked close, the gym windows buzzed under a boy's hand. He felt it and heard it at the same moment. Sound is a vibration, and a big one can shake the glass it passes through.

[warm and friendly] The storm moved on in half an hour. The posters were soaked, but the tadpoles did not mind at all. A tadpole lives in water and was on its way to becoming a frog either way. A robin hopped onto the wet grass to hunt for insects, the food chain from the poster back at work.

[warm and friendly] The judges gave every table a ribbon. In one afternoon they had seen matter change state, forces move things, a life cycle turning, weather arriving and sound shaking a window. The weather had done the demonstrating, and the judges had the good sense to watch it from indoors.
[warm] The shape of it.

[warm and friendly] Lily had to write a paragraph about her dog, Pepper, and she had a hundred things to say. He brings in the newspaper. He finds her lost shoes. He once ate a whole birthday cake. She wrote it all in one heap, and it sounded like a shopping list.

[warm and friendly] Her teacher asked one question. What is this paragraph about? My dog, said Lily. Yes, said the teacher, but what about him? Every sentence in the heap was true. Not one of them said the big thing.

[warm and friendly] So she wrote the big thing first. Pepper is the best helper in our house. That was the idea, and it went in the first sentence. Then the heap became proof. He brings in the newspaper. He finds my lost shoes.

[warm and friendly] Then she read each sentence and asked the test question: is this about the same idea? The newspaper, yes. The shoes, yes. The birthday cake? That was not helping. That was stealing.

[warm and friendly] The cake did not get thrown away. It got a paragraph of its own, with its own first sentence. Pepper is also a thief. Now Lily had two paragraphs, two ideas, and nothing in the wrong place.
[warm and friendly] Her teacher drew it as a table. The first sentence is the tabletop, the idea everything rests on. The details are the legs, and a leg from a different table makes it wobble.
[warm and friendly] That is the shape of a paragraph. One idea in the first sentence, details after it holding it up, and a new paragraph for every new idea.
[warm] The paper boat.

[warm and friendly] Marcus could fold a paper boat with his eyes closed. His friend Eli could not, so Marcus wrote the steps on a card for him. Fold the paper in half. Fold the top corners down. Fold the bottom strips up. Pull it open. Easy.
[warm and friendly] Eli tried it at the kitchen table. He got a paper hat, and then he got stuck. Pull what open? Every way he pulled, the hat tore. He brought Marcus the ripped hat and the card.

[warm and friendly] Marcus read his card and frowned. Every step on it was right, but his hands did more than it said. After the hat, you open it at the bottom and flatten it into a diamond. Then you fold the bottom corners up and flatten it again. He had skipped what he no longer noticed doing.
[warm and friendly] So he folded one slowly and wrote down every move as his hands made it. What you need: one sheet of paper. Then seven steps, in the order they really happen. Seven, not four.
[warm and friendly] Eli followed the new card without asking a single question. Hat. Diamond. Smaller diamond. Pull the top corners apart. The boat popped open, and it floated in the sink.

[warm and friendly] Explaining how to do something has two parts: say what is needed, then give every step in order. The test is to picture a stranger following your words. A missing step leaves them stuck, and steps out of order leave them with a mess.
[warm] I think, because.

[warm and friendly] Mia's class wanted a pet. When the teacher asked why, twelve kids shouted at once. Because pets are cool! Because! Just because! The teacher waited for the noise to stop. That is not a reason, she said. That is a wish.

[warm and friendly] Mia wanted the pet more than anyone. But she could hear that the shouting was not working. Wanting something was not the same as making a case for it. What did a case even look like?

[warm and friendly] Then Leo stood up for a hamster. I think we should get a hamster, because hamsters are fun. The class clapped. The teacher nodded and asked him for a second reason. Leo opened his mouth, closed it and sat down.

[warm and friendly] Mia put up her hand and said it in order. I think our class should get a fish. Because a fish would teach us to take care of something every day. Because a fish is quiet and will not bother the class next door.

[warm and friendly] Then she said it again, in new words. A fish would be the perfect classmate. The teacher wrote it on the board in four lines: what I think, a reason, a reason, and what I think again.
[warm and friendly] They voted, and the fish won. It got a name, Captain Bubbles, and a job chart.

[warm and friendly] That is how to give a reason. Say what you think. Say because, with two real reasons. Then say it again at the end in fresh words. A wish only gets clapped for. A reason gets a fish.
[warm] Georgette and the letter.

[warm and friendly] Georgette was eight, read everything, and had never written a real letter. Her grandmother lived a day's drive away and wrote every week in handwriting like lace. Georgette wanted to answer with something worth reading. Her first try was a page of loose facts that wandered like a lost cat. She had a lot to say and no idea where to put it.

[warm and friendly] Her teacher showed her the shape of a paragraph. Say the big idea in the first sentence. Then give details that hold it up. Georgette started over. Our new house is small, but it is perfect. My room has a window seat. The kitchen smells like toast. The yard has a tree made for climbing.

[warm and friendly] Then she read each sentence and asked the test question: is this about the same idea? The neighbor's dog barks at the mailman. That one was about the dog, not the house. It moved to a paragraph of its own, with its own first sentence.

[warm and friendly] Her second letter explained how to fold a paper boat. Fold in half, corners down, strips up, pull it open. Two weeks later her grandmother wrote back that she had made a very nice paper hat and worn it to the grocery store. Georgette laughed until her stomach hurt. She had skipped the steps her hands did without thinking.

[warm and friendly] So she folded a boat slowly and wrote down every move. What you need: one sheet of paper. Then all seven steps, in order, from the first fold to pulling the top corners apart. The next letter from her grandmother had a photo inside: a paper boat floating in her kitchen sink.

[warm and friendly] The third letter was a case. Georgette thought the family should visit at Christmas instead of summer. I think we should come at Christmas, she wrote, because the whole family is off school and work at once, and because you have never seen me in the Christmas play.

[warm and friendly] Then she said it again in new words, the way her teacher had shown her. Christmas is the one time we can all be at your table. Her grandmother read it twice and said yes the same afternoon.

[warm and friendly] Georgette kept every letter her grandmother sent in a shoebox under her bed. Some of them had paper boats tucked inside. Years later, when she was the grandmother people wrote to, she still had them, and she still answered every one in paragraphs.
[warm] Three bags.

[warm and friendly] Ben was helping at his aunt's apple stall at the farmers market. A customer pointed at three paper bags, five apples in each, and asked how many apples that was. Ben counted every apple with his finger. One, two, three. The customer sighed. Ben lost his place and started over.
[warm and friendly] His aunt could say the answer before he opened the second bag. Fifteen. Every time. Was she guessing? The apples smelled sweet, and the line was getting longer.

[warm and friendly] She tipped the apples onto the table in three rows of five. Five, ten, fifteen, she said, tapping one row at a time. Three groups of five is three fives added together: five plus five plus five. That is all multiplying is. Three times five is fifteen.
[warm and friendly] Rows and columns like that have a name, she said. An array. Count the rows, count how many are in each row, and multiply.

[warm and friendly] The next customer wanted four bags with three apples in each. Ben made four rows of three. Twelve. Then he turned the tray sideways, and the rows became three rows of four. Still twelve. Four groups of three and three groups of four were the same apples, seen from a new side.

[warm and friendly] The first number says how many groups. The second says how many are in each one. Whenever things come in equal groups, you do not have to count them one by one. Groups times how many in each group, and the counting is already done.
[warm] Seven times eight.
[warm and friendly] Every fact in the times table stuck for Lena except one. Seven times eight. She learned it every night and lost it every morning, like a sock that kept vanishing in the wash.
[warm and friendly] Her grandfather asked what seven times eight even meant. Fifty-six, she said. No, he said, what does it mean? Lena did not know. She had been memorizing a sound, not a thing.

[warm and friendly] He drew a rectangle of dots on a napkin, seven across and eight down. Then he turned the napkin sideways. Eight across and seven down. Seven eights and eight sevens were one rectangle, looked at two ways. Every fact works both ways, so learning half the table gets you the whole thing.

[warm and friendly] Then he showed her how to build the hard fact from easy ones. She already knew her fives: every fact ends in five or zero. Five eights are forty. She knew her twos, because twos just double. Two eights are sixteen. Forty and sixteen make fifty-six.
[warm and friendly] The rectangle split right down the middle to prove it: five columns on one side, two on the other, seven columns in all.
[warm and friendly] He had one more trick: say five, six, seven, eight, and there it is, because fifty-six is seven times eight. The numbers march in order, and Lena said it all the way to school.

[warm and friendly] The facts up to ten times ten are the tools every bigger problem uses. Practice a few at a time, a little each day. A fact you can picture, and build from facts you know, is a fact you keep.
[warm] Deal them out.

[warm and friendly] Twelve cookies, four friends, and nobody wanted to be the one who got fewer. Everyone grabbed. Somebody got five, somebody got just two, and the arguing started before anyone took a bite.

[warm and friendly] Grace took the plate back. There had to be a fair way. Twelve was too many to split by just looking. She could feel the warm cookies through the plate, and everyone was staring at her.

[warm and friendly] She dealt them out like cards. One for each friend, around the table. Then another round, and another. No favorites, no grabbing, no arguing. The plate was empty, and every plate had three. Twelve divided by four is three.

[warm and friendly] She could check it backward, too. Three cookies on each of four plates is three times four, and three times four is twelve. Dividing undoes multiplying. The same three numbers make both facts.

[warm and friendly] Then the doorbell rang. Two more friends, and now there were six. Nobody grabbed this time. Everyone looked at Grace. She asked herself the backward question: what times six makes twelve? Two. So each of the first four gave one cookie back, and all six had two.

[warm and friendly] Dividing is sharing out equally, one round at a time, like dealing cards. When a division looks hard, flip it around and ask the multiplying question: what times the divisor makes the total? The answer to that is the answer to this. Twelve divided by six is two, because six times two is twelve.
[warm] Column by column.
[warm and friendly] Hugo had 256 marbles in one jar and 378 in another, and he wanted one number for the whole collection. He added them in his head and got a different answer every time.

[warm and friendly] The trouble was the ones. Six and eight make fourteen, and fourteen will not fit in one column. He wrote the whole 14 there anyway, and the answer came out enormous and wrong. Where was the extra ten supposed to go?

[warm and friendly] His teacher showed him to go column by column, ones first. Six and eight is fourteen. Write the 4, and carry the ten to the tens column. Tens: five and seven and the carried one make thirteen. Write the 3, and carry the hundred. Hundreds: two and three and one make six. 634 marbles.

[warm and friendly] Every number up to a thousand is built the same way, from hundreds, tens and ones. 634 is six hundreds, three tens and four ones. Each column holds one kind, and a ten that spills over belongs next door.

[warm and friendly] Then his cousin asked for 125 marbles. Two steps: put the jars together, then give some away. Ones first again. Four ones are not enough to take away five, so Hugo borrowed a ten, and fourteen take away five is nine. Two tens take away two is zero. Six hundreds take away one is five. 509 left.

[warm and friendly] Adding and subtracting big numbers is small columns, in order. Carry when a column makes ten or more. Borrow when a column runs short. And read a two-step problem all the way through before you start.
[warm] Three ways to measure a puppy.

[warm and friendly] The shelter sent Ellie home with a new puppy named Noodle and a chart to fill in. How long is she? How heavy is she? How much water does she drink in a day? Ellie grabbed a ruler and started with the puppy, who did not want to be measured at all.

[warm and friendly] Fourteen inches, nose to tail, after four tries. Twelve inches make a foot, so Noodle was one foot and two inches long. Then Ellie held the ruler against the puppy again for the second question and stopped. A ruler cannot tell you how heavy something is.

[warm and friendly] She needed a different tool. The kitchen scale was too small, so her mom stood on the bathroom scale holding Noodle, then without her. The difference was six pounds. Pounds answer how heavy.

[warm and friendly] For the water, Ellie poured two cups into the bowl with a measuring cup in the morning. At bedtime she poured what was left back into the cup. One cup. So Noodle drank one cup that day. Cups answer how much liquid.
[warm and friendly] Her dad pointed at the gallon jug in the garage. Sixteen cups fill a gallon, he said, so that jug holds sixteen days of Noodle's water.

[warm and friendly] Three questions, three tools. A ruler for how long, a scale for how heavy, a measuring cup for how much. Every measurement starts with the question. Pick the unit that answers it, and the tool comes with it. A ruler on a puppy only ever answers one of the three.
[warm] The cars.

[warm and friendly] Kai said most cars on their street were red. His sister Ana said blue. They sat on the porch for ten minutes to settle it and called out colors as cars went by. Red, blue, blue, white, red, blue. By the end, neither could remember the count.

[warm and friendly] So they tried again. Ana drew a line for every car under its color, and when a color reached five, she drew the fifth line across the other four. Bundles of five. Counting a bundle takes one look.
[warm and friendly] This time the tallies said red four, blue six and white three. Blue had one bundle and one more line. Red had four lines and no bundle at all.

[warm and friendly] Then Ana turned the tallies into a bar graph. One bar for each color, as tall as its count. The blue bar stood tallest, taller than red by two, and nobody had to count anything again. The picture said it.
[warm and friendly] They showed their mom, and she asked what the bars were counting. Birds? Bikes? A graph with no labels is a riddle. So Ana wrote a title across the top and a color under each bar.
[warm and friendly] Kai made a pictograph too, with one little car standing for two real ones. Blue got three little cars. Red got two. White got one and a half.
[warm and friendly] Tallies count in fives so a long count stays easy. Bar graphs and pictographs turn counts into pictures, and a title and labels say what the pictures mean.
[warm] Frederick and the ants.

[warm and friendly] Frederick was eight and had an ant farm on his windowsill, a birthday present from his dad, along with a digital microscope he was not allowed to touch without help. Twenty-four harvester ants came in a tube. His dad said they had come without a queen, so the farm would not grow, but it would be busy.

[warm and friendly] On the third morning the ants had dug four tunnels, and they would not hold still to be counted. So Frederick stopped counting ants and counted groups. Four tunnels, six ants resting in each. Four groups of six. Twenty-four, without touching a single ant.

[warm and friendly] By the second week he had the times tables to ten taped above the farm, and he used them the way other kids used a calculator. Six groups of four was the same twenty-four ants seen sideways, because every fact works both ways. His sister asked what seven eights were. Fifty-six, he said, before she finished asking.

[warm and friendly] When his dad brought home a second, bigger farm, Frederick split the colony fairly. Twenty-four ants, two farms, twelve in each. Dividing was sharing out equally, and it undid the multiplying exactly: two groups of twelve made twenty-four again.

[warm and friendly] Every morning he held a ruler against the glass and measured the longest tunnel in inches. One morning the bigger farm's longest tunnel reached seven inches. He kept a tally chart of which farm dug farther each day, in bundles of five, and turned it into a bar graph. The bigger farm won by a lot. More room, more digging.

[warm and friendly] Then he read that a wild harvester ant colony can hold thousands of ants, and he wanted real numbers. He and his sister sat a careful step back from two anthills in the backyard, because harvester ants sting, and tallied every ant that went in for ten minutes at each hill. The first hill got 256. The second got 378.

[warm and friendly] He added them in columns, ones first. Six and eight is fourteen, so write the 4 and carry the ten. Five and seven and the carried one is thirteen, so write the 3 and carry the hundred. Two and three and one is six. 634 trips into the two hills in twenty minutes.
[warm and friendly] His dad found the sums penciled on the side of the farm and did not erase them. Frederick would be a biology professor one day. It started with a windowsill and a tally chart.
[warm] The talking toaster.

[warm and friendly] Arjun's uncle had a toaster that talked. When the toast was ready, it said, done, and the bread popped up. Arjun wanted to know how it decided what to say. His uncle said the toaster only knew three things, and those three explained every computer in the world.
[warm and friendly] The first thing was inputs. The lever going down, the dial set to four, the little button for bagels. Each one tells the toaster something. You do the telling.
[warm and friendly] The second thing was outputs. The heat, the ding, the toast popping up, the voice saying done. Each one shows you something. The toaster does the showing.
[warm and friendly] In between was a program, a list of steps the toaster follows exactly, in order. Dial at four means this much heat for this long. Then pop, then ding, then done.

[warm and friendly] Arjun turned the dial all the way to nine to see what would happen. The toaster did exactly what it was told, and the bread came out black. It never wondered whether he meant it. A program cannot guess. It follows the steps it is given, with the inputs it is given.

[warm and friendly] Then Arjun looked at his tablet. Touching the screen was an input. The picture on the screen and the sound from the speaker were outputs. The games were programs. It was the same toaster with more buttons.
[warm and friendly] Inputs tell a computer. Outputs show you. A program is the steps in between. Watch, car or toaster, every computer runs on those three.
[warm] Exactly what she was told.

[warm and friendly] Nina wrote instructions for a jam sandwich and handed them to her big sister, who promised to follow them exactly and add nothing. Step one: put jam on the bread. Her sister picked up the whole loaf, still in its bag, and smeared jam on the outside.

[warm and friendly] Nina shrieked. That was not what she meant! Her sister shrugged. It was what she wrote. Nina had never said to open the bag, or take out a slice, or open the jar. Every step she skipped, her sister skipped too.

[warm and friendly] The second try was longer. Open the bag. Take out two slices. Lay them flat. Open the jar. Spread jam on one slice. But Nina put the slices together before the jam step, and her sister spread jam on the top of a closed, empty sandwich.
[warm and friendly] Two steps in the wrong order, and the whole sandwich went wrong. Nina swapped them back.

[warm and friendly] The third try had eleven steps, every one in its place. Her sister followed them without making a single decision, and out came a perfect sandwich. Nina had written an algorithm: a list of steps, in order, that gets something done.
[warm and friendly] A computer follows an algorithm the way her sister did. It never guesses what you meant. If a step is missing, it skips it. If two steps are swapped, it swaps them.
[warm and friendly] An algorithm is steps in order. The order matters, and every small step must be there, because whoever follows it will do exactly what it says and nothing else.
[warm] One instruction, repeated.

[warm and friendly] Felix wrote instructions for a bead necklace: red bead, blue bead, red bead, blue bead. Eighty lines for eighty beads. His hand ached, and somewhere in the middle he had written blue twice in a row.
[warm and friendly] His teacher asked what all those lines had in common. Felix looked. Every pair was the same, red then blue, over and over. Eighty lines were really one pair of lines, forty times.

[warm and friendly] So he rewrote the whole thing in two lines. Repeat forty times: red bead, blue bead. That is a loop, a set of steps that runs again and again. Two lines instead of eighty, and no place for a mistake to hide.

[warm and friendly] Then his little sister wanted a bracelet: red, red, yellow, red, red, yellow. Felix hunted for the part that repeats. Not red, red. Not red, yellow. The part was three beads long: red, red, yellow. Repeat it six times, and she had eighteen beads.
[warm and friendly] A loop is also easy to change. When his sister wanted a longer bracelet, Felix did not rewrite anything. He changed six to eight, and the bracelet grew to twenty-four beads.

[warm and friendly] Loops are everywhere once you look. A song writes its chorus once and marks it to repeat. A staircase is one step, repeated. Even a clap, stomp, clap, stomp dance is a loop of two moves. Programs use loops to do a lot with very little.
[warm and friendly] Find the part that repeats. Write it once. Say how many times. That is a loop.
[warm] The robot birthday.

[warm and friendly] The robot came in a box on the morning of June's birthday party. It was small and white, with two blue lights for eyes, and her aunt had built it. The first thing it did was nothing at all. Nobody had told it anything. It sat on the table like a guest who had forgotten why it came.

[warm and friendly] June's aunt, who built robots for a living, showed her the three parts. The buttons on its back were inputs: you press them to tell the robot something. The little screen and the beep were outputs: that is how it shows you something. In between, a program waits for steps. No steps, no robot.

[warm and friendly] June wrote her first program on an index card and typed it in with the buttons. Forward two. Turn left. Beep. The robot rolled two squares across the checkered tablecloth, turned, beeped and stopped dead, because that was the end of the card. It did exactly what it was told, and not one thing more.

[warm and friendly] Serving the cake needed more steps than anyone expected. Pick up a plate. Put a slice on it. Drive to the next guest. Hand it over. Four steps, in order, once for every guest, and there were ten guests. Written out, that was forty lines, and June's hand hurt by line twelve.

[warm and friendly] Then her cousin noticed that the same four steps kept repeating. So June wrote them once, inside a loop: repeat ten times. Forty lines became five. The robot served ten plates without a single mistake, and the whole program fit on a card small enough for a pocket.

[warm and friendly] The only disaster was the juice. The card said pour the juice, and nobody had said take the cap off first. The robot tipped the bottle over every cup, very politely, and not a drop came out. Everyone laughed so hard that June's grandpa had to sit down.

[warm and friendly] June added one line above the pour: take off the cap. The juice poured, and the robot beeped once, which was the closest it could get to singing. Her aunt said June had just debugged her first program: she found the missing step and fixed it.

[warm and friendly] Every computer works like that robot. Inputs tell it, outputs show you, and a program is the steps in between. The order matters, every step must be there, and a loop lets a few lines do a lot of work.
[warm] Three levels.

[warm and friendly] On Saturday, Tomas hit a pothole on his bike, rode past a crew fixing the highway overpass and mailed a birthday card to his grandmother. Three ordinary things. Then his uncle asked him who fixes the pothole, who fixes the highway and who delivers the card.
[warm and friendly] The government, Tomas said. His uncle asked, which one? Tomas did not know there was more than one. It felt like a trick question, and the pothole was still there.

[warm and friendly] There are three, his uncle said, stacked like floors in a building. The ground floor is local: your city, led by a mayor and a city council. It fixes streets, runs the library and sends the fire truck. The pothole belongs to them.

[warm and friendly] The middle floor is the state: Texas, led by a governor and a legislature in Austin. It builds the highways, runs the state parks and gives out driver's licenses. The top floor is national: the United States, led by a president and Congress in Washington, D.C. It prints the money and delivers the mail.

[warm and friendly] Tomas wanted the pothole gone, so his uncle took him to a city council meeting. Tomas stood up and described the hole, how deep it was and where. A council member wrote it down. Two weeks later, a city truck filled it.
[warm and friendly] Local, state and national. Three levels, three leaders, three sets of jobs. The closer the level, the easier it is to walk in and be heard, even when you are nine.
[warm] Rule or law?.

[warm and friendly] Noah got told off twice in one day. Once at school for running in the hall, and once on the way home for stepping into the street before the walk signal came on. His dad said one of those was a rule and one was a law. Noah said they felt exactly the same.

[warm and friendly] They both told him what to do. They both had someone watching. But would a police officer ever stop a kid for running down a school hallway? Noah laughed. Of course not. So what made them different?

[warm and friendly] Who they cover, his dad said. A rule is for one group: a family, a class, a team. The school made the hall rule, and it stops at the school door. A law is for everyone in a city, a state or the whole country, and breaking it has a set punishment.

[warm and friendly] The walk signal law covers everyone in Texas. The state legislature in Austin made it. Laws for the whole country come from Congress. The President carries them out, and the courts decide what they mean when people disagree.

[warm and friendly] The next day, Noah's class voted on a field trip. Fourteen kids chose the zoo and ten chose the museum. More than half picked the zoo, so the zoo won by four. That is majority rule.
[warm and friendly] The museum kids groaned, but they still got to go, and they still get a vote next time. That is the deal that makes voting work.
[warm and friendly] Rule or law, ask who it covers.
[warm] The eleven dollars.

[warm and friendly] Hana had eleven dollars. Six came from chores and five from a birthday card. At the store she found the book she wanted for eight dollars and the ball she wanted for seven. She counted her money twice. It did not get any bigger.

[warm and friendly] She tried every trick. Maybe the ball was on sale. It was not. Maybe she could pay the rest next week. The cashier smiled and shook her head. Eight and seven make fifteen, and eleven is not fifteen.

[warm and friendly] That is scarcity. There is never enough for everything, so every choice gives something up. Hana chose the book. The ball stayed on the shelf, and the ball was the real cost of the book. The thing you give up has a name: the opportunity cost.

[warm and friendly] She still had three dollars, and she still wanted that ball. So on Saturday she set up a lemonade stand at the end of the driveway. Anyone in the country is free to start a business like that. It is called free enterprise.

[warm and friendly] She sold twelve cups at fifty cents each, six dollars in all, and paid her mom back one dollar for the sugar and cups. Now she had eight. She bought the ball for seven and dropped the last dollar into her savings jar.

[warm and friendly] Every time you spend money, time or attention, you are not spending it on something else. The trick is not to avoid that. It is to know what you are giving up, and to choose on purpose.
[warm] Mike and the crosswalk.

[warm and friendly] Mike was eight and walked to school past a corner where cars did not stop. There were no stripes and no light, just a sign nobody seemed to see. His big brother had been clipped there by a car's side mirror, and his arm was bruised for a week.

[warm and friendly] Mike did what nobody in his house had ever done. He went to a city council meeting in a shirt his mom ironed, stood at the microphone and held up a map he had drawn of the corner. His voice shook on the first sentence and steadied by the third. The corner needs a crosswalk, he said. The mayor listened from the long table.

[warm and friendly] The street belonged to the city, so the city could paint the stripes. The council talked it over for an hour and took a vote. Five hands went up for the crosswalk and two against. Five is more than half of seven, so the crosswalk won. That is majority rule, and the two who voted no still had to help make it happen.

[warm and friendly] The light was harder. The corner sat on a state highway, and a traffic light there needed the state's permission. That meant Texas, with its governor and its legislature in Austin. The city wrote to the state highway office, and then everyone waited.

[warm and friendly] When the answer came, Mike noticed the stamp on the envelope. The mail is run by the national government, the United States, led by a president and Congress in Washington, D.C. Three levels of government, three sets of jobs, and it took all three to fix one corner.

[warm and friendly] While he waited, Mike did chores and saved eleven dollars. At the store he wanted a book for eight dollars and a ball for seven. Eleven was not fifteen. He chose the book, and the ball was its real cost, the thing he gave up. That is called the opportunity cost.

[warm and friendly] He was learning early that there is never enough for everything. His teacher called that scarcity. Even eleven dollars had to choose. He was also learning that things get fixed by the people who show up, and that one did not have a fancy name.

[warm and friendly] The crosswalk went in the next spring, stripes first and the light a few months after. Mike watched the painters from the sidewalk. His brother crossed it first. Mike crossed it second, holding the new book. Nobody had to run.
[warm] A cup, seven ways.

[warm and friendly] Ines drew a cup, and her art teacher said, again. Ines drew it again. Again, said the teacher, but this time only lines. Then only a flat shape. By the fourth cup, Ines was sure she was being punished.

[warm and friendly] She was not. Each cup was built from just one of the seven elements of art, the pieces every picture is made of. The teacher lined them up across the table so Ines could see them side by side.

[warm and friendly] Line was just the edges, a mark traveling around the cup. Shape was the outline filled in flat, like a paper cutout. Form was shaded on one side, so the cup looked round enough to pick up.

[warm and friendly] Color turned it red. Texture made it rough, dragged on with a dry brush. Space put the cup small and far away, with a whole empty table around it. Value used no color at all, only light, dark and every gray between.

[warm and friendly] Then the teacher took the line cup and drew it twice more. Once with a thick, heavy line, and the cup looked loud and sure of itself. Once with a thin, wobbly line, and the same cup looked nervous. Ines laughed. One element had changed the mood.
[warm and friendly] Seven cups, and none looked like the others. Ines had thought art was talent. It turned out to be ingredients.
[warm and friendly] The elements of art are line, shape, form, color, texture, space and value. Look for them in any picture, from a scribble to a masterpiece, and you will see how it was built.
[warm] Three jars.

[warm and friendly] Ravi had three jars of paint, red, yellow and blue, and a picture in his head that needed orange, green and purple. He asked for more jars. His art teacher said the three jars already held everything.

[warm and friendly] He did not believe her until he mixed. Red and yellow made orange. Yellow and blue made green. Blue and red made purple. Three primary colors had made three secondary colors, and he had not opened a new jar.
[warm and friendly] Then he mixed blue with a little green and got blue-green, a color between the two. That kind is called tertiary: a primary mixed with the secondary beside it.

[warm and friendly] The teacher had him set the colors in a circle. One half glowed: red, orange and yellow, the warm colors, like fire and sun. The other half sat back: green, blue and purple, the cool colors, like water and shade.

[warm and friendly] Ravi painted a sunset with the warm half and a calm sea with the cool half. Then he put a small orange boat on the blue water, and it jumped off the page. Orange and blue sit across the wheel from each other. Complementary colors make each other look brighter.
[warm and friendly] For the sky he added white to red and got pink, a tint. For the night coming in at the edges he added black to blue, a shade.
[warm and friendly] Red, yellow and blue are the primaries, and every other color on the wheel can be mixed from them. Three jars hold the whole wheel.
[warm] Four looks.
[warm and friendly] Zoe looked at the painting for three seconds and said she did not like it. Her teacher said that was step four, and asked her to go back to step one.

[warm and friendly] Step one: describe. Say only what is there. A woman at a window. A letter in her hands. Gray light. A red chair. Zoe was not allowed to say whether any of it was good. Just what was there.
[warm and friendly] Step two: analyze. How is it made? The light comes in from the left and lands brightest on the letter. The chair is the only warm color in a room full of gray and blue.
[warm and friendly] Where did your eye go first, the teacher asked. To the letter. That is the focus, she said, and the painter put it there on purpose, with the brightest light in the whole picture.

[warm and friendly] Step three: interpret. What does it mean, and why do you think so? The letter matters to her. The red chair says the room is not as cold as it looks. Zoe had to point at the painting to prove each idea.

[warm and friendly] Step four: judge. Now the judging had something under it. Zoe still did not love the painting. But she could say what it was doing and how, and that the red chair was a small, smart choice.
[warm and friendly] Describe, analyze, interpret, then judge. Most people start at judging, the least interesting step, and stop there. Three looks before the verdict, and the verdict gets better.
[warm] Chloe looks at a picture.

[warm and friendly] Chloe was eight and already wore the brightest thing in any room, that day a yellow raincoat on a dry afternoon. Her grandmother had brought her to the museum for her birthday. In front of a big painting of a boat in a storm, Chloe said, before anyone asked, that she liked it.

[warm and friendly] Her grandmother, who was not Georgette but might as well have been, smiled and said that liking it was the last thing to say, not the first. Then she made Chloe look four times, one look at a time.

[warm and friendly] First look: what is in it? Chloe was only allowed to name what was there, like a detective taking notes. A small boat. Two people. A tall mast. Dark waves, a gray-green sea, a black sky and one bright red sail. No opinions yet. Just the list.

[warm and friendly] Second look: how is it built? The mast made a diagonal line, and diagonal lines feel like motion, which is why the boat seemed to tip. The waves were thick paint you could almost feel, which is texture. The red sail was the brightest color in the painting, the only warm one against all that cool gray-green. That was why her eye had gone there first. The painter had made it the focus on purpose.

[warm and friendly] Third look: what might it mean? Chloe thought about the two tiny people and the one bright sail. Hope in a storm, she said. Her grandmother asked why, and Chloe pointed. Because the only warm color in the painting is the thing that keeps them going. Her grandmother nodded slowly.
[warm and friendly] Fourth look: do I like it? Yes, still. But now she could say why, and the why was better than the yes. Her grandmother said most grown-ups never get past the yes.

[warm and friendly] At home Chloe tried to paint the storm from memory with three jars of paint. Blue and yellow made the green sea. Red, straight across the color wheel from green, made the sail burn, because complementary colors make each other look brighter. For the sky she added black to blue, a shade. Her painting was smaller and messier than the museum's, but it was hers.

[warm and friendly] Line, shape, form, color, texture, space and value: every picture is built from those seven. Chloe has looked four times ever since, and she still wears the brightest thing in the room, now that she knows how a bright spot pulls the eye.
[warm] The monster that was a coat.

[warm and friendly] The monster stood in the corner of Omar's room at eleven at night, tall and still with one arm raised, and Omar did not move for a full minute. Then his mother opened the door, and the light showed a coat on a hook.

[warm and friendly] It had been a coat all along. His eyes had reported a tall dark shape, and his brain, which does not like gaps, had filled the shape in with the scariest thing it knew. His teacher, Miss Adeyemi, said the next day that was the brain doing its job. The senses are reporters, she said. The brain decides what the reports mean, and in the dark it guesses.

[warm and friendly] She proved it with a drawing. Two lines the same length, one with arrowheads pointing in and one pointing out, and every child in the room was sure the second was longer. She measured them with a ruler. Same. The class laughed, because a brain fooled by two lines could certainly be fooled by a coat.

[warm and friendly] The second lesson was about Omar's own brain, which was eight years old and, Miss Adeyemi said, not finished. It would keep growing and changing until he was about twenty-five. Every time he practiced his piano scales, it built a stronger path for them, the way feet make a path across a field.

[warm and friendly] The third lesson came from Omar himself. He had been awake until eleven because of the monster and had slept six hours. By lunch he had lost his water bottle, snapped at his friend and forgotten his reading folder. A tired brain forgets, snaps and makes mistakes, Miss Adeyemi said. It is not a bad brain. It is a brain that needs about ten hours, and got six.

[warm and friendly] That night Omar hung the coat in the closet and shut the door. Then he hung it back on the hook, to see whether his brain would fall for it twice. It did not. He was asleep by nine, and in the morning the coat was only a coat.
[warm] Nine words, five days.
[warm and friendly] Priya studied her nine spelling words for an hour on Thursday night and got four right on Friday, and she decided, on the walk home, that she had a bad memory.

[warm and friendly] Her grandfather did not agree. He had been a mail carrier for thirty years and knew four hundred addresses by heart, and he said nobody is born with that. He asked how she had studied. On the couch, she said, with the tablet playing. That was the first problem, he said. Attention is the door to memory, and the door was closed.

[warm and friendly] The second problem was the hour. He drew a line on paper that fell like a slide: what you learn on Monday is mostly gone by Wednesday unless you meet it again. One long night puts the words in and lets them slide out. Small and often, he said. Three words a day, and each day say yesterday's again.

[warm and friendly] The third problem was the reading. She had read the list over and over, and reading feels like remembering when it is not. Close the book and say them, he said. If you can say a word, you have it. If you cannot, you know exactly which one to look at.

[warm and friendly] The next week she tried it, three words on Monday at the kitchen table with the tablet off. Three more on Tuesday, plus Monday's said out loud, and three more on Wednesday, plus the six. On Thursday she said all nine to the dog. On Friday she got nine right, and it had taken twelve minutes a day instead of an hour of nothing.

[warm and friendly] Her grandfather gave her one more trick for the phone number she could never keep. Ten digits, he said, are too many for a brain, which holds about seven things at once. Three chunks. She said it in three chunks, and has it still.
[warm] The smoke detector.
[warm and friendly] Ben lost the last game of the tournament by one point and threw his water bottle across the field, and for a few seconds he could not have told you why.

[warm and friendly] His coach, who had seen a hundred water bottles thrown, sat him down on the bench and asked what the feeling was called. Ben said he did not know, and the coach waited. Angry, Ben said at last, and when she asked what was under that, he thought for a moment and said sad, because he had wanted it.

[warm and friendly] Naming it did something. The coach said it always does: a feeling is a signal, and saying the name out loud uses the thinking part of the brain, which turns the volume down. Then she had him breathe in for four and out for four, five times, and his hands stopped shaking.

[warm and friendly] On the ride home Ben noticed the thought that had come with the anger. Everyone will think I am bad, it said. His father asked him to try a different thought on the same moment: that was one bad game. Same moment, he said, but the second thought felt different, and the second thought made him want to practice instead of quit.

[warm and friendly] Two weeks later, before his piano recital, the shaky hands came back, and Ben was ready for them. The coach had said some stress is useful: a little before a test gives focus and energy. He named it, nervous, breathed his fours, and played his piece with more care than he ever had in the living room.

[warm and friendly] The feeling that had thrown a water bottle was still there, his father told him, and it always would be. The job was not to make it go away. The job was to read it, like a smoke detector, and decide whether it was a fire or just toast.
[warm] The loud game.

[warm and friendly] The loud game was the best part of recess for Zara. In October she found out it was the worst part of recess for Hana, who had been playing it every day for a month without saying so.

[warm and friendly] Zara only found out because her teacher had given the class a question to try: how was that for you? She asked Hana on the walk back inside, expecting nothing, and Hana said the shouting made her stomach hurt. Same game, two minds, Zara thought, and neither of them was wrong. She had simply never asked.

[warm and friendly] There was a third girl, Mia, who kept score. Not in the game; in the friendship. Mia counted who sat with whom and who had been invited where. When Zara played with Hana at lunch, Mia said she was not a real friend anymore. That, said the teacher when Zara asked, is the sign: a healthy friendship feels safe, and one that keeps score does not.

[warm and friendly] The fight with Mia came on Thursday. Zara wanted to say you are mean and nobody likes you, and did not, because the class had practiced the sentence that works. I felt left out when you said I was not a real friend, she said, and I want us to both play. Mia said nothing for a while. Then she said okay.

[warm and friendly] It did not fix everything. Zara told her mother, who was the trusted adult in the house. Her mother said that some fights take two sentences and some take a month, and that Mia might be keeping score because she was afraid of losing. Zara had not thought of Mia being afraid of anything.

[warm and friendly] By November the three of them played a quieter game on Tuesdays and the loud one on Fridays, and Hana came to both. Zara still asked how was that for you, and the answers still surprised her, which she had decided was the point.
[warm] Chloe and the worry jar.

[warm and friendly] Chloe was fourteen the summer she looked after her cousin Nico for a week, and she had been told he was easy. He was eight, he was funny, and on the first night he cried for an hour about a spelling test that was five days away.

[warm and friendly] She did not know what to do, so she did what her mother did and asked what the feeling was called. Scared, he said, after a while. Then, remembering a poster from health class, she had him breathe in for four and out for four until his shoulders came down. Naming it and breathing did not fix the test. It fixed the hour.

[warm and friendly] The next morning she found the spelling list, twenty words, and Nico's plan to read it a hundred times on Thursday. Chloe knew that slide from her own tests. Four words a day, she said, at the kitchen table with the tablet off, and every day say yesterday's out loud first. Reading feels like remembering and is not.

[warm and friendly] She found a jar in the pantry and called it the worry jar. Any worry that came at bedtime went on a slip of paper and into the jar, to be read in the morning, when worries are smaller. The first night there were four slips. By Thursday there were two, and one of them was about a friend.

[warm and friendly] The friend was Leo, who had said Nico ruined a game of tag. Nico wanted to say Leo was a liar. Chloe gave him the sentence her class had practiced: what you felt, when, and what you want. I felt bad when you said I ruined it, and I want to play again. Nico practiced it on the dog, and then on Leo, who said okay.

[warm and friendly] By Wednesday she had noticed the pattern under everything. Nico was sleeping seven hours, because his parents were away and the house was strange. A tired brain forgets, snaps and cries. She moved bedtime to eight and read to him until he was gone, and Thursday was a different boy.

[warm and friendly] Thursday night the jar held one slip. It said, what if I get one wrong. Chloe wrote under it, then you got nineteen right, and put it back, and in the morning Nico read both lines and laughed.

[warm and friendly] He got twenty on Friday, and when his mother called that night Chloe told her all of it: the fours, the four words a day, the jar, the sentence, the bedtime. His mother was quiet and then said that was more than she had known to do, and asked where Chloe had learned it. School, Chloe said, and then, honestly, from you.
[warm] Can a robot be your friend.
[warm and friendly] The robot vacuum arrived in Room 8 on a Monday, and by Tuesday the class had named it Bolt and Rosa had asked the question that took the rest of the week. Can Bolt be our friend?

[warm and friendly] Miss Okafor did not answer, and instead she wrote two questions on the board, one above the other. How many legs does a spider have? Can a robot be your friend? The first one, she said, you can look up, and she let Diego look it up: eight. The second one nobody can look up, because it is a wonder question, and a wonder question you have to think through.

[warm and friendly] So what is a friend, she asked, and the class tried. Someone who is kind to you, said Rosa. Miss Okafor asked whether the crossing guard was kind to them, and everyone said yes. Then she asked whether the crossing guard was their friend, and the room went quiet. Kind, it turned out, was not enough. A not-example had shown them what the meaning still needed.

[warm and friendly] They tried again. A friend is someone who chooses you, said Diego. A friend is someone who knows when you are sad, said Rosa. Bolt, they agreed, was kind in its way, since it cleaned up the glitter, but it did not choose anyone, and it bumped into sad people exactly as often as happy ones.

[warm and friendly] On Friday Miss Okafor told them about a man named Socrates, who had lived long ago in a city called Athens. He spent his days asking people what their words meant. Most of them had never checked. His student Plato wrote the questions down, and people still read them two thousand years later. You checked, she said. That is the whole job.
[warm and friendly] The class voted that Bolt was a helper and not a friend, by nineteen to four. The four who voted friend had a because ready, which Miss Okafor said was the part that mattered.
[warm] Recess before lunch.
[warm and friendly] Sam wanted recess before lunch instead of after, and at the class meeting he said so, and Miss Okafor asked the question she always asked. Why?

[warm and friendly] Because everybody wants it, said Sam, and Miss Okafor said that was a headcount and not a reason. Because I said so, said Sam, grinning, and she said that was an order. Because I want to, he tried, and she said that was a wish, and Sam ran out of becauses and sat down.

[warm and friendly] The next day he came back with a real one. Because kids who run around first eat more of their lunch. Miss Okafor asked how he knew, and Sam had asked the cafeteria manager, who had counted the trays that came back full. On the days after gym, fewer trays came back full. That was a reason: it was about the thing, it was true, and somebody had checked.

[warm and friendly] Ana disagreed, and she had a because too. Because kids come in sweaty and cannot settle down to eat. Miss Okafor wrote both on the board and asked whether either one was about the wrong thing. Neither was. They were two real reasons pointing two ways, which happens more often than anyone likes.

[warm and friendly] So the class checked. For one week they had recess first, and the cafeteria manager counted trays and Miss Okafor counted minutes to settle. The trays came back emptier, and settling took four minutes instead of two. The class decided the emptier trays were worth four minutes.
[warm and friendly] Recess moved before lunch in October. Sam kept the tray count on the wall, next to the words Miss Okafor had written when he first stood up: how do you know?
[warm] The rabbit and the fish.

[warm and friendly] The class pet vote was supposed to take five minutes and had already taken twenty when Miss Okafor stopped it with a rule. Nobody could speak until they had said the other person's idea back, and the other person had said that is it.

[warm and friendly] Lena tried first. So you think we should get a fish, she said to Kofi, because fish are boring. No, said Kofi, that is not it. Lena tried again. So you think we should get a fish because nobody is allergic to a fish. Yes, said Kofi, that is it, and it was the first time all morning that anyone had heard him.

[warm and friendly] Then it was Kofi's turn. So you think we should get a rabbit because rabbits are soft and you can hold them. That is it, said Lena. Now they had two ideas with two becauses, and neither one was about the wrong thing, and the class had to pick.

[warm and friendly] Marcus, who had said nothing, asked the question that settled it. Is anyone allergic to rabbits? Two hands went up, slowly. Lena looked at the hands for a while and said that she had changed her mind, because a class pet that two people could not touch was not a class pet.

[warm and friendly] Somebody said Lena had lost. Miss Okafor said that changing your mind for a better because was one of the bravest things a thinker could do. The loudest idea was never the best one, she said; the one with the best because was. Lena and Kofi were best friends again by lunch, which had never really been in doubt.
[warm and friendly] The fish arrived on Friday. Lena named it, which everyone agreed was fair, and Kofi fed it, and the rule about saying it back stayed on the board for the rest of the year.
[warm] Three boxes and a fence.
[warm and friendly] The parade came down Main Street every October, and every October the fence by the bakery was the best place to watch it, if you could see over it.

[warm and friendly] Priya could see over it. Ben could see over it on tiptoe. Tomas, who was smallest, could see the fence. The bakery had three boxes, and Priya's first plan was one box each, which was equal, and Tomas stood on his box and saw a little more fence.

[warm and friendly] Ben said the plan was fair because everyone got the same. Priya looked at Tomas, who was not complaining, and said that fair had to mean everyone could see the parade, or what was the point. She gave Tomas her box. Now Tomas had two, Ben had one, and Priya had none, and all three of them could see the drums come around the corner.

[warm and friendly] That was the day Priya learned that fair is not always equal. Equal gives everyone the same thing. Fair gives everyone what they need for the same chance, and sometimes those are different. The way to tell is to look at the smallest person and ask whether it is working for them.

[warm and friendly] The rest of the day kept teaching. At the fire drill after school, the rule was no running in the hall, and the teacher ran, and everyone understood the exception because everyone could hear the reason. And when there was one brownie left and two people who wanted it, Ben cut and Tomas chose, and Ben cut it so evenly that you could not tell the halves apart.

[warm and friendly] Fair by need at the fence, a rule with a reason at the drill, and cut-and-choose at the bakery. Priya went home with no box and the best view on Main Street, which was the strangest fair of all.
[warm] Georgette and the wondering jar.

[warm and friendly] Georgette had taught for forty years, and when she retired she took one thing from her classroom: a glass jar with a slot in the lid. On Thursdays at the library she set it on a table, and any child in the wonder club could drop a question in.

[warm and friendly] The first rule of the club was that she would not answer. Every question was read aloud, and the club decided which kind it was. How far is the moon? A look-up question, and Dev looked it up. Is it wrong to lie to be kind? A wonder question, and nobody could look that up.

[warm and friendly] The second rule was what do you mean. When Lila said a lie was any untrue thing you said, Georgette asked whether an actor on a stage was lying. Lila thought and said no, because the audience knew. Then a lie needs more than untrue, said Georgette, and Lila added it on purpose, to fool someone, and the meaning got better.

[warm and friendly] The third rule was because. Nobody could say what they thought without a because, and Georgette sorted the becauses out loud as they came: a headcount, an order, a wish, a real one. The real ones were about the thing, and true, and somebody could check them. Dev learned to ask how do you know so kindly that nobody minded.

[warm and friendly] The week the club nearly broke up, two boys wanted the jar's last question to be theirs, and the argument went on until Georgette made each one say the other's idea back. It took three tries, and when they got there, they found that one boy wanted the question read and the other wanted to read it, two different things, and both possible.

[warm and friendly] Fairness came up every Thursday, because a jar of questions is a jar of turns. Equal turns were fair until a new child came who had never had one, and the club decided, without Georgette, that a first turn counted for more. The child who had wanted equal turns most was the one who suggested it.
[warm and friendly] The last cookie on the plate was settled the old way, one child cutting and another choosing, and the halves were so even that Georgette kept one on the table as a reminder.

[warm and friendly] In June a parent asked what the club was for, since it never reached an answer. Georgette lifted the jar, which was full again, and said that it taught four things: which questions to look up, what a word means, what a because is, and how to disagree with a friend. The answers, she said, they would find on their own.
[warm] The blade sharpener.

[warm and friendly] Priya and her cousin Jonah both mowed lawns on Elm Street that summer, and both charged the same: six dollars an hour. By July, Jonah had noticed something that did not seem fair. Priya was earning almost twice as much as he was.

[warm and friendly] The difference was not the mowing. It was what Priya had learned from her grandfather the winter before, on the workbench in his garage. She could take a mower blade off, sharpen it on the grinder, and balance it so the mower did not shake. Nobody else on Elm Street could do that.

[warm and friendly] So the neighbors paid her for two things. Six dollars an hour to mow, and eight dollars for every blade she sharpened, which took her fifteen minutes. Jonah worked out the arithmetic on the back of a flyer and stared at it. A skill, his grandfather told him, is money that shows up every hour you use it.

[warm and friendly] In August a windstorm came through and knocked down half the branches on the street. Everyone needed a chainsaw blade at once, and the hardware store had twelve. The price on the shelf went up by four dollars overnight. The blades had not changed. How many there were, and how many people wanted them, had.

[warm and friendly] Priya understood it before Jonah did. When something is scarce and wanted, it costs more; when the truck refills the shelf, the price comes back down. She did not raise her own prices for the neighbors, but she understood why the store had.

[warm and friendly] That winter Jonah spent his Saturdays in the garage, learning the grinder. Skills are human capital, his grandfather said, and human capital is the only thing you carry to every job you will ever have. By the next summer, Elm Street had two blade sharpeners, and both of them earned for two things.
[warm] The bike that cost forty-four dollars.

[warm and friendly] Marcus had planned the bike for a month. He knew the model, the color, and the price: sixty dollars, marked down from eighty for one week in June. He had forty dollars in his jar, and the week would end on Saturday.

[warm and friendly] His sister Dani, who was in high school and had a job, offered him a loan. Twenty dollars, she said, and you pay me back twenty-four by the end of summer. The four dollars was interest, the price of borrowing. Marcus thought about it overnight, wrote down how he would earn the twenty-four, and said yes.

[warm and friendly] His friend Theo went to the same store that Saturday with thirty dollars and no plan. He came out with a remote-control car that had been by the register, a bag of candy, and three dollars. The car broke on Tuesday. The bike Theo had been talking about since April was still sixty dollars, and he had three.

[warm and friendly] Marcus rode home. Every Saturday in July he mowed Miss Okafor's yard for six dollars, and every Saturday he handed Dani a share. By the middle of August he had paid back all twenty-four, and the bike was his with nothing owed on it.

[warm and friendly] Theo asked how it had worked. Marcus explained the two halves of it. The plan had told him what he wanted and what it cost before he walked in, so the register had no power over him. And the loan had been for something planned that he could pay back, with the interest counted before he said yes.

[warm and friendly] Credit is a tool, Dani told them both. Used for a plan, it gets you the bike. Used in the aisle, it turns a want into a debt, and the debt outlives the want. Theo wrote a list before his next trip to the store.
[warm] The cookie table.

[warm and friendly] Ana signed up for a table at the spring fair to sell cookies, and the first thing she learned was that the table itself cost money. Five dollars for the day, whether she sold one cookie or a hundred. Her mother called it a fixed expense: it did not move.

[warm and friendly] The flour, sugar, butter and chocolate chips were different. Every dozen cookies she baked used up more of them, so the more she planned to sell, the more they cost. Those were variable expenses, and they grew with the batch. Four dozen cookies cost her twelve dollars in ingredients.
