[warm and friendly] She priced the cookies at one dollar each and set out forty-eight of them under a sign. By two o'clock she had sold thirty-one. Her cousin ate two, which counted as expenses of a sort. At the end of the day she sold the last fifteen for fifty cents each to a man with three children.

[warm and friendly] At the kitchen table that night she did the arithmetic on a napkin. Money in: thirty-one dollars plus seven dollars and fifty cents, thirty-eight fifty. Expenses: five for the table, twelve for ingredients, seventeen. Profit: twenty-one dollars and fifty cents. Her mother made her do it twice, and it came out the same.

[warm and friendly] Ana divided the profit the way she divided her allowance, before it could disappear: ten to spend, eight to save, and three fifty for the animal shelter jar. The deciding took a minute and the money stayed where she had put it.

[warm and friendly] Next year, she said, she would bake five dozen and skip the cousin. Fixed expenses stay the same, variable ones grow with what you sell, and profit is what is left when both are paid. A napkin and a pencil are enough to run a table.
[warm] The paycheck with a hole in it.

[warm and friendly] Leo's first paycheck from the swimming pool snack bar was supposed to be one hundred dollars: ten hours at ten dollars an hour. The check said eighty-eight. He read it three times and then took it to his father, sure that someone had made a mistake.

[warm and friendly] Nobody had. One hundred dollars was his gross income, what he had earned. Eighty-eight was his net income, what he took home. The twelve dollars in between were taxes: some for income tax, some for payroll tax, listed in small print down the side of the stub.

[warm and friendly] Leo wanted to know where the twelve dollars had gone. His father drove him past the answer on the way home. The road they were driving on, the school, the park with the pool, and the fire station on the corner: taxes pay for the things everyone shares.

[warm and friendly] At the kitchen table they made a budget for the summer. Income on the left: eighty-eight dollars every two weeks. Expenses on the right: a bus pass, lunches, and the phone plan Leo had promised to pay for himself. The right side came to ninety-four.

[warm and friendly] A budget balances when the expenses fit inside the income, his father said, and this one did not. Six dollars over. Leo had three ways to close it: spend less, earn more, or move something to next month. He packed his lunches, and the six dollars vanished.

[warm and friendly] The rest went into a savings account instead of the jar in his closet, because the bank kept it safe and paid a little interest for leaving it there. By the end of the summer the account held more than he had put in, and Leo knew exactly where every dollar had gone.
[warm] Savanah and the egg money.

[warm and friendly] The first thing Savanah ever sold was an egg, and by fifteen she was selling twelve dozen a week at the Saturday market in town. The hens were hers, the feed was hers to buy, and the money in the coffee can was hers to keep, which taught her everything the can could teach.

[warm and friendly] The can had two kinds of expenses in it. The stall fee was eight dollars every Saturday, sold out or not: fixed. The feed went up with every hen she added, and the cartons went up with every dozen: variable. She wrote both kinds on the lid in pencil, so they would stop surprising her.

[warm and friendly] At three dollars a dozen, twelve dozen brought in thirty-six dollars. Eight for the stall, fourteen for feed and cartons, and the profit was fourteen. Her mother, who had kept the farm's books for twenty years, showed her the arithmetic once and never again. After that, the can and the pencil were Savanah's job.

[warm and friendly] In March a fox got into the coop and took four hens. That week she had seven dozen, not twelve, and half the county was short of eggs, because the fox had not been particular about whose coop. The grocer in town raised his price to four dollars. Scarce and wanted, her mother said, costs more.

[warm and friendly] Savanah kept her price at three. Her customers had come every Saturday for two years, and she wanted them there in two more. It was a choice, and it cost her seven dollars that week, the difference between three and four on seven dozen. She wrote the number on the lid and did not regret it.

[warm and friendly] Replacing the hens took money the can did not have. Her mother lent her forty dollars, and Savanah wrote out the terms herself before she took it: forty back by August, plus four dollars of interest, from the profit and nothing else. Credit, she understood, was borrowing against work she had not done yet.

[warm and friendly] By June the coop was full again, the loan was half paid, and the can had grown a second compartment, a jar with a lid, where a third of every Saturday's profit went and stayed. On the jar she had written one word: college. Her mother had told her what it cost, and Savanah had done that arithmetic too.

[warm and friendly] She paid her mother the forty-four dollars on the first Saturday of August, in the truck on the way to market, and her mother folded it into her pocket without counting it. That, Savanah thought, was what the whole summer had been for. Not the eggs. The trust in the folding.
[warm] The question about lunch.
[warm and friendly] Ruby brought her grandfather's compass to show and tell and talked for two minutes about the trip where he used it. The first question from the class was whether it was pizza day.

[warm and friendly] It was not pizza day, and it was not a question about the compass. Miss Tan wrote two words on the board, on topic, and gave the class a rule she called the beach rule. If someone tells you about the beach, where did you swim is a question about the topic. What is for lunch is a question about you. Both are allowed, she said, but only one is listening.

[warm and friendly] She showed them what listening looked like from the outside: eyes on the speaker, hands still, body turned toward the person. Then she told them the part nobody could see. Your mind on the words, she said, not on what you want to say next. And when it wanders, and it will, bring it back to the last thing you heard.

[warm and friendly] Ruby got a second turn, and this time the questions were about the compass. Did the needle always point north? What was the trip for? One comment came from Theo, who said his uncle had a compass on his watch, and Miss Tan said that was a comment that added to the talk. I like pizza, she said, would not have been.

[warm and friendly] That night Ruby practiced the other half of listening on her brother, who was reading a report about bees out loud for school. When he finished, she said the main idea back in her own words: bees make honey from flowers. Yes, he said, surprised. The flowers, the hive and the wax were the details. She had heard the whole thing.

[warm and friendly] The next show and tell was Theo's, a rock from a volcano, and Ruby asked the first question. Was it hot when they found it? It was not, but it was about the rock, and Theo talked for three more minutes because somebody had asked.
[warm] Four steps to the library.
[warm and friendly] Owen told the new girl how to get to the library in one breath: go down and then left and past the thing with the fish and it is right there. She ended up in the nurse's office.

[warm and friendly] Miss Alvarez had the class practice instructions the next morning with paper airplanes, and she read four steps fast, all at once, and let them fold. Half the planes had no wings. So she read the steps her way, with the number first: four steps. First, fold the paper in half, and next, fold the top corners to the middle. Then, fold the sides down for wings, and last, throw it. Now say them back to me.

[warm and friendly] The class said them back, and two children had the wings before the corners, and Miss Alvarez fixed it right then, before a single fold. That, she said, is why you say the steps back. A wrong step caught before you start costs one second. A wrong step caught at the end costs the whole airplane.

[warm and friendly] Owen tried the library again with the same new girl. Four steps, he said. First, walk to the end of this hall. Next, turn left. Then, go past the fish tank. Last, it is the door with the blue sign. Say them back. She said them back and turned right at the second step, and he fixed it, and she found the library.

[warm and friendly] Telling what happened worked the same way. When Owen told his mother about the field trip, he started with the part where the goat ate his map, and she could not follow it. He tried again in order. First we rode the bus, next we saw the cows, then the goat ate my map, and last we ate lunch on the hill. Now, she said, I can see it.

[warm and friendly] By spring Owen counted steps on his fingers without thinking about it, and the new girl, who was not new anymore, could get anywhere in the building. She said the steps back every time, which drove Owen a little crazy, and which was exactly the point.
[warm] Clover.
[warm and friendly] Maya's one-minute talk was going to be about everything: her rabbit, her cousin, the beach and a book. Her teacher, Miss Okoro, stopped her at the plan and asked her to pick one.

[warm and friendly] One topic, Miss Okoro said, three facts about it, and a sentence about why. Maya picked the rabbit, whose name was Clover, and found her three facts at the kitchen table. Clover eats hay every morning, she sleeps in a box in the kitchen, and she thumps her foot when the cat comes in. And why? Because she is quiet and brave. About a hundred words, which is a minute.

[warm and friendly] The first practice came out as rabbit, hay, box, thump, and Miss Okoro asked for complete sentences, with a who and a what. My rabbit eats hay every morning, has a who and a what. Rabbit, hay, is a list. Maya tried again, and the sentences made the rabbit sound like a rabbit instead of a shopping list.

[warm and friendly] Then came the four things that carry a sentence across a room. Eye contact, one person at a time, a whole sentence each. Rate, slower than felt normal. Volume, aimed at the boy in the back corner who never looked up. Enunciation, the ends of the words on, so thumping was thumping and not thumpin.

[warm and friendly] She brought one picture, a photo of Clover in her box, and held it up for the box sentence and put it down after. She practiced out loud three times, standing in her kitchen, with Clover watching from the box. The third time was the first time it felt like talking instead of reciting.

[warm and friendly] On the day the boy in the back corner looked up at the thumping part, because she had aimed it at him. Afterward he asked whether the cat was scared of the rabbit. It was. That was the best question Maya had ever been asked, and she answered it in a complete sentence.
[warm] The talking stick.
[warm and friendly] The class had five minutes to plan the garden and five people talking at once, and at the end of the five minutes nobody could say what anyone else had said.

[warm and friendly] Their teacher, Miss Bell, brought out a stick from the reading corner and gave it one rule: whoever holds it talks, everyone else listens, and it goes around the circle. The first time around was slow and strange. The second time around, the class had six ideas on the board, and Priya, who had not said a word all year, had given two of them.

[warm and friendly] The rules, Miss Bell said, are not there to slow you down. They are there so the quiet person gets heard and the loud person gets listened to. Everyone got a turn before anyone got two, and the boy who usually talked the most found out he had things to say when he waited.

[warm and friendly] Building on ideas was the next lesson. Instead of starting over each time, they used two sentences. I agree with Priya, and I want to add that the beans could go by the fence. Or, I think something different, because the fence is in the shade. Both took the last speaker seriously. Both kept the plan moving instead of going in circles.

[warm and friendly] The principal came in during the third planning day, and the class found out that polite talk works in every room. Good morning, Principal Reyes, said the stick holder, using her name. When she asked how the garden was going, Priya said it was going well and that the beans were going by the sunny fence. A full sentence. The principal stayed ten minutes.

[warm and friendly] The garden went in on a Friday in April with beans by the sunny fence, and the stick went back to the reading corner. It came out again whenever five people started talking at once, which was less and less.
[warm] Savanah and the fire chief.

[warm and friendly] Savanah volunteered on Friday mornings in a third-grade class near the hospital where she worked, and in March the teacher asked her to get the class ready for a visitor: the fire chief.

[warm and friendly] The first Friday she found out what the questions would be. A boy asked whether the chief liked pizza. Savanah did not say it was a bad question. She drew a fire truck on the board and asked which questions were about the truck and which were about the person asking. The pizza question, the class decided, was about the boy.

[warm and friendly] So they made a rule, on topic, and practiced it. She told them about a patient whose heart she had scanned at work, and they asked questions. Was the patient scared? What did the picture look like? Every question was about the story, and she answered every one, and the class found out that on-topic questions get longer answers.

[warm and friendly] The second Friday was listening you could see: eyes on the speaker, hands still, body turned. And the part you could not see, your mind on the words. She read a short report about how a fire truck pumps water and asked for the main idea back in their own words. The truck pushes water through the hose, a girl said. Yes, said Savanah. The rest was details.

[warm and friendly] The third Friday was instructions, because the class would walk to the fire station. She gave the route in one breath first, badly, and half of them pointed the wrong way. Then she gave it properly: five steps, she said first, with first, next, then and last, and had a boy say them back. He had step three wrong, and they fixed it in the classroom instead of on the sidewalk.

[warm and friendly] The fourth Friday was one-minute talks about helpers. One topic, three facts, why. A girl talked about her aunt the nurse in complete sentences, looking at one face at a time, with the ends of her words on, and Savanah understood the aunt better in one minute than she had from a year of hearing about her.

[warm and friendly] The last Friday before the visit was turns. Twenty-two children and one fire chief meant a talking stick, hands up, one voice at a time, and everyone gets a turn before anyone gets two. They practiced good morning, Chief, with the name, and a full sentence for every answer.

[warm and friendly] The chief came on a Tuesday and stayed forty minutes, because every question was about the truck or the job and every child said thank you. On the way out she asked the teacher who had prepared them. The teacher pointed at Savanah, who was, at that moment, listening.
[warm] The path of a loaf of bread.

[warm and friendly] Lucia was halfway through a peanut butter sandwich when her teacher asked the class where their lunch had come from. The store, Lucia said, and Miss Ortega smiled and asked where the store had gotten it.

[warm and friendly] So Lucia traced the bread backward, one step at a time. The store had bought it from a bakery, and the bakery had baked it from flour. The flour had come from a mill, where wheat is ground into powder, and the wheat had grown in a field in the Texas Panhandle.

[warm and friendly] Miss Ortega asked who had done each step, and the list surprised the class. A farmer had planted the wheat in the fall and harvested it in early summer with a combine. A truck driver had hauled it to the mill. A miller had ground it, a baker had baked it, and a grocer had set the loaf on the shelf.

[warm and friendly] Then she asked what the farm itself had used. Soil to grow in, Lucia said, and rain, and sunlight, and someone added diesel for the tractor. Miss Ortega wrote every answer on the board under the words natural resources and said a good farmer spends them carefully, because they have to last.

[warm and friendly] The peanut butter had its own path, which a boy named Omar traced. Peanuts grow underground on low green plants, and Texas grows a great many of them. They are dug, dried, roasted and ground, and the paste goes into a jar.

[warm and friendly] That night Lucia drew her sandwich as a flow chart, boxes and arrows from two fields to one plate, with a stick figure at every step for each worker. Her mother taped it to the refrigerator, where it stayed until the paper curled.
[warm] The cup in the closet.

[warm and friendly] Ethan was sure seeds needed light, so he set out to prove it with two cups of lima beans. One went on the sunny windowsill, and the other went into the dark hall closet, where nobody would bother it.

[warm and friendly] Both cups got the same soil, the same water and the same warm house. After a week Ethan opened the closet expecting nothing, and found two pale shoots pushing up through the dirt. The beans had sprouted in the dark.

[warm and friendly] His grandmother, who had gardened for fifty years, explained it at dinner. A seed carries its first food packed inside it, so it needs only water, air and warmth to start. Light matters later, once the shoot is up and the leaves have work to do.

[warm and friendly] The closet beans proved her right over the next week. Their stems grew long, thin and yellow, stretching for light that was not there, while the windowsill beans stood short, sturdy and green. Ethan moved the pale ones to the window, and in a few days they began to turn green.

[warm and friendly] The soil was the other surprise. His grandmother's compost pile, a heap of old leaves and vegetable peels, had turned in a year into dark crumbly earth. That is decomposition, she said, and the sand mixed into it came from rock worn down by wind and water over a very long time.

[warm and friendly] In January Ethan pointed at her pecan tree and asked if it had died. It was resting, she said, dormant until spring. In April the buds opened, and Ethan planted his beans beside it, in the dark soil the pile had made.
[warm] Four questions every morning.

[warm and friendly] Ava spent a long October weekend on her aunt's farm outside Waco, and every morning started with the same four questions. Did everyone have food, water, shelter and enough room? Her aunt said those four were the whole job, and everything else was details.

[warm and friendly] Water came first, because a cow can drink twenty gallons or more on a hot day, and the trough had to be full before breakfast. After that came hay for the cattle, grain for the hens, and a check that the barn doors had held through the night's wind.

[warm and friendly] Ava watched the cows eat and noticed their teeth, wide and flat at the back, grinding grass the way a mill grinds wheat. Her aunt said a cow's stomach has four parts to handle all that grass. The chewing Ava saw while the cows rested was cud, food brought back up to chew again.

[warm and friendly] The ducks were built differently. They crossed the yard clumsily on webbed feet, then slid into the pond and paddled away with no effort at all, which is what the webs are for. The hens had no webs and stayed well away from the water.

[warm and friendly] On Saturday one of the hens hatched the chicks she had been sitting on for three weeks, and her aunt explained the whole circle. An egg kept warm for about 21 days hatches into a chick. The chick grows into a young hen, and at about five months old she lays eggs of her own.

[warm and friendly] On the last morning a cold front blew in, and the cattle stood with their backs to the wind. Overhead a loose line of orange butterflies was heading south. Monarchs, her aunt said, on their way to Mexico for the winter. Ava added a fifth question to the list: what is the weather doing?
[warm] The squash that would not come.
[warm and friendly] Noah's squash plants were covered in yellow flowers by June, and not one of them turned into a squash. The flowers opened in the morning, closed by afternoon, and dropped off.

[warm and friendly] His neighbor, who kept bees, walked over to look and asked how many bees Noah had seen. He had not seen any. A squash flower has to get pollen from another flower, she said, and bees are the ones who carry it.

[warm and friendly] Until her bees found his yard, she showed him how to do their job with a small paintbrush, dabbing pollen from one flower into another early in the morning. Three days later the first tiny squash began to swell behind a wilting bloom.

[warm and friendly] Noah kept a tally on the garage wall, a mark for every squash he picked: four the first week, six the second and nine the third. His teacher helped him turn the marks into a bar graph, and the bars climbed like stairs, which pleased him more than he expected.

[warm and friendly] Then July brought a dry spell, three weeks without rain. The squash wilted every afternoon while the cactus by the mailbox looked exactly the same. Noah cut the top off an old milk jug to make a watering can, filled it from the rain barrel, and watered at the roots each evening.

[warm and friendly] By August the neighbor's bees had found the yard, the paintbrush went back in the drawer, and the tally reached forty-one. Noah put the peels and old stems in the compost bin for next year's soil, which his neighbor said was the whole idea of a farm, tiny or not.
[warm] Mike and the twenty-one days.

[warm and friendly] Mike kept a dozen laying hens and a rooster behind his house. In March the third-grade teacher down the street asked if he could bring the class some eggs that would hatch. He arrived with an incubator the size of a picnic cooler and twelve eggs.

[warm and friendly] The incubator kept the eggs at about 99.5 degrees, the warmth of a sitting hen, and the class took over the hen's other job. A hen turns her eggs many times a day, so the students marked each shell with an X on one side and an O on the other. They turned the eggs three times a day, and Mike came by on weekends to do it himself.

[warm and friendly] On day seven Mike brought a bright flashlight and darkened the room. Held against the light, nine eggs showed a web of thin red veins and a dark spot. Three were clear inside; they had never started, which happens even under a hen, and nobody had done anything wrong.

[warm and friendly] While they waited, the class planted radish seeds in paper cups so there would be something to watch. The seeds sprouted in four days with water, air and warmth. The students kept a tally of sprouts on the board and measured the tallest one each morning with a metric ruler.

[warm and friendly] A boy asked where the eggs at the store came from, if not from a class like this one. Mike walked them through it: big farms keep thousands of hens, and the eggs are collected, washed, checked under a light like theirs, packed in cartons and trucked to stores. The hens eat corn and soybeans grown on other farms.

[warm and friendly] On day eighteen they stopped turning the eggs, so the chicks could settle into place to hatch. On day twenty the first tiny crack appeared, and on day twenty-one the room went silent as a wet chick pushed its way out. By Friday seven of the nine had hatched.

[warm and friendly] The chicks moved to a box with a heat lamp, water and chick feed, kept at about 95 degrees the first week and a little cooler each week after. The students noticed beaks made for pecking seeds, and fluffy down starting to give way to real feathers on the wings.

[warm and friendly] After two weeks the chicks went home to Mike's yard, and the class came to visit in May. Mike promised the teacher a carton of eggs from the new hens in the fall, since a young hen starts laying at about five months old. The circle, he said, would close by Halloween.
[warm] The price of strawberries.

[warm and friendly] Every Saturday in April, Ana and her grandmother bought strawberries at the farmers market, and every Saturday a box cost $4. Then one week the sign said $6, and Ana asked the farmer why.

[warm and friendly] He explained that a late freeze had killed many of the blossoms on his plants. He had only half as many strawberries to sell, but just as many families wanted them. When there is not enough of something for everyone who wants it, he said, the price goes up.

[warm and friendly] By June the berries on the other farms were ripe, the market was full of strawberries, and the price fell back to $4. Ana wrote it in her notebook: scarce means more, plenty means less.

[warm and friendly] On the way out, they passed a man fixing the market's big refrigerator. Her grandmother said he had trained for four years to learn how refrigerators work. Skills that take years to learn usually earn more money, she said, and people call those skills human capital.

[warm and friendly] Ana thought about her own skills. She could bake banana bread with her grandmother, and a neighbor had already asked to buy a loaf for $5. That would be income, her grandmother said, money earned for work.

[warm and friendly] That night they talked about what Ana would do with the five dollars. She could spend it, save it, or share some of it with the food bank. Ana decided to choose before the money came, not after, and she drew three jars in her notebook to remind herself.
[warm] Three jars.
[warm and friendly] Leo turned nine and started getting an allowance of $10 a week. His mother gave him three jars and a rule: before the money was spent, every dollar needed a job.

[warm and friendly] Leo wanted a skateboard that cost $36. He decided that each week $5 would go in the spend jar, $4 in the save jar, and $1 in the share jar. His mother showed him how to find the time it would take: 36 divided by 4 is 9, so nine weeks.

[warm and friendly] He circled the weeks on the kitchen calendar and watched the save jar fill, one four-dollar stack at a time. By the fifth week it held $20, and he could already picture the skateboard rolling down the driveway.

[warm and friendly] In the sixth week, at the store with his dad, Leo saw a slushie and a small toy by the checkout. He bought both with his save money. It was unplanned spending, and it felt good for about an hour. His dad did not say a word, which Leo later decided was on purpose.

[warm and friendly] That night he counted again. The save jar was $4 short, so the skateboard would take ten weeks instead of nine. Leo was not happy, but he understood the trade: the slushie had cost him a week.

[warm and friendly] In the tenth week he bought the skateboard. On the same day the share jar held $10, and Leo chose where it would go. He and his dad took it to the animal shelter, where it bought a large bag of food.
[warm] The bank with the big door.

[warm and friendly] For her eighth birthday, Maya got $25 from her grandparents, and her dad took her to the bank to open a savings account. The bank had a heavy door, a quiet lobby, and a banker named Mr. Lopez who drew pictures while he talked.

[warm and friendly] A bank has three big jobs, he said. It keeps money safe, and the government protects the money in savings accounts. It lends money to people and businesses who need to borrow. And it pays interest to people who save, a little extra for letting the bank use their money.

[warm and friendly] He pointed out the window at the bakery next door. Last year the bakery had borrowed money from this bank to buy a new oven. The baker was paying it back a little each month, plus interest. The money savers like Maya keep in the bank is the money it lends.

[warm and friendly] Maya told him about the time she borrowed $5 from her brother for a movie ticket. She paid him back on Saturday, all $5, and he did not charge her anything extra. Mr. Lopez laughed and said that a bank would have charged interest, because that is how banks earn money.

[warm and friendly] At home, Maya kept her piggy bank for small spending money, since it was easy to reach. But it paid nothing, and once a dollar had gone missing behind the dresser. The savings account was harder to reach, which helped her leave the money alone.

[warm and friendly] A year later, her statement showed something new. Her account paid 2 percent a year, and 2 percent of $25 is 50 cents. Fifty cents was not much, Maya said, but she had not done anything to earn it, and she liked that.
[warm] Lemonade on Saturday.
[warm and friendly] Owen and Priya were nine when they rented a table at the neighborhood market for $5 a Saturday. They planned to sell lemonade for $1 a cup.

[warm and friendly] First they worked out the cost of one cup. Lemons, sugar and a paper cup came to 40 cents. The table cost $5 no matter how much they sold, so it was a fixed expense. Every cup they sold needed its own 40 cents of supplies, a variable expense.

[warm and friendly] The first Saturday was sunny, and they sold 30 cups for $30. Priya did the math in their notebook. The cups cost 30 times 40 cents, which is $12, and the table was $5, so the expenses were $17. Their profit was $30 minus $17, or $13.

[warm and friendly] The second Saturday it rained. They sold only 10 cups, made $10, and spent $4 on supplies. The table still cost $5, rain or shine, so their profit was just $1. Owen said that was the day he understood what a risk was.

[warm and friendly] For the third Saturday, Priya had an idea. A soccer tournament was being played at the park, so they set up next to the field. They sold 40 cups, spent $16 on supplies and $5 on the table, and made $19 in profit.

[warm and friendly] At the end of the month they split their profit evenly and wrote down what they had learned. Know your fixed expenses. Count your variable expenses. And go where the thirsty people are.
[warm] Georgette and the market table.

[warm and friendly] Georgette had been making peach jam for sixty years, ever since her own mother taught her in a farmhouse kitchen. One summer her grandchildren, Eli, who was ten, and Rosa, who was eight, asked if they could sell it. Georgette said yes, on one condition: they would learn how a business works.

[warm and friendly] They rented a table at the Saturday market for $10. Georgette explained that the table was a fixed expense, the same every week however many jars they sold. Each jar also needed peaches, sugar, a glass jar and a lid, about $2 in all, and that was a variable expense, because more jars meant more supplies.
[warm and friendly] They priced the jam at $6 a jar. Rosa worked it out on the chalkboard: each jar sold left $6 minus $2, or $4, to cover the table and maybe more.

[warm and friendly] On the first Saturday they sold 20 jars and took in $120. The supplies had cost $40 and the table $10, so the expenses came to $50. Their profit was $120 minus $50, or $70, and Eli cheered so loudly that the bread seller next to them laughed and bought a jar for her own breakfast table.

[warm and friendly] In the middle of the summer, the price of peaches went up. A late freeze that spring had killed many peach blossoms, so there were fewer peaches to sell. Each jar now cost $3 to make. Twenty jars still brought in $120, but the supplies cost $60 and the profit dropped to $50.

[warm and friendly] Georgette paid each grandchild $10 every Saturday for their work, money they had earned. Rosa set up three jars at home: $4 to spend, $5 to save and $1 to share. By the end of eight Saturdays, her save jar held $40, and she opened a savings account at the bank.

[warm and friendly] At the bank, Georgette pointed out their neighbor from the market, who had borrowed money for a new canopy to keep her booth dry. She would pay it back a little each month, with interest. That is credit, Georgette told them: useful when you need something now, but it always has to be paid back.

[warm and friendly] The last jar sold on the final Saturday in August. Eli asked his grandmother what had been the most valuable thing at the table all summer. Georgette tapped the recipe card in her apron pocket and said it was the sixty years of practice that went into every jar. Nobody could buy that at a market, she said.
[warm] The red bird in the gray sky.

[warm and friendly] Tomas had painted a whole sky of gray birds for the school poster contest, forty of them, and the poster looked like a wet sidewalk. His art teacher, Miss Delgado, stood beside it for a long time and then asked one question. Where does your eye go first?

[warm and friendly] Nowhere, Tomas admitted. The birds were all the same size, the same gray, the same distance apart. Repetition, Miss Delgado said, is a fine principle, but it needs a partner. A picture with only repetition is wallpaper.

[warm and friendly] She handed him a brush loaded with red. One bird, she said, any bird. He painted the third bird from the left red, and the poster changed while the paint was still wet. Every eye that came near it went to the red bird first. That is emphasis, she said. A focal point.

[warm and friendly] Then she showed him contrast. The red bird was small against the big gray sky, bright against dull, one against many, and each difference made the bird louder. Movement came next: he added a thin line of cloud that curved from the corner of the poster to the red bird, and the eye followed it like a road.

[warm and friendly] Balance was the last fix. The red bird sat on the left, so the right side felt empty, until Tomas painted a large, dull barn low in the corner. A big dull thing balanced a small bright thing, and the poster stopped tipping. Proportion he left alone; the birds were the right size for the sky.

[warm and friendly] The poster won second place, and Tomas kept the judge's note more than the ribbon. The elements are the building blocks, it said. The principles are how you stack them. Your red bird knows that.
[warm] Three pictures, one question.
[warm and friendly] The museum had three rooms on Priya's class list, and the docent gave the class one question to carry through all of them: what did the artist most want you to see?

[warm and friendly] The first room held a copy of a cave painting from Lascaux, in France, horses running across a wall that was painted about seventeen thousand years ago. The painter had used the bumps of the rock for the horses' bellies. Priya decided the main idea was movement: a whole herd, going somewhere, fast.

[warm and friendly] The second room held a print by Hokusai, made in Japan in the 1830s, a great wave curling over three small boats with a mountain far behind. The main idea, said Kofi, was that the sea was bigger than anybody. Priya thought it was the boats, still rowing. The docent said both, and that the wave was made of a hundred hooked lines, repetition doing the work of fear.

[warm and friendly] The third room held a story quilt by Faith Ringgold, painted cloth with a border of sewn squares and a story written along the edge. A family on a rooftop at night, in a city. The main idea was closeness, the class agreed: everyone on one blanket under one sky.

[warm and friendly] On the bus Priya asked the docent what her job was called. A museum educator, she said. Then she counted the other jobs the class had passed that day. An illustrator had drawn the map of the rooms; a graphic artist had made the signs; a photographer had shot the catalog; an architect had built the light into the ceiling.

[warm and friendly] Three pictures, three places, seventeen thousand years apart, and one question that worked on all of them. Priya wrote it on the inside cover of her sketchbook, where she would see it every time she opened it.
[warm] The concert with the eyes closed.
[warm and friendly] The fourth-grade orchestra let the third graders sit in on a rehearsal, and the conductor, Dana Reyes, began with a game. Close your eyes, she said, and tell me the family.

[warm and friendly] The first sound was air moving through a tube, high and clear. Woodwind, said Leo, before anyone else, and it was a flute. The second was lips buzzing into metal, bright as a shout: brass, a trumpet. The third was a bow drawn across a string, and the fourth was a stick on a drum skin. Strings and percussion. Four families, four sounds, and he had named them all with his eyes shut.

[warm and friendly] Then she played the same note on the flute and the trumpet, one after the other. Same note, she said, different color. That color is timbre, and it is how you know a friend's voice on the phone.

[warm and friendly] The orchestra played its piece next, and Dana Reyes stopped them twice to point at the page. Here is mezzo forte, she said, a little loud, not all the way. Here is piano, soft. The students who had played it loud all the way through looked at their shoes and then played it again, better.

[warm and friendly] Leo noticed something on the third time through. The beginning came back at the end, the same tune after a different middle. He drew three letters on his program, A, B, A, and showed his neighbor. The conductor saw it and held it up to the room. That, she said, is the form of the piece, and this third grader just drew it.

[warm and friendly] Four families you can tell apart with your eyes shut, a color called timbre, signs for how loud and how fast, and a shape you can draw with letters. Leo went home with the program in his pocket and the letters on the front.
[warm] The night the mariachi played.

[warm and friendly] The park in San Antonio held a free concert on the last Friday of every month. In October the band was a mariachi from the high school: trumpets, violins, a guitar and a big round-backed guitarrón.
[warm and friendly] Sofia's music teacher had given the class homework for the night: listen with a purpose. Write down four musical events, she had said, and name each one with the right word.

[warm and friendly] The first event came quickly. The violins carried the tune for a verse, and then the trumpets took it, bright and hard, and the whole sound changed color. A change of timbre, Sofia wrote. The second came when the chorus returned after the verse, the same tune again. A change of form.

[warm and friendly] The third song began slowly and then broke into a gallop, and the dancers in front of the stage began to spin. A change of tempo. And in the last song the band dropped to almost nothing, one guitar and one voice, before everyone came back at once. A change of dynamics, from piano to forte in a single bar.

[warm and friendly] Between songs Sofia noticed the manners of the crowd. Nobody clapped between the verses of a long song, phones stayed dark, and when the last chord rang, the whole park stood up. Her grandmother, standing beside her, hummed a song she had learned as a girl in Monterrey. Sofia wrote a fifth event that was not on the list: a folk song, passed from person to person.
[warm and friendly] Four events, five with her grandmother's, each with the right word beside it. Listening with a purpose, Sofia found, did not make the music smaller. It made it hers.
[warm] Chloe and the orchestra.

[warm and friendly] Chloe's art teacher gave the class an assignment that sounded impossible: draw a sound. Chloe took her sketchbook to the community orchestra's Thursday rehearsal, sat in the last row, and waited for a sound worth drawing.

[warm and friendly] The first thing she drew was not a sound but a shape: the orchestra itself, a half circle of chairs with the strings in front, the woodwinds behind them, the brass behind those, and the percussion along the back wall. Four families, arranged by how far their sound carries. The seating was a balance, she realized, big soft strings in front and loud brass held back where they would not drown the rest.

[warm and friendly] Then the conductor tapped the stand and the sound began, and Chloe found she could draw it after all. The strings were long smooth lines. The woodwinds were thin curves, air through a tube. The brass were short bright zigzags, lips buzzing into metal. The percussion were dots, a stick on a skin. Timbre, the color of each sound, turned into a line of its own.

[warm and friendly] In the slow middle section a single oboe took the tune while everyone else went to piano, almost nothing, and Chloe's pencil went to the oboe player the way every ear in the hall did. Emphasis, she wrote in the margin. One bright thing against a soft field. The conductor was arranging sound the way her teacher arranged a picture.

[warm and friendly] When the opening tune came back after the middle, she drew the whole piece as three blocks: a wide one, a narrow one, a wide one. ABA, the concertmaster told her afterward, looking over her shoulder. You drew the form. Most people my age cannot hear it, and you drew it.

[warm and friendly] She came back for the concert on Saturday and learned the other half of listening. She sat before the first note, kept her phone dark, and held her clapping through the pause between the movements, because the pause was inside the piece, not after it. At the last chord she clapped until her hands stung.

[warm and friendly] The oboe player found her in the lobby, saw the drawings, and asked what the zigzags were. The trumpets, Chloe said. The player laughed and said that was exactly right, and that she had never seen her own instrument drawn before, a smooth curve with a thin reed of a line inside it.

[warm and friendly] The orchestra hung the drawings in the lobby for the rest of the season, four families in four kinds of line, and a small card underneath that Chloe wrote herself. The elements are the building blocks, it said. The principles are the organizers. Music uses them too.
[warm] One minute.

[warm and friendly] Noah had seen the movie. His friend Eli had not, and Eli's bus was one minute away. Tell me the story, Eli said. Noah started at the very beginning, with the hero's breakfast, and the bus was already turning the corner.

[warm and friendly] He could not do it. There were two hours of movie, and he loved all of it: the dog, the joke about the boots, the song in the market. If he left any of it out, was it even the same story?
[warm and friendly] The bus squealed to a stop, and he had thirty seconds. He grabbed the three questions his teacher always asked. Who was it about? What happened? How did it end?

[warm and friendly] A girl lost her map, crossed a desert without it, and found the hidden city by following the stars. No breakfast, no dog, no song. Eli said, oh, that sounds good, and got on the bus knowing exactly what the movie was about.

[warm and friendly] Noah tested the rest. Could he cut the joke about the boots and still have the story? Yes, so it was a detail. Could he cut the lost map? No. Without it, there was no desert and no story.
[warm and friendly] He had almost added, and it was the best movie ever. He was glad he had not. That was his opinion, not the story.

[warm and friendly] A summary keeps the big events and drops the small details. It stays in order and leaves your opinion out. The test is the bus stop: if a friend hears it in a minute and knows the story, you summarized it.
[warm] The muddy boots.
[warm and friendly] When Tessa came downstairs, her brother's boots were by the door, caked in mud to the ankles. Her mom looked at them and sighed. Nobody said a word about where he had been.

[warm and friendly] And yet Tessa knew. Puddle jumping, on the way home from school, the way he always did after rain. Nobody had told her. How could she be so sure of something she had not been told?

[warm and friendly] Because she had two things. A clue in front of her, the mud on the boots. And something she already knew, that her brother could not pass a puddle without jumping in it. A clue plus what you know makes an inference.

[warm and friendly] Her little sister had a different idea. Mom sighed because the car is broken, she said. Tessa looked around. No clue anywhere said anything about a car. That was not an inference. It was just a guess.

[warm and friendly] That night, Tessa read a story that began: Maya grabbed her umbrella and sighed at the window. It never said rain. It never said Maya was unhappy. Tessa knew both before she reached the next line.
[warm and friendly] The umbrella was the clue for rain. The sigh was the clue for unhappy. Tessa knew what umbrellas and sighs mean, and the writer had trusted her to know.

[warm and friendly] Writers do not say everything. They show muddy boots and a sigh, and they trust you to work out the rest. An inference is a clue in the text plus what you already know. No clue, no inference.
[warm] Brave as a lion.

[warm and friendly] Rosa's friend Maya had stood up to the biggest kid in school without blinking. Rosa wanted to write it down, and the word brave did not seem big enough. Brave was what you called someone at the dentist.
[warm and friendly] She tried adding more brave. Very brave. Really very brave. It got longer and weaker every time. The bravest thing she had ever seen was turning into a pile of dull words.
[warm and friendly] Then she stopped describing Maya and compared her to something else. Maya is as brave as a lion. The little word as made it a simile, a comparison that uses like or as.

[warm and friendly] Then she went further. Maya is a lion. No like, no as. Maya simply was one, for the length of the sentence. That is a metaphor: saying one thing is another thing it plainly is not.

[warm and friendly] Neither sentence is meant to be taken literally. Maya has no mane and no tail. But both put a lion in the reader's head, fast, and a lion says more than a page of very brave ever could.

[warm and friendly] Once she knew the trick, Rosa heard it everywhere. At lunch her brother said the cafeteria was a zoo. A metaphor. Her teacher said the hallway was as quiet as a library. A simile. Neither was meant literally, and both were perfectly clear.
[warm and friendly] Like or as makes a simile. Saying one thing is another makes a metaphor. Both compare, and both let a reader feel what plain words only describe.
[warm] Road signs.

[warm and friendly] Jamal read the science chapter twice and could not have told you what it was about. The words were fine one at a time. Together they felt like a road with no signs, and he kept missing the turns.

[warm and friendly] His teacher told him to stop reading the sentences and read the little words between them instead. First. Then. Because. As a result. However. Jamal thought she was joking. Those were the words you skipped.

[warm and friendly] They were the signs. First, then and finally meant a sequence, one step after another, like the steps of a volcano erupting. Because and as a result meant cause and effect: this happened, so that happened.

[warm and friendly] Both, unlike and however meant comparing, two things set side by side. And the words problem and solved meant a problem and its solution. Four shapes, and the little words told him which one he was on.

[warm and friendly] Jamal went back to the chapter. The first section said first, then, finally: a sequence. The next said because three times in one paragraph: causes and effects. The last said unlike and however: a comparison of two kinds of volcanoes. He knew what was coming before it came.
[warm and friendly] When he saw because, he knew an effect was on its way. When he saw however, he knew a difference was coming. The chapter made sense on the first try.
[warm and friendly] Every text is built one of a few ways, and signal words tell you which. Read the signs, and you will know the shape of the road before you walk it.
[warm] The wrong page.

[warm and friendly] Priya needed the word jungle for her report and opened the dictionary to G, because the word starts with the same sound as giraffe. Nothing. She flipped forward and back until the pages blurred. The dictionary was enormous, and the word was hiding.

[warm and friendly] Her dad asked how jungle was spelled. J, U, N, G, L, E, she said. Then why look in G? Because jungle and giraffe start with the same sound, she said. But not the same letter. A dictionary does not care how a word sounds. It only cares how it is spelled.

[warm and friendly] So she went to J. But J still had pages and pages. Her dad showed her the second letter trick. Words that start with the same letter are sorted by the next one: bat, bed, bin. JA came first, then JE, JI, JO, and last, JU.
[warm and friendly] Then she noticed two words printed in bold at the top of every page. She had never once looked at them. They were guide words: the first and last words on that page.

[warm and friendly] One page said jumpy at the top left and junk at the top right. Jungle comes after jumpy, because N comes after M. It comes before junk, because G comes before K. So it had to be on that page, and there it was.

[warm and friendly] A dictionary is sorted by the first letter, then the second, then the third. Guide words name a page's first and last entries, so you never have to read a page to know if your word is on it.
[warm] The icy road.

[warm and friendly] The bus was twenty minutes late, and Owen's toes were frozen. When it finally came, the driver said the road was icy. Owen wrote it in his journal as two facts. The road was icy. The bus was late. They sat there like strangers.
[warm and friendly] His teacher read it and asked which one caused the other. Owen said, both? The ice and the lateness had happened at the same time, and he could not see which came first.

[warm and friendly] The ice came first. The road was icy, so the bus was late. Or the same two things the other way round: the bus was late because the road was icy. The ice was the cause, the thing that made something happen. The late bus was the effect, the thing that happened.
[warm and friendly] So points forward, from the cause to the effect. Because points back, from the effect to the cause. Ask why, and you find the cause. Ask what happened, and you find the effect.

[warm and friendly] That afternoon the storm got worse, and one cause started knocking over effects like dominoes. The ice closed the bridge. It canceled soccer practice. It sent Owen home early, and school was called off the next day.
[warm and friendly] Owen added them all to his journal, each with an arrow pointing back to the ice. One cause, five effects, counting the late bus.
[warm and friendly] A cause makes something happen, and an effect is what happened. Pick the right little word, so or because, and the two strangers in a journal become one story.
[warm] Two minutes first.

[warm and friendly] Marcus had a chapter on volcanoes to read and ten minutes before dinner. He started at the first word and was still on the first page when his mom called. Reading was a wall, and he had barely scratched it.

[warm and friendly] The next night his dad showed him a trick. Don't read the chapter yet, he said. Just look at it. Marcus thought that was cheating. How could looking at a chapter tell you what it said?

[warm and friendly] He read the headings first: what a volcano is, why it erupts, kinds of volcanoes. Then the captions under the pictures, and then the words in bold, the ones the book wanted him to learn. Two minutes, and he knew the shape of the whole chapter.
[warm and friendly] When he did read it, every sentence had a place to go. The bold word magma showed up, and he already knew it was important.

[warm and friendly] Then his dad showed him the back of the book. The index listed every topic in alphabetical order, with the pages where it appeared. Marcus found lava on three different pages in ten seconds. The glossary, a tiny dictionary just for this book, told him that magma is melted rock underground and lava is the same melted rock once it reaches the surface.
[warm and friendly] At the front, the table of contents listed the chapters in order. The volcano chapter was the fourth.

[warm and friendly] Headings, bold words and captions guide you through a page. The contents, the index and the glossary guide you through a whole book. Read the signposts first, and you never get lost.
[warm] The letter with the missing lines.

[warm and friendly] The letter was two pages long and said almost nothing directly. That was the point. It began with the weather, which is how you know someone has something else to say. It came from a grandmother who had just moved three hundred miles away.

[warm and friendly] The grandchild who read it had learned to summarize: keep the big events, drop the details. A summary is short on purpose. The big events were three: a move, a new garden and a question about visiting. Everything else, the rain, the neighbor and the price of tomatoes, was detail.

[warm and friendly] Then came the reading between the lines. The letter never said she was lonely. It said the house was quiet at night and that the garden was slow to grow when there was nobody to show it to. That is an inference: a guess with a clue behind it.

[warm and friendly] She wrote that the new town was as strange as a shoe on the wrong foot, a simile, because it compares with as. Later she wrote that the days were a long gray hallway, a metaphor, because it says the days were one. Both told the truth better than plain words would have.

[warm and friendly] The letter had a shape too. First the move, then the garden, then the question, with signal words holding it together: first, after that, finally. Structure is a map. A reader who knows the shape can find the question without reading every line twice. Hers was on the last page.

[warm and friendly] One word the reader did not know, disconsolate, sent them to the dictionary. The guide words at the top of each page, the first and last words on it, walked them there: past dirt, past disagree, to a page that began with disco and ended with discord. Disconsolate: unable to be comforted.

[warm and friendly] The words the grandmother chose did something the facts alone could not. A reader who only summarized would know she moved and planted a garden. A reader who inferred would know she missed them, and that the question at the end was not really about June. It was about whether anyone would come.

[warm and friendly] The reply went out that afternoon, in the same shape: first the news, then the feelings, finally the answer. It said yes. The visit was arranged for June, and the next letter from the grandmother began with the weather again, and then said, plainly, that the garden was finally growing. It had someone to show it to.
[warm] Five kinds before breakfast.

[warm and friendly] Amir had to find five kinds of energy for homework, and he was sure it would take all day. Energy sounded like something in a power plant, or a rocket. Not something you would find at home before breakfast.

[warm and friendly] He stood in the kitchen with a pencil and nothing on the page. The lamp was on. The toaster was ticking. His dad was listening to the radio, and the fan was turning. He had been in this room a thousand times and never seen energy in it.

[warm and friendly] Then he looked again. The lamp gave off light. The toaster glowed with heat, and he could smell the bread starting to brown. The radio made sound. The outlet fed the fan electrical energy, and the fan turned it into spinning blades: mechanical energy, the energy of moving things.
[warm and friendly] Five kinds, one kitchen, before he had even eaten. But the best part was what came next. Every machine in the room took in one form and gave out another.

[warm and friendly] The lamp took in electrical energy and gave out light, plus a little heat, which is why the bulb was warm. The toaster turned electrical energy into heat. The radio turned it into sound. The fan turned it into motion.
[warm and friendly] Amir rubbed his cold hands together and felt them warm up. Motion into heat. He tapped a spoon on his bowl. Motion into sound. He was a machine too.
[warm and friendly] Energy comes in forms you can name, and machines change one form into another. Ask of anything: what form goes in, and what comes out?
[warm] The loop.

[warm and friendly] Jade had a battery, a bulb and two wires. The instructions said the bulb would light. She hooked one wire from the battery to the bulb and waited. Nothing. She wiggled it. Still nothing. The bulb sat there like a glass egg.

[warm and friendly] She checked the battery. It was new. She checked the bulb. It was fine. Everything worked, and nothing worked. Her brother said the electricity was stuck in the battery, which did not help.

[warm and friendly] Then she noticed the second wire. It ran from the bulb back toward the battery and stopped an inch short. She touched it to the battery. Light! She lifted it. Dark. Electricity did not want a road. It wanted a loop, from the battery, through the bulb and back home.

[warm and friendly] Her brother wanted a turn, so she let him close the gap. He tried a plastic straw between the wire and the battery first. Dark. Then a metal paper clip. Light. The metal let electricity through. The plastic stopped it.

[warm and friendly] Metals like copper, iron and aluminum are conductors: they carry electricity. Rubber, plastic, wood and glass are insulators: they block it. That is why a wire is metal inside and plastic outside. The metal carries the flow, and the plastic keeps it away from your hand.
[warm and friendly] Jade taped a paper clip to the board so she could swing it on and off the wire. Now she had a switch. Open, dark. Closed, light.
[warm and friendly] Every circuit is a loop, and electricity flows only when the loop is complete. Break it anywhere, and the light goes out.
[warm] The sandcastle.

[warm and friendly] Sofia built the best sandcastle of her life on the first day of vacation. Three towers, a moat, and a wall you could stand a shell on. She came back every morning to check on it, and every morning it was a little less castle.

[warm and friendly] At the end of the beach stood a rocky cliff. Waves slammed into it, and in its cracks lay sand and broken shell. Sofia asked her grandpa a question she had never thought to ask. Where does sand even come from?

[warm and friendly] From rock, he said. Water, ice, wind and plant roots crack rock into smaller and smaller pieces over many years. That breaking is called weathering. Most beach sand is bits of rock and shell broken down that way.

[warm and friendly] By the fourth day, the waves had carried half of her castle out to sea. By the last day there was nothing left at her spot at all. Carrying pieces away is called erosion, and water does most of it.

[warm and friendly] And yet, farther down the beach, a fresh bank of sand had piled up where none had been. Where the water slowed down, it dropped what it was carrying. Dropping the pieces somewhere new is called deposition.
[warm and friendly] Sofia pressed a shell into the new sand bank. Her castle had not vanished. It had moved.
[warm and friendly] Break, carry, drop. Weathering, erosion and deposition shape every hill, canyon and beach on Earth. A sandcastle shows in one week what a mountain shows in a million years.
[warm] The right tools.

[warm and friendly] At the zoo, Ravi watched a duck paddle across the pond and then walked into the desert house, where a cactus stood covered in spines. He thought both looked ridiculous. Feet like paddles. A plant like a pincushion. Why would anything grow that way?

[warm and friendly] He asked the keeper whether the duck minded its silly feet. She asked him a question back. What would happen to a duck with feet like a chicken? He pictured it paddling hard and going nowhere.

[warm and friendly] Every strange part, she said, is a tool for a problem. Webbed feet push against the water like oars. The cactus has a thick stem that stores water for the dry months, and its spines keep thirsty animals from biting in.

[warm and friendly] In the next room, a small desert fox with enormous ears was curled up asleep. Ravi guessed the ears were for hearing. They do help, the keeper said, but they also let heat escape, and that keeps the fox cool in the desert sun.
[warm and friendly] An adaptation is a part or a habit that helps a living thing survive where it lives. The fox has a habit too. It sleeps through the hot day and hunts in the cooler night.
[warm and friendly] Then she asked one more question. What if you moved a polar bear to a forest? Its white fur hides it on snow. Among green trees, it would stand out.
[warm and friendly] When something looks odd, ask two questions: what problem does this place give it, and how does this part solve it? The answers turn the strangest creatures into the smartest.
[warm] The piano.

[warm and friendly] The movers could not lift Grandma's piano into the truck. Two of them strained until their faces went red, and the piano rose about an inch. Nina watched from the driveway, sure the piano was staying.

[warm and friendly] Then they pulled a long metal ramp from the truck and laid it against the back. They rolled the piano up it, slowly, and it went in. Nina did not understand. The piano weighed the same as it had a minute ago. Where had the weight gone?

[warm and friendly] Nowhere, the mover said. The ramp made a trade. Instead of lifting the piano straight up four feet, they pushed it along twelve feet of ramp. Less force, more distance. The work, the push times the distance, stayed about the same.

[warm and friendly] That ramp is a simple machine, an inclined plane. Nina counted the others that day. The dolly under the boxes rolled on wheels and axles. The crowbar that opened a crate was a lever. Next door, a flag went up its pole on a pulley.
[warm and friendly] Every one made a job easier without an engine, and every one made the same trade. A long lever handle moves far so the other end can move a little and push hard.
[warm and friendly] There are six simple machines: the inclined plane, the wedge, the screw, the lever, the wheel and axle, and the pulley. None of them gives you something for nothing.
[warm and friendly] Machines do not make jobs smaller. They make them possible, by stretching a hard push into a long, easy one.
[warm] Four tests.

[warm and friendly] Leila's teacher tipped a box onto the table: a nail, a cork, a coin, a metal spoon, a wooden spoon and a sugar cube. Sort them, she said. Leila lined them up by size. Then by color. Neither felt like science.

[warm and friendly] The teacher set out four tools beside them: a magnet, a bowl of water, a mug of hot water and a thermometer. Try each test on each object, she said, and write down what happens. Leila thought the answers would be boring.

[warm and friendly] The magnet grabbed the nail and ignored the cork. Iron is magnetic, and cork is not. In the bowl, the cork floated and the coin sank with a clink. The cork is less dense than water, and the coin is more.

[warm and friendly] Then she stood both spoons in the hot water. In less than a minute, the metal handle was too warm to hold. The wooden handle stayed cool. Metal conducts heat fast. Wood insulates, and keeps the heat from traveling.

[warm and friendly] Last, she stirred the sugar cube into a cup of water. It shrank, then vanished. It had not disappeared. It had dissolved, spreading through the water in pieces too small to see. Leave the cup on a sunny sill until the water dries up, and the sugar is left behind.
[warm and friendly] The thermometer measured the hot water. Mass, volume and temperature are properties you measure with tools. Floating, magnetism, conducting and dissolving are properties you test.
[warm and friendly] Every kind of matter has properties. Measure what you can, test the rest, and a box of odd objects sorts itself.
[warm] The strings.

[warm and friendly] Mr. Ortiz laid cards on the classroom floor: grass, grasshopper, mouse, snake, bird and hawk. Each student held a string running from a thing that gets eaten to the thing that eats it. Grass to mouse. Mouse to snake. Mouse to hawk. Grass to grasshopper to bird to hawk. Snake to hawk.
[warm and friendly] Soon the strings crossed everywhere. It looked less like a chain and more like a spider web, which, Mr. Ortiz said, was the whole idea.
[warm and friendly] Then he picked up the mouse card. Three strings dropped to the floor. The class expected the hawk to fall too. It ate mice, after all. But the hawk card did not move. Why not?

[warm and friendly] Because the hawk still had the snake and the bird. A food chain is one line. A food web is all the lines at once, and an animal that eats more than one thing has more than one string holding it up. A web bends where a chain would break.

[warm and friendly] The arrows in a food web run the same way as the strings, from the eaten to the eater. They show where the energy goes. And every string, followed back far enough, starts at a plant.
[warm and friendly] Mr. Ortiz added one last card: mushrooms. Decomposers break down dead plants and animals and return them to the soil, which feeds the grass. The web closed into a loop.
[warm and friendly] More links mean more ways to survive a loss. That is why a meadow full of different living things stays alive.
[warm] The night the lights went out.

[warm and friendly] At seven the lights went out on the whole street. The first thing anyone learned was which energy was which: the lamp had been light, the heater heat, the radio sound, the fridge motion, and all of it had been electrical until the line went down.

[warm and friendly] The second thing was a circuit. The flashlight only lit when the switch closed the loop, and when the batteries went in the wrong way round, nothing. Electricity needs a complete path from the battery, through the bulb and back. Open the switch and the path is broken.

[warm and friendly] The youngest child wanted to use a metal spoon to fix a loose wire. The oldest said no. Metal is a conductor, which is why the wires inside a cord are copper, and rubber and plastic are insulators, which is why the cord is wrapped in them. Nobody touched the wire.

[warm and friendly] Outside, the storm that had cut the line was doing other work. Rain was carrying the garden soil down the path: erosion, said the oldest child, who had done it in a tray at school. At the bottom, by the gate, it was piling into a small bank: deposition.

[warm and friendly] Water had done the first part too, long before the storm. The rock by the gate was cracked where ice had frozen in it winter after winter and pushed it apart. Breaking rock down is weathering. Carrying the pieces away is erosion. Dropping them somewhere else is deposition. The path had all three.

[warm and friendly] The moths on the porch had gone quiet, and the owl in the pine did not care about the dark at all. Its large eyes gather what little light there is, and its soft-edged feathers make almost no sound. An adaptation is a body part or behavior that helps a living thing survive where it lives.

[warm and friendly] The last thing was the pump. The basement was taking on water, and the hand pump worked with a lever, a bar with a long handle that turns on a fixed point. It took a lot of pulling to lift a little water, but it lifted it. A lever trades distance for force.

[warm and friendly] When the lights came back at midnight nobody was scared of the dark anymore. They had seen energy in five forms and a loop that must be closed. They had met a conductor and an insulator, land broken and carried and dropped, animals fitted to the night, and a machine that makes a hard job possible.
[warm] The big thing first.

[warm and friendly] Sam wrote a paragraph about dogs. They fetch. They guard the house. They guide people who cannot see. My cat sleeps all day. It was all true, and his teacher wrote one question in the margin: what is this paragraph about?

[warm and friendly] Sam was annoyed. It was about dogs, obviously. But when he read it again, he saw that every sentence was a fact standing on its own. Nobody had told the reader what the facts added up to.
[warm and friendly] So he wrote the big thing first. Dogs make good helpers. That is a topic sentence, and it makes a promise: the rest of the paragraph will show how.
[warm and friendly] Then the facts followed, and suddenly they were not loose facts. They were three ways of proving one idea. Fetching helps. Guarding helps. Guiding helps most of all.

[warm and friendly] Then Sam asked the test question of every sentence: does this back up the first one? My cat sleeps all day. No. It was true, and funny, but it was about a cat, not dogs helping. It moved to a paragraph of its own.
[warm and friendly] His teacher called the topic sentence the sign on the door. It tells you what is inside the room. Every sentence after it has to belong in that room.
[warm and friendly] Write the big thing first. Then make every sentence after it back the big thing up. A reader will know where they are going from the very first line, and so will you.
[warm] Longer recess.

[warm and friendly] Lena wanted a longer recess, and so did everyone. When the principal visited, half the class shouted it at her. She smiled and said, tell me why, and the room went quiet. Wanting something, it turned out, was not a reason.

[warm and friendly] Lena went home and tried to write why. The first draft said recess should be longer because it should. She read it back and felt her face go hot. It was the same shout, written down.
[warm and friendly] The second draft had a shape. Her opinion came first: I think recess should be longer. Then reason one, with a helper word: first, we think better after we have run around.
[warm and friendly] Then reason two: also, friends who play together get along better in class. The little words first and also held the reader by the hand, one step at a time.

[warm and friendly] Then a closing sentence that said the opinion again in new words: give us twenty more minutes outside, and you will get better students back. Her dad read it and said it sounded like a lawyer wrote it.
[warm and friendly] The principal read it twice, then read it to the teachers. Recess grew by ten minutes the very next week, and nobody had to shout.

[warm and friendly] An opinion paragraph is an opinion, two reasons and a closing sentence. Say what you think at the start, prove it in the middle, and say it again at the end. That is how a wish becomes an argument.
[warm] The bird in the house.

[warm and friendly] A sparrow flew in through the open door, and the whole afternoon turned upside down. That night Ava had to write about something that happened. She wrote: a bird got in and then it got out. Her teacher wrote back: I was not there. Let me see it.
[warm and friendly] Ava did not know what that meant. It was true. A bird got in and got out. But reading it back, she could not see the bird either, and she had been standing right under it.
[warm and friendly] So she wrote it again in three parts. The beginning said who and where: our living room, a hot afternoon, the door propped open. Then a sparrow shot in like a thrown ball.

[warm and friendly] The middle said what happened. It circled the lamp twice, landed on the curtain rod, and everyone in the room froze with their hands up. The cat crouched under the couch, tail twitching.
[warm and friendly] The end said how it turned out. Dad slid the window open, and after one more circle the bird found the light and was gone. Nobody breathed until it was over the fence.
[warm and friendly] Her teacher circled one line: everyone froze with their hands up. Ava had not written that they were scared. She had shown it, and the reader felt it anyway.

[warm and friendly] A small story has a beginning, a middle and an end. Show what happened with words a reader can see: not a bird got in, but a sparrow like a thrown ball. Your reader was not there. Your words take them.
[warm] Mike writes it down.

[warm and friendly] Mike was nine and spent the summer hauling scrap with his uncle for money the house needed. The truck was old, the metal was heavy, and by July his hands had stopped hurting. He did not think of any of it as something to write about.

[warm and friendly] When school started, the first assignment was a paragraph with a topic sentence. A topic sentence tells the reader what the whole paragraph is about. Mike wrote the only big thing he knew: hard work is not the same as hard. Then the details: the truck, the weight, his hands.

[warm and friendly] His teacher showed him how the details held the topic sentence up, the way posts hold up a fence. Take one away and the paragraph leans. Put in a detail that does not belong, like the sandwich he ate in June, and the reader stops trusting the fence. A good paragraph stays on its topic from the first sentence to the last.

[warm and friendly] The opinion paragraph was harder, because Mike had opinions and no practice saying them nicely. Recess should be longer. Reason one: kids think better after running. Reason two: kids get along better after playing. Then say the opinion again, a new way, at the end.

[warm and friendly] His teacher wrote good in the margin, and underneath, one question: how do you know? Mike added a fact. After recess, his class had finished a math page faster than before it. An opinion with a reason is stronger. An opinion with a reason and a fact is harder to argue with.

[warm and friendly] The small story was about the bird that got into the house that August. Every story needs a problem, and a bird in the living room is a good one. Beginning: the door left open in the heat. Middle: the bird on the curtain rod and everyone frozen. End: his uncle opening the window, and the bird finding its way out into the yard.

[warm and friendly] Revising was the part Mike liked least and learned most from. He read the story out loud and heard where it dragged. He cut two sentences about the curtain, added the sound of the wings, and changed went to flew. The story got shorter and better at the same time.

[warm and friendly] Mike had not known a summer of scrap could be a story. It turned out everything could, if you gave it a beginning, a middle and an end, and then read it out loud and fixed what you heard. He kept every page in a folder with the truck drawn on the front.
[warm] Three kitchens.

[warm and friendly] When Diego's class was asked what the first Texans ate, he said buffalo, because that was the picture in every book. His teacher put a map of Texas on the wall and asked where. Diego waved his hand over the whole state.

[warm and friendly] Then she pointed at three places. The wet forests of the east. The dry, open plains of the north and west. The gray, marshy coast. Would a buffalo hunter do well in a marsh? Would a fisher do well on a dry plain? Diego was not so sure anymore.

[warm and friendly] In the wet east, rain fell often and the soil was rich. The Caddo farmed corn, beans and squash, and they lived in villages of tall, round houses made of grass. People who farm can stay put.

[warm and friendly] On the dry plains, the Comanche followed the buffalo on horseback. They rode into Texas in the 1700s, on horses whose ancestors had come over with the Spanish. The herds kept moving, so the people carried tipis they could pack.
[warm and friendly] Along the coast, the Karankawa fished the bays from dugout canoes and gathered shellfish. They moved with the seasons, camping wherever the food was best that season.

[warm and friendly] Many nations lived in Texas, and they traded, fought and made peace with one another for centuries. When Spain, Mexico and the United States arrived, each found peoples already at home.
[warm and friendly] Land decides a way of life. Look at where a people lived, and you can guess what they ate, what they built and how far they moved. The map was the first cookbook.
[warm] The mission bell.

[warm and friendly] The bell in the old mission near San Antonio had rung every morning for about a hundred years, since Spain built the mission, its walls and the little farm around it. Lucia's great-great-grandmother had heard it as a girl. The bell never changed.

[warm and friendly] Spain had claimed Texas in the 1500s. From the 1690s on, it built missions and forts to spread its faith and hold the land, and San Antonio grew up around them. Lucia had never known any flag on the pole but Spain's.

[warm and friendly] Then, in 1821, Mexico won its independence from Spain. One morning the bell rang under a new flag on the same pole. Texas was part of Mexico now. Lucia wondered how a place could belong to one country at breakfast and another by lunch.

[warm and friendly] Mexico had a problem. Texas was huge and had few settlers, and an empty land is hard to hold. So Mexico opened the door to American settlers. Stephen F. Austin brought the first three hundred families in the 1820s.

[warm and friendly] They came, and kept coming. Within about ten years, Americans outnumbered the Tejanos, the Texans of Mexican descent like Lucia's family. The newcomers disagreed with Mexico City about laws, language and slavery.
[warm and friendly] The bell rang over more and more faces that had never seen Spain or Mexico. One of the old missions had another name by then: the Alamo.
[warm and friendly] Two flags in a row, Spain and then Mexico, and the roots of a third growing under the same bell. The missions are still standing, and some still ring their bells.
[warm] The thirteen days.
[warm and friendly] Mike wanted to know why the most famous battle in Texas was one Texas lost. Georgette poured the tea, spread an old map on the table and put her finger on San Antonio.

[warm and friendly] In the fall of 1835, she said, Texans rose up against Mexico. Late that winter, Santa Anna's army surrounded the Alamo, an old mission in San Antonio. On March 2, 1836, while it was still under siege, Texans signed a declaration that Texas was free.

[warm and friendly] About two hundred defenders held the Alamo for thirteen days. On March 6, the army broke through, and the defenders who fought were killed. A few women, children and one enslaved man named Joe survived to tell what happened.

[warm and friendly] Georgette slid her finger east to a bend where two waters met. About six weeks later, here at San Jacinto, Sam Houston's army attacked on the afternoon of April 21. The battle lasted eighteen minutes. Santa Anna was captured the next day, and Texas was free.
[warm and friendly] Mike looked from one finger to the other. So why remember the loss?

[warm and friendly] Because the Texans at San Jacinto did, Georgette said. They charged shouting, Remember the Alamo, and the name carried them. Many Texans believe those thirteen days also bought the rest of Texas time.

[warm and friendly] For nine years Texas was its own country, the Republic of Texas, and Sam Houston was elected its first president. That is why its flag has one star. Georgette folded the map. Some defeats are not the end of a story. They are part of the price of the ending.
[warm] The 28th star.
