[warm and friendly] Mia found an old flag in her grandfather's attic with twenty-eight stars on it, not fifty. He told her the twenty-eighth star was Texas. For nine years Texas had been a country of its own. Then, in 1845, it joined the United States as the twenty-eighth state.

[warm and friendly] Mexico had never accepted that Texas was free, and a fight over the border helped start a war between the United States and Mexico in 1846. When it ended, the border was the Rio Grande.

[warm and friendly] But the story was not a straight line. In 1861 Texas left the Union to join the Confederacy in the war over slavery. Mia asked whether the star came off the flag. It did not. The United States never removed the stars of the states that left.
[warm and friendly] When that war ended, freedom did not reach Texas the day it was declared. Mia asked how freedom could be late. The news traveled slowly, and some people did not want it heard.

[warm and friendly] On June 19, 1865, Union soldiers arrived in Galveston with the order that every enslaved person in Texas was free. That day became Juneteenth, a holiday that began in Texas and now belongs to the whole country.

[warm and friendly] Then, in 1901, at Spindletop near Beaumont, oil roared out of the ground, and Texas changed again. Six flags had flown over Texas by then: Spain, France, Mexico, the Republic of Texas, the Confederacy and the United States.
[warm and friendly] Statehood in 1845, the Confederacy in 1861, Juneteenth in 1865 and oil in 1901. History is a line with bends in it.
[warm] Six flags over one town.

[warm and friendly] The town had been a town for a very long time. Before the roads, the Caddo farmed corn, beans and squash on the river flats to the east, and the Comanche rode the plains beyond. People had lived on this ground for thousands of years before anyone raised a flag over it.

[warm and friendly] Then a mission bell rang, and Spain called the place its own for more than a hundred years, though the priests were few and the settlers fewer. For a few years a French explorer named La Salle kept a fort on the coast, and France claimed the land too. His fort did not last, but his flag is still counted.

[warm and friendly] In 1821 a new flag went up: Mexico, newly free of Spain. Mexico opened the door to families from the north, and Stephen F. Austin led the first of them to farms along the Brazos. More came than anyone planned, and they brought their own ideas about how they wanted to be governed.

[warm and friendly] The arguments turned into a war. In October 1835 a cannon at Gonzales fired under a flag that said come and take it. In March 1836 the Alamo fell. In April, at San Jacinto, the fight took eighteen minutes, and the town belonged to a new country, the Republic of Texas, with a single star on its flag.

[warm and friendly] The Republic had to do everything a country does, with very little money. It printed its own paper money, which soon lost most of its value. It moved its capital more than once and chose Austin in 1839. Sam Houston led it twice, and people argued about joining the United States the whole time.

[warm and friendly] Nine years after San Jacinto the star joined twenty-seven others. Texas was the 28th state. Sixteen years after that, in 1861, Texas left the Union and joined the Confederacy, and the town sent its young men to the Civil War. After the war, on June 19, 1865, a Union general announced in Galveston that the enslaved people of Texas were free, and Juneteenth began.

[warm and friendly] The flags in the town square today tell the whole story in cloth: Spain, France, Mexico, the Republic, the Confederacy and the United States. Six flags, but more than six peoples, because the Caddo and the Comanche were here before any cloth went up a pole.

[warm and friendly] The children who walk past them on the way to school are walking the same ground the Caddo farmed. One of them stopped to count the stars on the last flag. Fifty. The single star is still there too, on the Texas flag beside it.
[warm] Twenty-three boxes.

[warm and friendly] The art teacher asked Leo to count the crayons in the supply room. There were 23 boxes with 4 crayons in each. Leo started multiplying in his head, lost the number and started again. Twenty-three fours is a lot to hold at once.

[warm and friendly] He tried counting the crayons one at a time and got to thirty before the teacher came back. This was going to take all afternoon. The boxes smelled like wax, and he was tired of them already.

[warm and friendly] Then he broke the 23 into pieces he could handle: twenty boxes and three boxes. Twenty boxes of four is 80 crayons. Three boxes of four is 12. And 80 plus 12 is 92. Two easy multiplications and one addition, instead of one hard one.
[warm and friendly] The teacher was impressed, so she gave him a harder one. The markers came in 14 bags of 23. Now both numbers were big. Leo broke both of them. Twenty and three. Ten and four.

[warm and friendly] He multiplied every piece by every piece. Twenty times ten is 200. Twenty times four is 80. Three times ten is 30. Three times four is 12. Then he added them: 200, 80, 30 and 12 make 322 markers.
[warm and friendly] He checked with a picture: a rectangle 23 wide and 14 tall, cut into four smaller rectangles, one for each piece. The four areas added up to the whole.
[warm and friendly] Every big multiplication is a set of small ones in disguise. Break the numbers into tens and ones, multiply each piece, then add the pieces together.
[warm] Sharing in rounds.
[warm and friendly] Grace had a sheet of 96 stickers and four friends waiting. She did not want to hand them out one at a time. That was 96 moves, and her friends were already bored.
[warm and friendly] So she tried a bigger step. Could everyone get twenty? Four twenties is 80. Yes. She peeled off twenty for each friend and had 16 left. Sixteen was a much smaller problem than 96.
[warm and friendly] Second round. Four more each used up all 16. Twenty and four: every friend had 24, and the sheet was empty. Share the big part first, see what is left, then share that.

[warm and friendly] Her teacher showed her the written way, one digit at a time. How many fours fit in 9, the first digit? Two, with 1 left over. Bring down the 6 to make 16. How many fours fit in 16? Four, exactly. The digits made 24. The same answer, in a tidier tower.

[warm and friendly] The next day her little brother added one more sticker to the sheet, 97 in all. Everyone got 24 again, and one sticker was left in her hand. That leftover is the remainder: 97 divided by 4 is 24, remainder 1.
[warm and friendly] To check it, Grace multiplied back. Four times 24 is 96. Add the remainder, 1, and you get 97. The check came out exactly.
[warm and friendly] Long division shares a big number in steps. Share what you can, bring down what is left, and always check by multiplying back and adding the remainder.
[warm] Twelve chairs.

[warm and friendly] Dev had to set out twelve chairs for the school play, in equal rows. He put them in one long row of twelve and stepped back. It looked like a bus. He tried five rows and had two chairs left over with nowhere to go.
[warm and friendly] Some numbers of rows worked, and some did not, and he could not tell which until he had dragged every chair. There had to be a way to know first.

[warm and friendly] He wrote down the ones that worked. One row of twelve. Two rows of six. Three rows of four. Four rows of three. Six rows of two. Twelve rows of one. The numbers that worked were 1, 2, 3, 4, 6 and 12.
[warm and friendly] Those are the factors of twelve, his teacher said: the numbers that go into it exactly, with nothing left over. Five was not a factor. That was why two chairs had nowhere to go.

[warm and friendly] For the next show, the class wanted chairs in rows of four. Four, eight, twelve, sixteen, twenty: any of those numbers of chairs would fill the rows exactly. Those are the multiples of four, what four makes when you count by it.
[warm and friendly] Then a latecomer brought a thirteenth chair. Dev tried every row he could think of. Only one long line worked. Thirteen has exactly two factors, itself and one, so it is prime.
[warm and friendly] A factor goes into a number exactly. A multiple is what a number makes. A prime has exactly two factors. And a prime number of chairs only ever makes one long line.
[warm] The quarter.

[warm and friendly] June found a quarter on the sidewalk and asked her dad why it was called that. Because it is a quarter of a dollar, he said. But he also called it twenty-five cents, and the price tag at the store said 0.25. Three names, one small coin.
[warm and friendly] She lined up four quarters, and they made a dollar. So one quarter was one fourth of the whole. But twenty-five? And that dot in 0.25? None of it looked like a fourth.

[warm and friendly] Her dad drew a dollar as a hundred pennies in a square, ten rows of ten. A quarter covered twenty-five of them. Twenty-five out of a hundred can be written as a fraction, 25/100, or as a decimal, 0.25. One fourth, twenty-five hundredths and 0.25 are the same money.
[warm and friendly] A decimal is a fraction with 10 or 100 on the bottom, he said, written with a point instead of a line. The first place after the point is tenths. The second is hundredths.

[warm and friendly] So a dime is one tenth of a dollar, 0.1. Three dimes are 0.3, and so are thirty pennies, 0.30. The zero at the end changes nothing, because three tenths and thirty hundredths are the same amount.

[warm and friendly] Then he gave her a puzzle. Which is more, 0.7 or 0.65? June said 0.65, because 65 looks bigger than 7. Her dad lined up the points. Seven tenths against six tenths. Seven dimes beat six dimes and a nickel. The tenths decide first.
[warm and friendly] Fractions and decimals are two names for one amount. Read decimals place by place, tenths first.
[warm] Half and a quarter.

[warm and friendly] Two boxes came back from the party. Half a pizza in one, a quarter of a pizza in the other. Mateo wanted to know how much pizza that was altogether. He wrote one half plus one fourth, then stopped. Halves and fourths were different sizes.

[warm and friendly] He tried adding the tops and the bottoms and got two sixths, which was less pizza than he had started with. That could not be right. The cheese was cold, and the math was getting worse.

[warm and friendly] So he cut. One slice of the pizza wheel through the half, and it became two quarters. Now every piece was a quarter. Two quarters plus one quarter is three quarters. Same bottoms, so he added the tops and kept the bottom.

[warm and friendly] The next weekend there were leftovers from two parties: seven quarter slices in all. Seven fourths. Mateo laid them out. Four quarters made one whole pizza, and three quarters were left over. Seven fourths is one and three fourths.
[warm and friendly] His sister ate three of the slices. Seven fourths take away three fourths is four fourths. Same bottoms, so he subtracted the tops. Four fourths was exactly one whole pizza.

[warm and friendly] At the end, he looked at a pizza cut into eighths with four slices left. Four eighths. Both numbers could be divided by four, so four eighths was the same as one half. Simplify at the end, and the answer gets easier to read.
[warm and friendly] Fractions add and subtract when their pieces are the same size. Same bottoms: work with the tops, keep the bottom.
[warm] Around and inside.

[warm and friendly] Hannah's mom asked her to measure the new garden bed so they could buy fence wire and soil. Hannah walked around the edge with a tape measure: four feet, three feet, four feet, three feet. Fourteen feet. She wrote down fourteen and thought she was done.

[warm and friendly] At the store, fourteen feet of wire was exactly right. Then her mom picked up the soil bags and asked how many square feet the bed was. Hannah said fourteen. Her mom tilted her head. Was it, though?
[warm and friendly] The wire went around the edge. The soil filled the inside. Those were two different questions, and one number could not answer both.

[warm and friendly] At home, Hannah drew the bed on grid paper, one square for every square foot. Four rows of three squares. Twelve squares. The bed covered twelve square feet, not fourteen. That was the area. The fourteen feet around the edge was the perimeter.
[warm and friendly] They had bought soil for fourteen square feet, so two square feet of soil were left in the bag. Her little brother used them to plant a single sunflower by the back steps.

[warm and friendly] Then her mom gave her a harder one: a square sandbox, five feet on every side. Around the edge: five, five, five and five, twenty feet. Inside: five rows of five, twenty-five square feet. Hannah did not mix them up this time.
[warm and friendly] Perimeter is the walk around the edge, measured in feet. Area is the surface covered, measured in square feet. Before you measure, ask which one the question wants.
[warm] The door.

[warm and friendly] Kai's homework asked for an acute angle, a right angle and an obtuse angle from around the house. He looked at the clock, the table and the roof and could not find any. He even checked under the bed. Angles seemed to live only on worksheets.

[warm and friendly] Then his little sister opened his door a crack to spy on him. The door and the wall made a thin wedge. Kai pushed it a bit wider. A bigger wedge. He pushed it straight out. A square corner.
[warm and friendly] The door had been drawing angles the whole time. Barely open, a small wedge: acute, less than a right angle, like the tip of a pizza slice. Kai drew it in his notebook.
[warm and friendly] Straight out from the wall: a right angle, 90 degrees, the corner of a square. Pushed farther: obtuse, wider than a right angle but not yet flat, like a chair tipped back.
[warm and friendly] Then he swung it all the way back until it lay flat against the wall beside it. A straight angle: 180 degrees, two right angles side by side.

[warm and friendly] His sister pointed at the top and bottom edges of the door. They ran side by side and never met, like railroad tracks. Parallel. The edge of the door met the floor in a square corner. Perpendicular. Kai wrote both words down before he forgot them.
[warm and friendly] Angles are everywhere two lines meet. A right angle is 90 degrees, acute is smaller and obtuse is wider. Open any door, and you can see all of it.
[warm] Chloe and the mural.

[warm and friendly] Chloe was nine and had been given a wall. The community center wanted a mural, her art teacher had said she could plan it, and planning turned out to be arithmetic. The wall was 23 feet wide and 4 feet high, and she wanted a row of 4 birds for every foot of it.

[warm and friendly] That was 23 times 4. She broke it into 20 times 4 and 3 times 4, eighty plus twelve, ninety-two birds. Breaking a number apart by place value turns a hard multiplication into two easy ones. She drew ninety-two birds on graph paper and lost count twice.

[warm and friendly] The paint came in cans that each covered 96 square feet. Area counts the squares that would cover a flat shape, and a rectangle takes length times height: 23 times 4, which she already knew was 92 square feet. One can would cover the wall once, with 4 square feet to spare. Two coats meant two cans.

[warm and friendly] The birds needed to be arranged in equal rows. Factors are numbers that multiply together to make another number. Twelve chairs can go one by twelve, two by six or three by four. Ninety-two birds could go one by ninety-two, two by forty-six or four by twenty-three.

[warm and friendly] Not three by anything, she found, because 92 is not a multiple of 3. She tried dividing and got 30 with 2 left over. A remainder, her teacher said, is what is left when things will not share out evenly. Chloe chose four rows of twenty-three.

[warm and friendly] The sky took a quarter of the wall and the grass a fourth. She wrote each as 0.25, a decimal, and added them: 0.50, the same as a half. Chloe had never cared about fractions and decimals until they told her where the horizon went. The birds would fly across the half in between.

[warm and friendly] On painting day, twelve volunteers came. Chloe split the ninety-two birds among them: 92 divided by 12 is 7 with 8 left over, so eight people painted eight birds and four painted seven. Nobody had to paint a fraction of a bird. Division, she decided, was fair sharing with a pencil.

[warm and friendly] The mural is still on the wall of the center. The birds are a little uneven, and she likes that now. Every time she walks past, she counts them, and every time there are ninety-two. She thinks of the numbers underneath the paint: the product, the area, the factors, the remainder and the decimals that put the sky in its place.
[warm] The pizza of notes.

[warm and friendly] Bea counted the notes in one measure and got seven. The measure was only supposed to hold four beats, so she decided the music was broken. Her teacher asked her to add the notes up instead of counting them.

[warm and friendly] A whole note is the whole pizza: four beats. A half note is half the pizza: two beats. A quarter note is one slice: one beat. An eighth note is half a slice: half a beat. Each note lasts half as long as the one before it.

[warm and friendly] Bea's seven notes were one quarter note and six eighth notes. The quarter was one beat. The six eighths were half a beat each, and six halves make three. One beat plus three beats. Four beats. Not broken at all.
[warm and friendly] The number of notes did not matter at all. What mattered was how long each one lasted, and how they added up.

[warm and friendly] She drew the measure as a pizza and every note as a piece, and the pieces always filled the plate. When they did not fill it, she had miscounted, and the empty space on the plate showed her where.

[warm and friendly] Four quarter notes fill a measure of four beats. So do two half notes, or one whole note, or eight eighth notes. Notes are fractions of a measure, and they add up the same way fractions do.
[warm and friendly] Whole, half, quarter, eighth: four beats, two, one and a half. A measure is a plate that has to be full.
[warm] The ladder of letters.

[warm and friendly] Luis could play any note if you told him its name, but he could not find the name on the page. Five lines, four spaces, and a dot somewhere on them. It looked like a fence with a bird on it.

[warm and friendly] His teacher called the staff a ladder. Some ladders you climb with your feet. This one you climb with your eyes. Every rung and every gap between the rungs has a letter, and every note sits either on a line or in a space.
[warm and friendly] The lines of the treble staff, from the bottom up, are E, G, B, D and F. To remember them, she said: Every Good Boy Does Fine. Luis said it three times on the walk home.
[warm and friendly] The spaces, from the bottom up, are F, A, C and E. They spell a word you already know: face. Four letters, four spaces, one face.

[warm and friendly] And the ladder went up in pitch. A dot higher on the staff was a higher note. Luis put his finger on the bottom line, E, and climbed, naming each rung and gap as he went: E, F, G, A, B, C, D, E, F.
[warm and friendly] By the end of the week, the bird on the fence had turned into a note he could name and play without stopping to count.
[warm and friendly] Five lines and four spaces; lines E, G, B, D, F; spaces F, A, C, E. Higher on the staff is higher in pitch. Learn two sayings, and you can name any note on the staff.
[warm] Four Italian words.

[warm and friendly] Nora played the piece exactly as written, every note right, and her teacher said it sounded like a grocery list. Nora asked what was missing. Her teacher pointed at four words she had skipped because they were not notes.

[warm and friendly] Forte means loud. Piano means soft. Those two are dynamics: how loud or soft to play. The piano got its name from them, her teacher said. Its full name, pianoforte, means soft-loud, because it could play both.

[warm and friendly] Allegro means fast. Adagio means slow. Those two are tempo: how fast the music goes. A composer writes the words right on the page so every player in the orchestra plays it the same way.

[warm and friendly] Nora played it again with the words. The opening was piano and adagio, soft and slow, like someone tiptoeing into a room. The middle was forte and allegro, and the room filled with people and noise.
[warm and friendly] Same notes, same order. But now it sounded like a piece of music instead of a list. Her little brother, who never listened to her practice, came to the door to hear the ending.
[warm and friendly] Her teacher played two examples. A lullaby, piano and adagio, soft and slow. A march, forte and allegro, loud and fast. Nora could have guessed the words just from hearing them.
[warm and friendly] Forte is loud, piano is soft; tempo is speed, allegro fast and adagio slow. The notes say what to play. The Italian words say how, and how is most of the music.
[warm] The school concert.

[warm and friendly] The concert began the way every rehearsal had, with the teacher tapping a pencil on the stand: tick, tick, tick, tick. The beat came first, before any note, and the twenty-two players found it the way you find a heartbeat, without looking. Every piece they would play that night rested on it.

[warm and friendly] The first piece was all quarter notes, one beat each, four to a measure. The time signature at the start said so: a 4 over a 4, four beats in every measure, and a quarter note gets one. Nobody rushed. Rushing is what happens when players stop listening to the beat.

[warm and friendly] The second piece had a solo, and the soloist read it off the staff the way she had learned in September. Every Good Boy Does Fine named the lines from the bottom up, and FACE spelled the spaces. Reading music is reading a map of sound: higher on the staff means higher in pitch.

[warm and friendly] The half notes held for two beats, and the eighth notes came in pairs, two to a beat, quick as footsteps. The rests were the hardest part. A rest is a beat of silence that still counts, and the whole band had to keep counting through it and come back in together.

[warm and friendly] At the end of the solo a whole note sat for four full beats while the room held still. Four beats is a long time to hold one sound, long enough to hear your own breathing. The soloist let it ring, then lowered her flute. Nobody clapped yet, because the page had one more piece on it.

[warm and friendly] The last piece was marked forte and allegro, loud and fast, and the drums took it at a run. In the middle the music swelled, a crescendo, each measure louder than the one before, until the trumpets were shining.

[warm and friendly] Then, on the final page, a word nobody had noticed in rehearsal: piano. It means soft. The whole band dropped to a whisper, and the piece ended slow, adagio, on one long note that faded until nobody could tell when it stopped. Loud is easy. Soft, played together, takes a whole band listening.

[warm and friendly] The applause was forte. Nobody had told it to be. Afterward the teacher said the band had played the notes right all year, but tonight they had played the music: the loud and the soft, the fast and the slow, and the silence in between.
[warm] The night librarian.

[warm and friendly] Ezra stayed up late finishing a game, and the next morning he could not remember what his teacher had said the day before. He had listened. It had gone in. It just was not there anymore.

[warm and friendly] His mom said the brain has a librarian who only works nights. All day long, new memories pile up on her cart: a spelling word, a math trick, a friend's joke. At night, while you sleep, she files them onto shelves where you can find them later.
[warm and friendly] Skip the night, and the cart stays full. Some things slide off before they are ever filed. That is why a tired morning feels like a cart with a wobbly wheel.
[warm and friendly] Ezra asked how long her shift was. For a kid his age, nine to eleven hours of sleep a night. Growing bodies and busy brains need all of it, every night.
[warm and friendly] And screens off an hour before bed, his mom said. The light from a screen tells the brain it is still daytime, and the librarian does not clock in.

[warm and friendly] That week Ezra went to bed on time and left his tablet in the kitchen. On Friday, he remembered every word on the spelling test, even the ones he had studied the night before, and it felt easy.
[warm and friendly] Sleep is when the brain sorts and stores what you learned. Study, then sleep, and more of it stays. Nine to eleven hours, and the screen goes off first.
[warm] The serving size.

[warm and friendly] Isla compared two cereal boxes and picked the one with less sugar on the label: nine grams against fourteen. Easy choice. Her dad asked her to read the very first line before she decided. Serving size: half a cup on hers, one cup on the other.

[warm and friendly] Every number on a label is per serving. Nine grams in half a cup was eighteen grams in a whole cup. Her cereal had won a race it should not have, because it had run only half the distance.

[warm and friendly] Then her dad showed her the ingredients list. Ingredients are listed from most to least, so the first word is what the food is mostly made of. Her box began with sugar. The other began with whole grain oats.
[warm and friendly] Isla felt a little tricked. The label had told the truth twice, in small print. She had just read the big number first, like almost everyone does.

[warm and friendly] Her dad turned the box over. Protein, he said, from beans, eggs, fish or meat, builds and repairs muscle. Fruits and vegetables bring vitamins. A good breakfast has more than cereal in the bowl.
[warm and friendly] Isla chose the oats, sliced a banana on top and poured herself a glass of milk. She read the serving size on every box in the pantry that weekend, just to catch them.
[warm and friendly] Check the serving size first, because every number is per serving. Then the sugar, then the first three ingredients. The small print tells the real story.
[warm] The top of the stairs.

[warm and friendly] Andre raced up four flights of stairs at the library and wanted to know what his heart had done about it. He pressed two fingers on the inside of his wrist, below his thumb, and felt his pulse thumping. His aunt, a nurse, showed him how to count.

[warm and friendly] Count the beats for fifteen seconds, she said, then multiply by four. At the top of the stairs, Andre counted 36 beats in fifteen seconds. Thirty-six times four: 144 beats a minute.
[warm and friendly] Why so fast? Working muscles need more oxygen, and blood carries it to them, so his heart pumped faster to send more blood.

[warm and friendly] Then his aunt had him rest and count again one minute later: 28 beats, or 112 a minute. His heart was already settling. How quickly a heart slows back down after hard work is called recovery, and it is one of the best signs of fitness.
[warm and friendly] Andre decided to try an experiment. For a month he played hard for about an hour every day: soccer, biking, tag with his cousins. It all counted, even in pieces.

[warm and friendly] Then he raced the same stairs and counted again. Nearly as fast at the top. But one minute later, his pulse had dropped much further than before. Training makes the heart stronger, so it pumps more blood with every beat, and the body learns to calm it down faster after hard work.
[warm and friendly] Muscles at work need more blood, so the heart speeds up. An hour of active play a day trains it, and a fit heart settles fast.
[warm] Twenty, twenty, twenty.
[warm and friendly] Zara's eyes ached after homework, and she could not fall asleep after watching videos in bed. She figured that was just how screens were. Everybody she knew had tired eyes.

[warm and friendly] Her school nurse gave her three rules that fit on one sticky note. The first was for her eyes. Every twenty minutes, look at something twenty feet away for twenty seconds. Staring at something close keeps the focusing muscles in your eyes working hard, and looking far away lets them relax.
[warm and friendly] The second rule was for sleep. Screens off an hour before bed, because the light from a screen tells the brain it is still daytime. Zara moved her phone charger to the kitchen.
[warm and friendly] The third rule was not about her body at all. Anything she shared online, a photo, a message, where she was, went past a trusted adult first. And never her address or her school.
[warm and friendly] Zara asked why. What goes online stays online, the nurse said. A photo can be copied and passed around long after you delete it, by people you will never meet.

[warm and friendly] A week later, Zara's eyes felt better by the end of homework, and she fell asleep faster. She stuck the note on her desk where she could see it, and one on her little brother's tablet too.
[warm and friendly] Screens are useful and fun, and they have costs. A break every twenty minutes, off an hour before bed, and nothing shared without a trusted adult.
[warm] The week the phone charged and I did not.

[warm and friendly] The notebook started as a dare from a teacher: one week, write down when you sleep, what you eat, when you move and when you look at a screen. No rules, no grades, just the truth on paper. The notebook was small enough for a pocket. Monday was honest and a little embarrassing.

[warm and friendly] Nine hours of sleep, but the last hour before sleep had been a screen, and the morning felt like wading. Children need about nine to twelve hours of sleep. The brain, the teacher had said, files the day at night, and Monday's files were still on the desk.

[warm and friendly] Tuesday was the cereal. Twelve grams of sugar per serving, and the serving was half of what went in the bowl, so the bowl held twenty-four. Sugar was the second ingredient on the list, and ingredients are listed from most to least, so there was a lot of it. Reading a label is reading the truth about food.

[warm and friendly] Wednesday was the stairs. Sitting still, the heart beat twelve times in ten seconds, seventy-two a minute. At the top of the stairs it was twenty-five in ten seconds. A minute later, eighteen. After two minutes, thirteen. The heart came back fast, and that, it turned out, was the whole point.

[warm and friendly] A heart that recovers quickly is a heart that is getting stronger. Kids need about an hour of moving every day, and it does not have to happen all at once. Recess counted. So did the walk to the bus and the stairs, twice.

[warm and friendly] Thursday was the screens. The tablet had been on for two hours straight, and the eyes felt dry and tired. The teacher's rule: every twenty minutes, look at something twenty feet away for twenty seconds. The eyes need to change focus, the way legs need to change position.

[warm and friendly] Thursday dinner was a plate the notebook could be proud of: half of it fruits and vegetables, green and orange, a quarter grain, a quarter protein, and water instead of soda. Nobody had planned it that way. The notebook had just made the plate easier to see.

[warm and friendly] By Friday the notebook had a rule in it that nobody had assigned: the phone charges overnight, and so do I. Screens off an hour before bed, eyes up every twenty minutes, half the plate green and orange, an hour of moving in whatever pieces the day allowed. Nothing in the week had been hard. It had only needed to be written down.
[warm] A face, a flower, a fence.

[warm and friendly] Felix drew a face and folded the paper down the middle. The two halves matched. Then he drew a flower from above, and no fold worked. It matched all the way around its center instead. His teacher said he had found two of the three kinds of balance by accident.

[warm and friendly] A face is symmetrical: the same on both sides of a line. It feels calm, like the front of a cathedral. A flower seen from above is radial: everything spreads from a center, like a wheel.

[warm and friendly] The third kind took a tree. Felix drew a big, quiet tree on the left side of a page and a small, bright red bird on the right. Different things, but the page felt even. That is asymmetrical balance, and it feels alive.

[warm and friendly] Then he drew the garden fence. Picket, picket, picket: a shape repeated with a rule, which is pattern. He painted every fourth picket red, and the fence had a beat. Pattern with a beat is rhythm, the same word musicians use.

[warm and friendly] Last, he painted one picket bright yellow in the middle of the fence. Everyone who looked at the drawing looked there first. Change one thing in a pattern and the eye goes straight to it. That is emphasis, made out of almost nothing.
[warm and friendly] Balance is how a picture stands still. Rhythm is how it moves.
[warm and friendly] Balance can be symmetrical, radial or asymmetrical. Pattern is repetition with a rule, and rhythm is pattern with a beat. A face, a flower and a fence hold it all.
[warm] The road into the distance.

[warm and friendly] Clara drew a road, and it lay flat on the page like a ribbon. She wanted it to go somewhere. Her teacher said a page has no depth, so depth has to be faked, and there were four fakes and one ruler.
[warm and friendly] Overlap: the near tree covers part of the far one, so the far one must be behind. It is the simplest trick, and the strongest. Clara tried it with two trees.

[warm and friendly] Size: the near tree is drawn bigger, and the far tree smaller. Placement: the far tree sits higher on the page. Detail: the near tree has every leaf, and the far one is a pale green smudge.

[warm and friendly] Then the ruler. Clara drew a horizon line where the sky met the ground. She picked one point on it, the vanishing point. The road's two edges ran toward that point until they met, and every fence post and rooftop leaned toward it too.
[warm and friendly] The road left the page. It went somewhere now, over a hill and out of sight, and Clara wanted to walk it.

[warm and friendly] Her teacher pointed at the gaps between the trees. The trees were positive space, the shapes of the things. The gaps were negative space, the shapes around them. Artists plan the empty parts as carefully as the full ones.
[warm and friendly] Overlap, size, placement and detail make a flat page look deep. Perspective lines everything up to a vanishing point on the horizon. Depth is a trick, and the trick has rules.
[warm] The handprint.

[warm and friendly] On the cave tour, Theo saw a red hand on the wall, outlined in paint that someone had blown around their fingers more than twenty-five thousand years ago. Before writing. Before farms. Theo asked why anyone would do that.

[warm and friendly] Nobody knows for certain, the guide said, and that was the beginning of a long answer. People made art before they wrote a single word, and every culture since has made it, never for only one reason.
[warm and friendly] Some art records. Painted animals running across a cave ceiling may show the animals people knew and hunted.
[warm and friendly] Some art honors: a carving of a queen, a statue of a leader, a painting for someone who died. Some art teaches: a church window full of stories for people who could not read.
[warm and friendly] Some art decorates: a pot with a pattern, because plain was not enough. And some art questions: a painting that made a whole city argue about what was fair.

[warm and friendly] Theo asked about masks. The guide said one mask might hide a face at a festival, another might hold an ancestor's spirit, and another might hang on a wall as a portrait. Same object, three meanings. So always ask who made a thing, when and for whom.

[warm and friendly] Art records, honors, teaches, decorates and questions. The hand on the wall might have been any of those. It might have simply meant, I was here. It is one of the oldest messages we have, and it still reads.
[warm] Chloe draws the road home.

[warm and friendly] Chloe was nine and could not make the road home look like a road. It sat on the page like a ribbon, flat and the same width all the way up. She had drawn it five times, and five times it looked like something lying on the paper instead of going into it.

[warm and friendly] Her teacher drew a dot on the horizon and said everything runs to it. The road wide at the bottom, thin at the top. The near tree big and detailed, the far tree small and plain. Overlap, size, placement, detail. The page was suddenly deep enough to walk into.

[warm and friendly] That dot is called a vanishing point, her teacher said, and painters in Italy worked out its rules about six hundred years ago. Before that, many pictures stacked things up the page to show distance. After it, a flat wall could look like a window. It was one of the biggest ideas in the history of art, and it fit on a single dot.

[warm and friendly] The next lesson was balance. Her own face was symmetrical, nearly the same on both sides. A flower spread from the middle: radial balance. The fence along the road was a pattern, a post, a post, a post. She had been drawing all three for years without knowing they had names.

[warm and friendly] Knowing the names made her choose them on purpose. She gave the farmhouse at the end of the road two matching windows, symmetry, and a round flower bed by the door, radial. The fence posts marched toward the vanishing point, each one a little smaller than the last.

[warm and friendly] Color came next. Her teacher showed her that far-off hills look paler and bluer than near ones, because there is more air between you and them. Artists call it atmospheric perspective. Chloe painted the near field a strong green and the far hills a soft blue-gray, and the distance deepened again.

[warm and friendly] The last lesson was the oldest pictures in the world: hands on cave walls. At a cave in France, people painted spotted horses and outlined their own hands beside them more than twenty thousand years ago, a story told with no words long before writing.

[warm and friendly] Chloe put her own hand on the road drawing and traced it. Art tells a story, her teacher had said. Hers was about the way home, the near tree and the far hill and the point where the road disappeared, and the hand said who had walked it. She signed it small in the corner, the way the painters did.
[warm] Two prices.

[warm and friendly] Marcus wanted a cupcake for two dollars fifty and a cookie for one dollar thirty-five. He added the numbers the way they looked on the sign, digits pushed together, and got a total that made the girl at the table laugh. It was more than a pizza.

[warm and friendly] He tried again in his head and got a different number. The line behind him was growing and his coins were sweating in his hand. Numbers with a dot in them seemed to have their own rules.

[warm and friendly] The girl wrote the two prices one above the other and lined up the dots. Cents under cents, dollars under dollars. Then she added column by column, just like whole numbers, and the dot stayed where the dots were. Three dollars eighty-five.

[warm and friendly] Marcus paid with a five-dollar bill, and now the change was his problem. He wrote 5 as 5.00, because a whole number has a hidden decimal point at its end, and zeros can fill the empty places without changing anything. Five dollars minus three eighty-five, cents under cents: one dollar fifteen.

[warm and friendly] He checked it the fast way before he walked off. Two fifty is about two and a half, one thirty-five is about one and a half, and together they make about four. Three eighty-five is close to four, so the answer made sense. An estimate cannot give the exact answer, but it catches a silly one.

[warm and friendly] Decimals are money, and money lines up. Put the decimal points under each other, add or subtract each column, and carry the point straight down. Every other rule you know for whole numbers still works.
[warm] Half of a half.

[warm and friendly] There was half a pizza left in the box, and Priya was allowed half of it. She ate her share and felt cheated. It was one slice. Half of something should be big, she thought, and this was small.

[warm and friendly] She tried to write what she had eaten. Half of a half. A half times a half? That gave her one over four, which was a quarter, and a quarter was smaller than either half she had started with. How could multiplying make something smaller?

[warm and friendly] Because of meant multiply, and she was multiplying by a fraction. Half of a whole pizza is big. Half of half a pizza is a quarter, and the box agreed: two cuts, four pieces, one in her hand. Tops times tops, bottoms times bottoms, one over four.

[warm and friendly] Her mother was baking and wanted two thirds of a recipe that called for three quarters of a cup of flour. Priya tried the rule. Two times three is six, three times four is twelve: six twelfths. Simplified, that is one half. Half a cup, less than the recipe asked, which made sense, because she was making less.

[warm and friendly] Then she tried a whole number. Three friends each ate a quarter of a pizza. A whole number is itself over one, so three over one times one over four is three over four. Three quarters of a pizza, gone.

[warm and friendly] When you multiply by a fraction, you take a part of something, and a part is smaller. Tops times tops, bottoms times bottoms, then simplify if you can. And when a problem says of, it is telling you to multiply.
[warm] Cartons of 24.

[warm and friendly] Owen had 288 eggs and cartons that held 24. His aunt wanted to know how many cartons to order. Owen started filling cartons by hand to count them and gave up around the fourth one. There had to be a faster way.

[warm and friendly] Dividing by a number like 4 was easy. Dividing by 24 felt impossible. Twenty-four was too big to see how many times it fit into anything, and there were far too many eggs to count one by one.

[warm and friendly] So he guessed. Ten cartons would hold 240 eggs. That left 48. Two more cartons would hold exactly 48. Ten and two: twelve cartons. He checked it backward, twelve times twenty-four is 288, and the answer stood.

[warm and friendly] The next week there were 300 eggs. Owen guessed with rounder numbers: 24 is close to 25, and four 25s make 100, so 300 would need about twelve cartons. Twelve cartons held 288, and 12 eggs were left over. A remainder.

[warm and friendly] The remainder changed the answer. Twelve eggs would not fit in twelve full cartons, so his aunt needed thirteen, and the last one was half full. Division gives a number, and the question decides what to do with what is left. His aunt said that was the most useful thing he had learned all week.

[warm and friendly] Dividing by a two-digit number is guessing well. Estimate how many times the divisor fits, take that much away, bring down what is left and estimate again. Then multiply your answer back and see if it lands.
[warm] Sugar cubes.

[warm and friendly] Lena's job was to count the sugar cubes in the box before the party. She lifted them out one at a time and lost count at nineteen. Then she put them back and lost count again. The cubes were sticky and the party was in an hour.

[warm and friendly] Her grandmother asked how many were in one layer. Lena looked at the top: four across, three deep. Twelve. And how many layers? She looked at the side. Two. She still did not see how that helped.

[warm and friendly] Twelve cubes in a layer, two layers. Twelve twice is twenty-four. She had counted the whole box in two looks. The length times the width gave one layer, and the height told her how many layers to stack.

[warm and friendly] At the party her grandmother brought out a bigger box. Five across, four deep, three layers. Lena did not lift a single cube. Five times four is twenty in a layer, and three layers of twenty is sixty.

[warm and friendly] Her grandmother said scientists count the same way, with tiny cubes one centimeter on each side. A box that holds sixty of them has a volume of sixty cubic centimeters. The cube is the unit, and the answer counts how many would fit.

[warm and friendly] The volume of a box is length times width times height, and the reason is the sugar cubes. Picture one layer, then count the layers. Every box, tank and room is filled the same way, one layer at a time.
[warm] Three east, two north.

[warm and friendly] The treasure map said the prize was at 3, 2 and nothing else. Jamal stood at the start of a park laid out in straight paths and had no idea what the two numbers wanted from him. Three what? Two what?

[warm and friendly] He tried walking two paths and then three and found himself at a bench with nothing under it. He tried three and then two in every direction and found another bench. The map was either broken or he was.

[warm and friendly] His sister took the map. Across first, then up, she said. Three blocks east along the bottom, then two blocks north. The corner she reached had a small stone with an X on it. Two numbers, one point, and the order was the whole secret.

[warm and friendly] The map had a second clue: 0, 4. Jamal laughed. Zero across meant no walking east at all. He walked four blocks straight north from the start and found a flag on a lamppost. The start of the park, where both numbers are zero, is called the origin.

[warm and friendly] His sister wrote the pairs the way mathematicians do, in parentheses with a comma: (3, 2) and (0, 4). The first number goes along the x-axis, across the bottom. The second goes up the y-axis. Every point on the plane has exactly one address.

[warm and friendly] The coordinate plane works exactly like that park. The first number says how far across, the second says how far up, and swapping them lands you somewhere else. Two numbers, one point, always across first.
[warm] The package.

[warm and friendly] Two friends solved 3 + 4 × 2 and got two answers. Sam added first and got fourteen. Eli multiplied first and got eleven. They argued until the teacher came over, and each was sure the other had broken something.
[warm and friendly] Sam said you read left to right, like a sentence. That seemed fair. Eli said multiplying came first. That seemed like a rule someone had made up. Who decided?

[warm and friendly] The teacher drew a box around the 4 × 2. Think of it as a package, she said. It arrives already wrapped. Multiplication and division are packages, so their answer, eight, is ready before any adding starts. Then add the three. Eleven. If you want to add first, you need parentheses to say so.

[warm and friendly] Sam got his fourteen back, with parentheses. (3 + 4) × 2 means add first, because the parentheses say so: seven, then fourteen. Both boys had been right about something. Sam had been right about the answer to a different question.

[warm and friendly] The teacher wrote one more: 12 ÷ 3 × 2. Division and multiplication are equal partners, she said, so go left to right. Twelve divided by three is four, and four times two is eight. Doing the multiplying first would give two, and two is wrong.

[warm and friendly] Parentheses first, then multiply and divide from left to right, then add and subtract from left to right. It is a rule everyone agreed to so that a math sentence means one thing everywhere, and the package is how to remember it.
[warm] The dimes.

[warm and friendly] Maya multiplied five dollars by a tenth and got fifty cents. She was certain something had gone wrong. Multiplying was supposed to make things bigger, and fifty cents was much smaller than five dollars.
[warm and friendly] She did it again and got fifty cents again. She tried it on the calculator and it said 0.5. The machine was on the other side. She stared at the dot as if it might move.

[warm and friendly] Then she thought about dimes. A tenth of a dollar is a dime. Five dollars, a tenth each: five dimes. Fifty cents. The answer was smaller because a tenth of something is smaller than the thing. Multiply the digits as whole numbers, five times one is five, then give the answer as many decimal places as the question had.

[warm and friendly] Her teacher gave her a harder one: 0.5 times 0.4. Five times four is twenty, and the question had two decimal places, one in each number, so the answer needs two: 0.20. Half of four tenths is two tenths, the same thing.

[warm and friendly] Then one that grew: 2.5 times 3. Twenty-five times three is seventy-five, one decimal place, 7.5. Maya checked it with money: three people each paying two dollars fifty spend seven dollars fifty. Times a number bigger than one, the answer grows. Times a number smaller than one, it shrinks.

[warm and friendly] Multiplying by a decimal less than one makes a number smaller, and that is correct, not broken. Multiply the digits, then count the decimal places in the question and put that many in the answer. The dimes never lie.
[warm] Ten beans.

[warm and friendly] Rosa grew ten bean sprouts for the science fair and measured each one. Four centimeters, four, three, four, five, four, seven, three, four, five. She wrote the ten numbers in a row and stared at them. They told her nothing.

[warm and friendly] Her teacher asked which height was most common and which sprout was the odd one. Rosa started counting the fours on her fingers and lost track. Ten numbers was enough to get lost in.

[warm and friendly] So she drew a line, numbered it, and put one dot above each measurement. The dots stacked. The pile at four was tallest by far, five dots high. And one lonely dot sat above seven, the surprise sprout that had beaten everyone. She could see the whole experiment in one look.

[warm and friendly] Her teacher showed her what else the dots could say. The most common height, the mode, was four. The range, tallest minus shortest, was seven minus three: four centimeters. Lined up from shortest to tallest, the middle fell between the fifth and sixth sprouts, and both were four.

[warm and friendly] The seven made her curious. That cup sat closest to the window and got the most sun. A line plot cannot say why a dot is alone. It shows you where to look, and then you go and look.

[warm and friendly] A line plot stacks one dot per measurement, so the common answer piles up and the odd one stands alone. A line graph is different: it joins points to show how one thing changes over time. Pick the picture that matches the question.
[warm] The bake sale.

[warm and friendly] The bake sale needed a table, a cash box and a price list, and the price list was where the decimals lived. Brownies were 1.25, lemonade 0.75. A brownie and a lemonade: line up the points, add the cents, add the dollars, 2.00. The first customer paid with a five, and the change was decimals in reverse: 5.00 minus 2.00, three dollars back.

[warm and friendly] Six lemonades for one family meant multiplying a decimal: six times 75 cents. Six times 75 is 450, and the price had two decimal places, so the answer did too: 4.50. Four dollars fifty, which the family's youngest checked by counting out eighteen quarters.

[warm and friendly] The brownies came from a recipe that made a tray, and half the tray had been eaten by breakfast. Half of what was left went to the sale: half of a half, a quarter of the tray. Multiplying by a fraction had made the brownies fewer, which is exactly what fractions do.

[warm and friendly] The cookies came in boxes of 24, and 288 cookies had been baked: how many boxes? Ten boxes used 240, two more used the 48, twelve boxes on the table. Checked backward, twelve times twenty-four was 288, and nobody had to count a single cookie twice.

[warm and friendly] The table sat on a grid painted on the gym floor, and the lemonade stand was three across and two up from the corner, the point (3, 2). The cash box was a box: four cookies long, three wide, two layers high, room for twenty-four cookies.

[warm and friendly] Every hour someone made dots on a line plot for the brownies sold: eight, ten, eleven, nine. The tallest stack showed the busiest hour was the third, just after lunch, and next year the brownies would be ready for it. A line plot does not tell you why. It tells you where to look.

[warm and friendly] Thirty-eight brownies sold at 1.25 each came to 47.50. At the end, the total came from a long sum with parentheses in it, and the parentheses went first: 38 times 1.25, then the lemonade, then the cookies. The sale had made 143 dollars and 50 cents.

[warm and friendly] Decimals, fractions, division, a grid, a box, a line plot and parentheses. Nobody at the table would have called it a math test, but every number on it was one. The class counted the money twice anyway, on two sheets of paper side by side, and both said the same thing. That was the best part.
[warm] What it was really about.

[warm and friendly] The reading test asked what the story was about, and Kai wrote two friends. He was proud of that answer. The story was about two friends who fought and made up. What else could it be about?

[warm and friendly] His teacher marked it half right. Half. He had named exactly who was in the story. He went back and read it a third time, looking for the half he had missed, and found only the same two friends.

[warm and friendly] Then she asked a different question. Not who is in it, but what does it say? The friends fought, said awful things, and were still friends by the last page. The story was saying that a real friendship can survive a fight. That was the theme, the thing the story said about life. The friends were only the topic.

[warm and friendly] Kai tried again with the next story, about a girl who lied to win a race and then could not enjoy the medal. He wrote honesty. His teacher said honesty was still only a topic, one word. A theme is a whole sentence: winning by cheating takes the joy out of winning.

[warm and friendly] Later Kai noticed that two very different books, one about a soldier and one about a dog, said the same thing: loyalty costs something. Different topics, one theme. The theme was the part that could travel from book to book.

[warm and friendly] Every story has both. The topic is what it is about: two friends, a dog, a war. The theme is what it says about being alive, and you find it by looking at what changed by the end. Name the topic, then ask what the story wanted you to know.
[warm] Two cameras.

[warm and friendly] Ana had to write about the afternoon the storm came, and she wrote it two ways by accident. In the first draft she wrote, I saw the storm coming. In the second she wrote, she saw the storm coming. Her teacher said both were fine and they were completely different.

[warm and friendly] How could the same afternoon be different depending on one word? The storm was the storm. The window was the window. Ana read both drafts aloud and could feel the difference but could not name it.

[warm and friendly] Her teacher explained with cameras. When you write I, the camera is on your head. The reader sees only what you see and feels what you feel. That is first person. When you write she, the camera is on a tripod in the corner. The reader can see the whole room, including you. That is third person.

[warm and friendly] Then her teacher showed a third camera, a rare one. You see the storm coming. That is second person, and it puts the reader inside the story as the one doing things. Directions and some games use it, but most stories do not.

[warm and friendly] Third person has two kinds of tripod too. One can only see inside one character's head. The other can see inside everyone, knowing what each person thinks. Ana rewrote the storm from that all-knowing corner and found out her little brother had been scared the whole time.

[warm and friendly] I and we mean first person. He, she and they mean third person. The point of view decides what the narrator can know and what the reader gets to see, so choose the camera before you choose the words.
[warm] Break a leg.

[warm and friendly] Right before Theo went on stage for the school play, his friend Maya grabbed his arm and said, break a leg. He froze. He had known Maya since kindergarten and she had never wished him harm before.

[warm and friendly] He spent the first scene worrying about his legs. Had she cursed him? Was there a loose board? By the second scene he had said all his lines without falling, and Maya was grinning at him from the wings.

[warm and friendly] Afterward she explained. Break a leg means good luck in the theater. Nobody breaks anything. It is an idiom, a phrase whose meaning is not in its words at all. You cannot work it out. You learn it by meeting it, the way you learn a nickname.

[warm and friendly] Theo started collecting them. His grandmother said he had his head in the clouds when he forgot his lunch. His coach said the test would be a piece of cake. His dad told him to hold his horses when he rushed. None of it was about clouds, cake or horses.

[warm and friendly] Maya said other languages have their own. In Spanish, estar en las nubes, to be in the clouds, also means daydreaming. But many idioms do not travel. Translate break a leg word for word into another language and the actor might really worry.

[warm and friendly] Raining cats and dogs. Piece of cake. Hit the hay. Every language is full of idioms, and each one means something its words do not say. When a phrase makes no sense taken literally, ask what it means to the people who use it.
[warm] Point to the line.

[warm and friendly] In the book club, Priya said the boy in the story was scared. Marcus said he was not, he was just tired. They argued for five minutes and got nowhere, because each was sure and neither had anything but being sure.
[warm and friendly] The teacher asked one question. Where? Priya said, in the middle somewhere. Marcus said, you can just tell. The teacher waited. Being sure, it turned out, did not count.

[warm and friendly] Priya opened the book and hunted. Page twelve: his hands shook as he reached for the door. There it was. Not a feeling about the boy but a line the author had written, and it showed fear more directly than any other line in the chapter. Marcus read it and gave in.

[warm and friendly] Then Marcus found his own line on page fifteen: he yawned twice at dinner. Tired had evidence too. The teacher smiled. A story can hold more than one truth. The boy was scared at the door and tired by dinner, and both claims now stood on something.

[warm and friendly] The last step was to explain. Priya wrote her claim and the line in quotation marks with its page number. Then she added one sentence saying how the line proved it: shaking hands are what fear does to a body. Claim, evidence, explanation.

[warm and friendly] A claim about a text needs a line from the text behind it. Point to the page. Pick the line that shows the claim most directly, not the one that sort of hints at it. Evidence is what turns being sure into being right.
[warm] Two storms.

[warm and friendly] Owen read two things about the same storm. A poem said the sky broke open and the street became a river. The newspaper said two inches of rain fell in one hour. He decided one of them was lying.

[warm and friendly] Which one? He had been in the storm. The street had felt like a river. But two inches did not sound like much, and nobody had seen the sky break. He could not make the two texts agree.

[warm and friendly] His mother said they did not have to. The poem was telling how the storm felt. The newspaper was telling what the storm measured. Both were true, and side by side they were the whole storm: the feeling and the facts. What they shared was the event. How they differed was the job each one was doing.

[warm and friendly] Owen wanted proof anyway, so he found a third source: the rain gauge in his own backyard. It held just over two inches. The newspaper had measured right. And the photo on the newspaper's front page showed a car up to its doors in water, which the poem had said first.

[warm and friendly] His mother asked why each writer wrote. The reporter wanted readers to know what happened, so every sentence carried a number, a time or a place. The poet wanted readers to feel the storm, so every line reached for a picture. The purpose shaped the words.

[warm and friendly] To compare two texts, ask what they share, how they differ, and what the difference shows. When they seem to disagree, a third source often settles it. Two texts on one subject are not a contest. They are two windows on the same room.
[warm] The cousin.

[warm and friendly] A letter to the school newspaper said classes should start later. Lena agreed before she finished the first line. Then she got to the reason. The writer's cousin went to a school that started later and liked it.

[warm and friendly] Lena wanted the letter to be right. But she could hear her teacher's voice asking, and how many cousins is that? One. One cousin, who liked something. Was that enough to change the whole school's day?

[warm and friendly] It was not. A claim is held up by reasons, and reasons are held up by evidence. One cousin's opinion is a story, not evidence. Sitting on the desk next to the letter was a study of two thousand students who slept more and did better when school started later. That was evidence. The writer had never opened it.

[warm and friendly] Lena opened the study herself. It said who was studied, how many, and for how long, and it compared schools that started earlier with schools that started later. Good evidence tells you where it came from, so you can check it.

[warm and friendly] She wrote her own letter back. She agreed with the claim, added the study as her evidence, and answered the strongest reason against it: buses would have to change their routes. An argument that answers the other side is harder to knock down.

[warm and friendly] When you read an argument, find the claim, then the reasons, then ask what holds each reason up. Without evidence, an argument is only an opinion with good posture. With it, even a short letter can change a school.
[warm] The play.

[warm and friendly] The class was putting on a play about two friends who fight over a bicycle and make up. The topic was two friends. The theme, which took a week of rehearsal to find, was that friendship survives a fight. The topic was two words; the theme was a sentence.

[warm and friendly] The play had come from a short book, and the class read both. The book spent three pages inside the younger friend's head. The play had no room for that, so it showed her feelings in what she did: she walked past the bicycle twice without looking at it. Same story, two different jobs.

[warm and friendly] The script was in first person for one scene, the narrator saying I, and the audience only knew what she knew. Then the camera moved to the corner: third person, she and he, and suddenly the audience could see the bicycle hidden behind the shed that neither friend could. That was the whole trick of the play.

[warm and friendly] One line said the older friend had cold feet. A first grader in the front row asked why nobody brought him socks. An idiom, said the narrator, not skipping a beat. It means he was nervous. The audience laughed, and the first grader learned a new phrase.

[warm and friendly] When a parent asked afterward how they knew the ending was happy, the cast pointed to the last line. The two friends ride off on the bicycle together, one pedaling and one on the handlebars. A claim about a story needs a line behind it, and that line was the evidence.

[warm and friendly] The week before, someone had written to the principal asking to cancel the play because it took time from math. The class read the letter the way they had learned. The claim was clear. The reason was time. The evidence was missing: no numbers, no schedule, nothing anyone could check.

[warm and friendly] So the class wrote back, and this time the evidence was there: rehearsals had happened at lunch, and not a minute of math had been lost. The principal read both letters and let the play go on. An argument with evidence beat one without. The class pinned both letters to the bulletin board, side by side.

[warm and friendly] After the last bow, the teacher said the play had used every skill of the year: theme, point of view, idioms, evidence, comparing two versions and weighing an argument. The first grader in the front row said it was a good play. That was also true.
[warm] Two glasses.

[warm and friendly] Theo stirred a spoon of sand into one glass of water and a spoon of salt into the other. The sand swirled, then sank. The salt swirled, then was gone. Same spoon, same water, and one of them had disappeared.

[warm and friendly] Where did the salt go? He looked from the side and from the top. Nothing. He was ready to say it had stopped existing until he took a sip and pulled a face. It was in there, all right, in every drop.

[warm and friendly] The sand had made a mixture. Each part kept its own properties, and he could pour the water off and leave the sand behind. The salt had made a solution, a special mixture where one part dissolves so completely into the other that you cannot pick it out, though you can still taste it.

[warm and friendly] His sister showed him how to get the salt back. She poured some of the salty water into a shallow dish and set it on a sunny windowsill. Three days later the water was gone and a crust of white crystals was left. Evaporation had pulled the solution apart.

[warm and friendly] Theo kept adding salt to a fresh glass to see how much would vanish. Spoon after spoon disappeared, until one spoonful sat on the bottom and stayed. The water could hold no more. Warm water, his sister said, would have held a little more before it stopped.

[warm and friendly] A mixture keeps the properties of its parts and can be separated. A solution is a mixture where one part dissolves and spreads evenly through the other. Sand and salt look alike in the spoon and behave nothing alike in the glass.
[warm] Top, lamp, marble.

[warm and friendly] Ava could not keep the three things straight. A day, a month, a year. They were all just time, and the sky did not come with labels. Her dad cleared the kitchen table and turned off every light but one.

[warm and friendly] He set a spinning top near the lamp. Which side of the top is lit? The side facing the lamp. Now watch the top spin. Every side gets its turn in the light and its turn in the dark. Ava said, day and night. He nodded. One spin, one day.

[warm and friendly] Then he carried the spinning top in a slow circle around the lamp. One lap, one year. Then he rolled a marble in a small ring around the top. One ring, about one month, and the marble was the moon. Three motions, three clocks.

[warm and friendly] Then her dad crouched to the height of the top and asked her to watch the marble. As it went around, Ava saw its lit side full, then half, then a thin sliver, then dark. The marble never changed shape. She was seeing different amounts of its sunny half. Those are the phases of the moon.

[warm and friendly] There was one more trick. As the marble circled, her dad turned it slowly so the same painted dot always faced the top. The real moon does that too, spinning once for every trip around Earth, which is why we always see the same face.
[warm and friendly] The Earth spins for day and night, circles the sun for the year, and the moon circles the Earth for the month. Once you have seen it on a table, you never lose it in the sky.
[warm] The lake that would not stay.
[warm and friendly] Chloe had decided to paint the lake once a day for a year. Same spot, same hour, sunrise. She wanted to see if a place could hold still.

[warm and friendly] It could not. In July the shore crept out and the rocks showed. In October the lake climbed back and swallowed them. On cold mornings a white mist rose off the water like the lake was leaving.

[warm and friendly] It was leaving. That mist was the lake, evaporating, becoming air. It rose, cooled, and gathered into cloud. The cloud drifted over the hills and fell as rain into the streams that ran back into the lake. What Chloe thought was one still thing was a loop she was standing inside.

[warm and friendly] On the coldest mornings the grass by her easel was wet though it had not rained. Water vapor in the air had touched the cold grass and turned back into drops: condensation, the same step that builds a cloud. In February the rain came down as snow, and in March the snow melted and ran back to the lake.

[warm and friendly] Some rain never reached the lake by the streams. It soaked into the ground and moved slowly through the soil and rock underneath, feeding the springs that bubbled up by the shore. Trees drank it too, and breathed some of it back out through their leaves.
[warm and friendly] Her three hundred and sixty five paintings were not one lake. They were the same water, caught at different points on its journey.
[warm and friendly] The water in your glass has been a cloud, a river, and a lake, and it will be again. Nothing is used up. It only moves.
[warm] Eyes and wheels.

[warm and friendly] Diego's homework asked which of his traits were inherited and which were learned. He had brown eyes, like his dad. He could ride a bike, like his dad. Both came from his dad, he figured, so both were inherited.

[warm and friendly] His dad laughed and asked how the bike riding had gone at first. Diego remembered. Twenty falls, two scraped knees, one bent pedal. His dad had not handed him the skill. He had handed him the bike.

[warm and friendly] That was the difference. Brown eyes came from his parents before he was born, and no amount of practice could change them. That is inherited. Riding came from falling twenty times and getting up twenty-one. That is learned. The question that sorts them is simple: could this have been practiced?

[warm and friendly] Diego tried the question on animals. A spider spins its first web without ever seeing one, so that behavior is inherited; scientists call it instinct. His neighbor's dog sits when told, but only because someone taught it with a hundred treats. That is learned.

[warm and friendly] Some things mix both. Height is mostly inherited, but good food helps a body reach it. Diego inherited long legs from his mom, but how fast he runs also depends on how much he practices. The legs came first. The speed came from the track.

[warm and friendly] Inherited traits come from parents. Learned traits come from practice and experience. Every living thing has both, and the way to tell them apart is to ask whether it could have been learned at all.
[warm] The rope that did not move.

[warm and friendly] Two teams pulled on the rope with everything they had, and the flag in the middle did not move an inch. Faces were red. Shoes were digging into the grass. Kai, watching from the side, thought nobody was pulling at all. How could that much effort add up to nothing?

[warm and friendly] The coach asked him the same thing. Both teams were pulling hard, so why did the flag stay put? Kai said maybe the rope was stuck. The coach shook his head and pointed at the small girl beside Kai.

[warm and friendly] She walked over and grabbed the end of one team's rope. The flag slid across the line and the other team stumbled forward. Two equal pulls had canceled out, balanced, and the flag had no reason to move. One more pull tipped the balance, and the motion changed.

[warm and friendly] The coach added one more idea. Why did both teams dig their shoes into the grass? Friction, the force that grips where two surfaces rub. On a wet floor in socks, both teams would have slid, pulled along by the rope instead of holding against it.

[warm and friendly] Then he rolled two carts across the field, one empty and one full of water jugs, and pushed each just as hard. The empty cart shot away. The full one crept. The same push moves a lighter thing more. Gravity was pulling on both the whole time, holding them to the ground.

[warm and friendly] A force is a push or a pull that changes motion. Balanced forces cancel and nothing changes. Unbalanced forces make things start, stop, speed up or turn. The flag was never stuck. It was perfectly balanced, until it was not.
[warm] The shell on the mountain.

[warm and friendly] Two thousand feet up a mountain trail, Nadia found a seashell pressed into the rock. A seashell. She checked the map in case the sea was nearby. The nearest ocean was three hundred miles away.

[warm and friendly] Had somebody carried it up and dropped it? It was inside the rock, not on it. Had the sea once come up this high? That was a lot of water. Her uncle told her the shell had never moved. The rock had.

[warm and friendly] The rock was made of layers, like pages in a book, each one laid down as mud and sand on an old sea floor. The shell had settled into one of those layers when this place was under water. Then, over millions of years, the land rose, and the sea floor became a mountain with the shell still in it. Deeper layers were older; the shell's layer said the place had once been a shallow sea.

[warm and friendly] Her uncle said fossils come in more than one kind. Some are the hard part itself, turned to stone. Some are only a print, like a leaf pressed into mud that hardened. Some are tracks, the footprints of an animal that walked across soft ground and left.

[warm and friendly] Coal was made in a similar way, he said, from swamp plants buried in layers and squeezed for millions of years. The energy in it first came from sunlight those plants caught long ago. That is why coal is called a fossil fuel.

[warm and friendly] Fossils are traces kept in layered rock. The deeper the layer, the older it is, and every fossil says what its place was like when it formed. A shell on a mountain is not a mystery. It is a page from the mountain's own book.
[warm] The trip to the lake.

[warm and friendly] The lake trip started with lemonade. Sugar in water: it vanished, but the drink was sweet. Sand from the shore in the bucket: it sank and could be poured off. A solution and a mixture, before the tent was even up. A cup left in the sun dried to a sticky ring, the sugar staying behind when the water left.

[warm and friendly] That night the moon came up over the water, and the youngest wanted to know why it changed shape. A ball, a flashlight, a slow walk around the campfire: the moon circles the Earth, and we see its lit side from different angles. It was full that night, the oldest said, because the moon sat on the far side of Earth from the sun.

[warm and friendly] In the morning the tent was wet on the inside. Nobody had spilled anything. The night air had cooled, and the water in it had turned to drops: condensation. By noon the drops were gone again, up into the air, and the clouds building over the far hills were the same water on its way back. The lake was one stop on a loop that never ends.

[warm and friendly] After lunch they took the canoe out. Paddling on one side only sent the canoe in a slow circle, and paddling on both sides together sent it straight. Every stroke pushed water back, and the water pushed the canoe forward. When everyone stopped, the canoe slowed and drifted still, the water dragging against the hull until the push was used up.

[warm and friendly] On the far shore the rocks lay in flat layers, like a stack of books on its side. In one of them the youngest found a tiny shell pressed into the stone. A fossil, which meant this ground had once been under water. The layers below it were older still.

[warm and friendly] That evening the cousins skipped stones. The trick was a flat stone thrown low and fast with a spin, so it bounced instead of sinking. Nobody was born knowing it. Every cousin learned it that afternoon, one sunk stone at a time.

[warm and friendly] On the last day the cousins compared: two had brown eyes like their fathers, inherited; all of them could now skip a stone, learned. The drive home passed a field of sunflowers turned toward the sun, and the youngest, who had been paying attention, said that was inherited too. Nobody argued.

[warm and friendly] Back home, the youngest made a list of everything the lake had taught. A solution and a mixture. The moon. The loop of water. A push and a drag. A shell in stone. And the difference between what you are born with and what you practice. It was a longer list than the one for school, and nobody had assigned it.
[warm] The tour.

[warm and friendly] New families were coming to see the school, and Diego was asked to write a guide. He wrote everything he knew in one long paragraph: the gym, the library, the lunch line, the garden, the smell of the art room. His teacher read it and said she felt lost.

[warm and friendly] Lost? It was all there. He had not left anything out. But when he read it back, he could not find the library either. It was buried between the lunch line and the garden with nothing to mark the door.

[warm and friendly] So he wrote it like a tour. An introduction that said what the school was: the entrance. One paragraph for the gym, one for the library, one for the garden: the rooms, each with its own idea and its own details. A conclusion that invited them to visit: the exit. Now a reader could walk through it.

[warm and friendly] Then he added signs. A heading over each paragraph, like the names over real doors: The Gym, The Library, The Garden. A small map with the rooms labeled. A caption under his photo of the garden. Readers who skimmed could still find their way.

[warm and friendly] His teacher crossed out one sentence: the library is the best room. Informational writing gives facts, she said, and best is an opinion. He changed it to something a reader could check: the library has four thousand books and a reading corner by the window.

[warm and friendly] An informational piece is a building. Introduction with the topic, a paragraph for each part, a conclusion at the end. Each paragraph holds one idea and the details that belong to it. Write it like a tour and nobody gets lost.
[warm] Five paragraphs.

[warm and friendly] Rosa had one paragraph about why the class should have a pet, and it was a good one. Her teacher asked for five. Rosa thought that meant saying the same thing five times, and her second paragraph was the first one in different words.
[warm and friendly] By the third she had run out of ways to say it. The essay was getting longer and emptier at the same time, like a balloon. There had to be a reason for five.

[warm and friendly] There was. Paragraph one: the opinion. Our class should have a pet. Paragraphs two, three and four: one reason each, with room to explain it. It teaches us to care. It calms the room. It is fun. Paragraph five: the opinion again, carried by the three reasons behind it. Five jobs, five paragraphs.

[warm and friendly] Her teacher said each reason needed something to stand on. It calms the room became: when the class next door got a fish tank, their teacher said the loudest part of the day got quieter. A reason with an example is harder to wave away.
