[warm and friendly] Rosa also thought about who would read it. The principal would decide, and the principal would worry about weekends. So Rosa added a sentence to her conclusion: families could sign up to take the pet home, one weekend each.

[warm and friendly] An opinion essay is an introduction with the opinion, one paragraph per reason, and a conclusion that says it again with the reasons behind it. Linking words like first, also and finally carry the reader from one to the next. Five is not more of the same. It is five different jobs.
[warm] The moment.

[warm and friendly] Sam wrote about the day he learned to ride a bike in three sentences. My dad took the training wheels off. I rode. It was fun. It was all true and it took eight seconds to read, which felt wrong for the biggest day of that summer.

[warm and friendly] His teacher asked which part had mattered most. The moment his dad let go, Sam said. She asked how long that moment had taken. About two seconds. And how many words had he given it? Two.

[warm and friendly] He wrote it again and slowed down at the right place. First the scene: a Saturday, the driveway hot, the wheels in the grass. Then the build: the wobble, his dad running beside him, the hand on the seat. Then the moment, stretched out: the hand gone, the front wheel shaking, and the second where it stopped shaking. Then what changed: he was a rider now.

[warm and friendly] His teacher pointed at one word: fun. Fun tells, she said. Show it instead. Sam crossed it out and wrote what his body did: the wind in his ears, his mouth open, a laugh that came out before he could stop it. The reader could feel the fun without being told.

[warm and friendly] Then he added the one thing his dad said, in quotation marks: You are doing it by yourself. Real words from a real person made the moment sound true. Sam kept the whole story on one page, and it took a full minute to read.

[warm and friendly] A personal narrative sets the scene, builds to the moment, and says what changed. The secret is pace. Move quickly through the ordinary parts and slow right down at the moment that mattered, so the reader lives there as long as you did.
[warm] Georgette and the class pet.

[warm and friendly] Georgette was ten and had decided the class needed a pet. She could not just ask. Her teacher said a good case is built, not wished for, so Georgette started building. She began with a question she could not answer yet: what does a class pet really need?

[warm and friendly] She wrote an informational piece first, three paragraphs on how hamsters live, with an introduction that walked the reader in and a conclusion that walked them out. Her teacher said it read like a tour of a house. That was the idea. Informational writing gives facts, not feelings.

[warm and friendly] The facts had to come from somewhere. Georgette used two sources, a library book and a page from an animal shelter, and wrote down which fact came from which. When they disagreed about how long hamsters live, she wrote down both: two to three years, said one, and up to four, said the other.

[warm and friendly] Then the opinion essay. Paragraph one: our class should have a pet. Paragraphs two, three and four: one reason each, it teaches care, it calms us, it is fun. Paragraph five: all of it again, with the reasons behind it.

[warm and friendly] Her first draft had a hamster that was very, very, very cute. Revising, she cut two of the verys and added a reason instead. Editing, she found three missing capitals and a their that should have been there. Revising changes what you say. Editing fixes how it is written.

[warm and friendly] The class voted. The hamster arrived in October and was named after a poet Georgette liked, which nobody else in the room had heard of. She wrote a care schedule for the wall: who feeds it, who cleans the cage, which family takes it home each weekend. It hung by the door all year.

[warm and friendly] The personal narrative came last, and it was about the moment the hamster escaped and she found it in her coat pocket after an hour of everyone searching. Set the scene, build to the moment, say what changed. She slowed the moment down the way her teacher showed her: the empty cage, the whole class on hands and knees, then a small warm weight moving in her pocket.

[warm and friendly] What changed was that Georgette learned she could make a room of people do something with five paragraphs. She kept every draft in a folder, the messy ones too, because the messy ones showed how the good ones were made. She never forgot it.
[warm] Three rows.

[warm and friendly] Maya had to learn thirteen colonies for a test, and thirteen felt like a lot of names to hold. She tried a song. She tried flashcards. By Thursday she could remember nine, and never the same nine.

[warm and friendly] Her grandfather looked at her map and asked what the weather was like in each place. Maya said she was studying colonies, not weather. He asked again, and she looked at where they sat along the coast.

[warm and friendly] They fell into three rows. New England up top, cold and rocky, where people fished and built ships and lived in tight towns. The Middle colonies in between, with rich soil for wheat and busy ports. The South, warm and wide, with big farms along slow rivers. Settled between 1607 and 1732 by people wanting land, faith or a fresh start, and the land told each row how to live.

[warm and friendly] Her grandfather added one more pattern. The colonists were far from the king, so they learned to govern themselves. Virginia had an elected assembly, the House of Burgesses, from 1619. New England towns held meetings where settlers argued and voted on local matters. That habit of deciding for themselves would matter later.

[warm and friendly] And not everyone came by choice. In the South especially, the big farms depended on enslaved Africans, brought by force and denied every choice the colonists prized. The three rows were shaped by weather and soil, and also by who was made to do the work.
[warm and friendly] Thirteen colonies in three regions, each with its own way of living, shaped by its own weather and soil. Learn the three rows first, and the thirteen names have somewhere to hang.
[warm] Four steps to a war.

[warm and friendly] Eli's family had a very old teapot that nobody used, and a story to go with it. In 1765 his ancestors had to pay a new tax on paper, stamps and later tea, and they had never been asked. No vote, no say, just a bill.
[warm and friendly] They grumbled and paid and grumbled more. Eli wondered why grumbling turned into a war. Plenty of people pay taxes they hate. What made these people different?

[warm and friendly] It happened in steps. In 1765, taxes with no vote. In 1773, colonists dumped tea into Boston Harbor rather than pay, and the teapot went on a shelf for good. In 1775, shots at Lexington. And on July 4, 1776, a declaration that governments exist to serve the people, and a people may change one that does not.

[warm and friendly] Eli found more steps in between. In 1770, British soldiers fired into a crowd in Boston and five colonists died, and the colonists called it a massacre. In 1774, Britain closed Boston Harbor to punish the tea party, and delegates from twelve colonies met in Philadelphia as the First Continental Congress.

[warm and friendly] The colonists had a slogan for all of it: no taxation without representation. They were not against every tax. They were against taxes voted by a Parliament across the ocean, where they had no members at all.

[warm and friendly] Taxes without a vote, then protests, then shots, then a declaration. Each step made the next one possible, and none of them was the whole story alone. A war is rarely one event. It is a staircase, and the teapot sat on the first step.
[warm] The second plan.

[warm and friendly] The country's first plan of government, the Articles of Confederation, could not even pay its own bills. Nadia could not believe it. A whole country with no way to collect money, no way to settle fights between states, no one in charge.

[warm and friendly] She asked why they did not just fix it. Her teacher said they tried, and every fix needed every state to agree, and one state always said no. The plan was so weak that even fixing it was impossible.

[warm and friendly] So in 1787, fifty-five delegates met in a hot hall and wrote a second plan. It gave the country three branches: a Congress to make laws, a President to carry them out, and courts to judge them. Each branch could stop the others, so no one branch could take over. Then a Bill of Rights was added to protect what the government could never touch.

[warm and friendly] The big states and the small states nearly broke the meeting apart. Big states wanted votes by population. Small states wanted one vote each. The answer was a compromise: two houses of Congress, the House of Representatives by population and the Senate with two senators from every state.

[warm and friendly] The plan still had to be approved. Nine of the thirteen states had to say yes, and in 1788 the ninth one did. Some states agreed only after a promise that a list of rights would be added. In 1791 the first ten amendments, the Bill of Rights, kept that promise.

[warm and friendly] The Constitution was written after the Articles failed: three branches that check each other, and a Bill of Rights added soon after. The point was never that the government would be strong. The point was that no part of it could be too strong.
[warm] Doubling the map.

[warm and friendly] In 1803 the United States bought a piece of land from France for fifteen million dollars, and the country doubled in size overnight. Priya thought that sounded like a great deal. Her teacher asked what the country planned to do with all that empty space.

[warm and friendly] Nothing, at first. Nobody lived there but the peoples who had always lived there, and few Americans knew what was in it. A map twice as big is not twice as useful if the new half is blank.

[warm and friendly] Then the blank half filled. Trails carried wagons west through the plains. In 1848 gold turned up in California, and tens of thousands rushed to it. A war with Mexico added the southwest, and railroads would later follow the trails. By 1850 the country reached the Pacific Ocean, and the map that had doubled was full to the far edge.

[warm and friendly] First came the explorers. In 1804 Lewis and Clark set out up the Missouri River with a small crew, helped along the way by guides like Sacagawea, and reached the Pacific in 1805. Their maps and notes filled in some of the blank half.

[warm and friendly] The filling had a cost. The land was never empty to the nations who lived there. As settlers moved west, the government forced many Native peoples off their homelands, including the Cherokee on the Trail of Tears in 1838. The railroad that crossed the continent in 1869 carried more settlers still.

[warm and friendly] The Louisiana Purchase doubled the country in 1803; trails, gold and war carried it to the Pacific by 1850. A country grows twice: once on paper, and once when people go and live in the lines.
[warm] The split.

[warm and friendly] In a shoebox in the attic Marcus found a letter from 1862, written by a soldier to his sister. The soldier wrote that the country had split in two and he did not know if it would ever be one again. Marcus read it three times. A country can split?

[warm and friendly] It can. Between December 1860 and June 1861, eleven southern states left the Union over slavery, which they wanted to keep and expand. The rest of the country said no. Neither side would give in, and the argument became a war.

[warm and friendly] The war lasted four years. In 1863 President Lincoln declared the enslaved people in the rebelling states free. In 1865 the South surrendered, more than six hundred thousand soldiers had died, and the 13th Amendment ended slavery everywhere in the country. The soldier's sister got her letter. The country got itself back, changed.

[warm and friendly] Marcus looked up the soldier's years. The war had begun at Fort Sumter in April 1861. In July 1863 the Union won at Gettysburg, in Pennsylvania, and that November Lincoln gave a two-minute speech there about a nation that should not perish.

[warm and friendly] Five days after the main Southern army surrendered in April 1865, Lincoln was shot at a theater in Washington, and he died the next morning. He did not live to see the 13th Amendment ratified that December, or the long work of rebuilding the South that came after.

[warm and friendly] A split over slavery, war from 1861 to 1865, emancipation in 1863, and an amendment that ended slavery for good. The letter in the shoebox is how history reaches a boy in an attic: one family at a time.
[warm] The ship in the family tree.

[warm and friendly] Rosa's great-great-grandmother came to America at nineteen with one bag, and Rosa wanted to know what was in it. Clothes, her grandmother said. A photograph. And the recipe for the bread the family still baked every Sunday.

[warm and friendly] Rosa tried to picture the trip. A ship packed with strangers, and a harbor she had only seen in books. Then Ellis Island, where they checked your eyes and your papers and let you through or sent you home. Why would anyone take that risk for a bag and a recipe?

[warm and friendly] For work, mostly. Around 1900 the cities were full of factories that needed hands, and millions came for them. They lived in tenements, one room for six people, one window, and worked long days. They also brought their food, their music and their words, and the cities grew larger and louder and more mixed than any cities had ever been.

[warm and friendly] Rosa looked it up. Ellis Island opened in 1892, and about twelve million people passed through it before it closed. On the other coast, many who crossed the Pacific came through Angel Island in San Francisco Bay, where some were held for weeks or months.

[warm and friendly] The cities strained to hold everyone. Some neighbors helped. In Chicago in 1889, Jane Addams opened Hull House, where new arrivals could learn English, leave their children in a nursery and find help getting work. The newcomers built the cities that had not been ready for them.

[warm and friendly] Around 1900 immigrants arrived through Ellis Island, worked in factories, lived in tenements and reshaped the cities. Every family that came changed the country a little, and the bread on Rosa's table is the proof that the change is still going on.
[warm] Fourteen hours.

[warm and friendly] Lena's history project was a shirt. Before machines, a skilled seamstress needed about fourteen hours of hand sewing for one fine shirt, more than a full day of work. After machines, a factory could turn out a hundred in a day. She wrote the two numbers down and did not believe them.

[warm and friendly] Fourteen hours for one, and a hundred in a day. How could anything speed up that much? And if shirts changed that fast, what else did? She started a list and it would not stop growing.

[warm and friendly] Steam engines turned the machines, so a factory no longer had to sit beside a river. The telegraph carried news across the country in seconds instead of weeks. Railroads carried the shirts, and everything else, to towns that had never seen a factory. The light bulb stretched the working day past sunset. Each invention pushed the others faster.

[warm and friendly] Machines also changed who worked, and for how long. Many factories hired children, some younger than ten, for twelve-hour days, because they were paid little and their small hands fit between the machines. It took decades of protest before laws kept young children out of factories.

[warm and friendly] The speeding up kept going. In 1913 Henry Ford set car parts moving past his workers on a line. Building one Model T dropped from about twelve hours to about an hour and a half. Every worker did one job, over and over, and the car came to them.

[warm and friendly] Factories, steam, the telegraph, the railroad and the light bulb moved work and life faster than anyone had known. A shirt in a day was not the whole story. It was the first thing people noticed in a world that had started to run.
[warm] The road from the coast.

[warm and friendly] The first of them came off a ship in 1620 and built a house on the coast, in the New England row of what became thirteen colonies. The winters were long, and half of the first settlers did not live to see spring. Their grandchildren farmed rocky fields and fished the cold water, and voted in town meetings on everything from roads to the minister's pay.

[warm and friendly] Their great-grandchildren paid a tax on tea they had no vote about, and in 1773 one of them was on a dark harbor tipping crates into the water. In 1775 the fighting started at Lexington and Concord, a day's ride away, and two of the family's sons marched.

[warm and friendly] In 1776 the family signed nothing but heard the Declaration read aloud in a market square. In 1787 they argued about the Constitution at the dinner table: a stronger plan than the first one, three branches, each able to stop the others.

[warm and friendly] In 1803 a cousin went west into the Louisiana Purchase, fifteen million dollars for land that doubled the country, and did not come back. His letters, when they came, told of rivers wider than the town and of the nations who had lived there long before him. His grandson crossed the plains in a wagon in 1849, headed for California gold.

[warm and friendly] In 1861 two brothers of the family fought on opposite sides. In 1865 the one who lived came home to a country that had ended slavery at the cost of more than six hundred thousand lives. His brother never came home; his name is carved on a stone in the town square with forty others.

[warm and friendly] The next generation went to work in the mills. A daughter ran a loom in a factory town where the machines never stopped and a whistle told everyone when to eat. Her husband laid track for the railroad that, by 1869, crossed the whole continent.

[warm and friendly] Around 1900 the family changed again. A young man from Italy came through Ellis Island with one bag, found work in the city, and married the loom worker's granddaughter. He brought a recipe and a language, and the family took both. From then on, holiday dinners were louder and better.

[warm and friendly] The house on the coast is a museum now. Visitors can walk from its door down the old road inland, the same road the family took west, to war, to the mills and back again. It runs all the way to Texas, and every mile of it is someone's story.
[warm] The scoreboard.

[warm and friendly] Ana kept score at the park with a flip board. HOME on one side, VISITORS on the other, and numbers she changed every time someone scored. Her brother said the board was a computer program with two variables.

[warm and friendly] A variable is a named box that holds a value and can change. The box called HOME held 3. When the home team scored, the box still said HOME and the value became 4. The name stayed; the number moved.

[warm and friendly] Ana saw why the name mattered. The program did not need to know the score ahead of time. It needed to know where to look. Add one to HOME, whatever HOME holds. The board could keep score for a game that had not been played yet.

[warm and friendly] Her brother showed her a second trick. TOTAL could be HOME plus VISITORS, worked out fresh every time either one changed. At 4 to 2 the total was 6. At 5 to 2 it was 7, and nobody had to count again.

[warm and friendly] He also said the names should tell you what the boxes hold. A box called X could be anything. A box called HOME could only be one thing. Math uses letters the same way: n plus 3 works for any n, the way the scoreboard works for any game.
[warm and friendly] A variable is a named box that holds a value and can change. The name stays, the value moves, and a program that uses the name works for a score it has never seen.
[warm] The thermostat that never sleeps.

[warm and friendly] Owen asked who turned the heat on at night when everyone was asleep. His father pointed at the thermostat and said it had been making the same decision every few seconds since they moved in. Nobody had touched it in weeks.
[warm and friendly] The decision was one sentence. IF the room is colder than the setting, THEN turn the heat on. ELSE, turn it off. A condition, and two roads.

[warm and friendly] That is all the thermostat knows, and it is enough. It checks, picks a road, checks again. Owen wrote the same sentence for his game: IF the player touches the star, THEN add a point, ELSE keep going. The thermostat had taught him the shape of every choice a computer makes.

[warm and friendly] His father showed him a harder choice on the sprinkler timer. IF it is six in the morning AND the ground is dry, THEN water the lawn. Both parts must be true. At six on a rainy morning, the sprinklers stay off.

[warm and friendly] Owen added one to his game. IF the player touches the star AND the timer is still running, THEN add a point. Late stars no longer counted. Before that, a player could grab a star after the clock ran out and still score. One small word, AND, had made the rule fair.
[warm and friendly] IF a condition is true THEN a step runs. ELSE is the other road. AND means both parts must be true. A program chooses the way a thermostat does: check, pick, check again.
[warm] Facing the wall.

[warm and friendly] Lena's robot was supposed to reach the flag in the corner. It drove forward, turned, drove, and stopped with its nose against the wall. Lena rewrote the whole program from scratch. It hit the wall again.

[warm and friendly] Her teacher told her to stop rewriting and start reading. One step at a time, out loud, with her finger on the line and her eye on the robot. Forward two. Good. Turn right. Good. Forward four.

[warm and friendly] Forward four was the bug. The room was three squares wide. One number, one wrong step, and everything after it had been right and useless. She changed the four to a three and the robot found the flag. Debugging was not rewriting. It was reading.

[warm and friendly] The next day a friend's robot had a different problem. It reached the corner and then turned the wrong way. Every number was right, but two steps were in the wrong order: turn, then forward, instead of forward, then turn. A bug can be a wrong value or a wrong order.

[warm and friendly] After each fix, Lena ran the whole program again, start to finish, not just the step she changed. A fix can break something that used to work. Testing again is the only way to know. Her teacher called it checking your work, the same as in math.
[warm and friendly] Debugging is reading the steps one at a time and checking each. The bug is usually one small wrong thing, and rewriting everything hides it instead of finding it.
[warm] The game that kept score.

[warm and friendly] The class built a game in a week. On Monday it had a ball and a paddle and no memory: every point was forgotten the moment it was scored. The ball bounced, the paddle moved, and nothing that happened mattered to anything that happened next.

[warm and friendly] Tuesday brought variables: a box named score, a box named lives, and the game began to remember. Score went from 0 to 5 to 8, and lives went down from 3 to 2 when the ball got past. The names stayed the same all game long; only the numbers inside them changed.

[warm and friendly] Wednesday was for deciding. IF the ball touches the paddle THEN bounce, ELSE lose a life. IF lives is 0 THEN show the end. The game did not decide anything by itself; it asked yes-or-no questions the class had written and took whichever road the answer pointed down.

[warm and friendly] The questions had to be asked again and again, many times every second, or the ball would slip past the paddle between two checks. So the whole program sat inside a loop: move the ball, check the paddle, check the lives, draw the screen, and start again. A loop is a set of steps a program repeats.

[warm and friendly] Thursday, the game was wrong. It ended after two lost balls, not three. Nobody deleted anything. They read the steps one at a time, and found the line that checked lives before taking one away instead of after. One line moved, and the game was fixed.

[warm and friendly] Then they tested it the way players would try to break it. One student held the paddle at the very edge. Another pressed two keys at once. A third just let the ball go by, to see whether the end screen appeared. Every test that passed was one less surprise on Friday.

[warm and friendly] Friday was for playing, and for one last box. A variable named best kept the highest score anyone had reached, and IF a new score beat it, THEN best took the new number. By lunch the best score was 41, and a quiet student who had written the loop held it.

[warm and friendly] The game was simple, but it held the whole of programming: boxes that remember, questions that decide, a loop that keeps asking, and a careful reading when something goes wrong. Everything bigger is built from the same four parts. The class kept the game on the classroom computer, and the best score has changed hands eleven times since.
[warm] Two blues to one yellow.

[warm and natural] Chloe found the green in a market far from home: a deep, wet, leaf green that she mixed by accident on a scrap of card. Two blobs of blue, one blob of yellow. She wanted a whole jar of it.

[warm and natural] So she poured in more blue and more yellow, a bit of each, and stirred. The jar turned a green she did not want. Too yellow. She added blue. Too blue. The scrap of card sat there, still perfect, still tiny.

[warm and natural] The card had the answer. Two to one. The mix did not care how much paint there was. It cared about the proportion: for every two parts of blue, one part of yellow. Four blues and two yellows is the same green. Twenty and ten is the same green. Two and two is a different green.
[warm and natural] Chloe measured the jar in spoonfuls, two blue for every one yellow, and got her leaf green by the pint.

[warm and natural] At the paint shop she used the same idea on prices. Three small jars cost 12 dollars, so one jar cost 4. A big jar held as much as four small ones and cost 13 dollars. Four small jars would have cost 16, so working out the price of one, a unit rate, showed the big jar was the better buy.

[warm and natural] She also noticed that two to one meant the green was two thirds blue. Two parts out of every three were blue, and one part out of three was yellow. A ratio compares the parts to each other; a fraction compares a part to the whole.
[warm and natural] A ratio is a recipe that ignores size. It is why a photo can be printed as a poster and still be the same picture.
[warm] How many halves.

[warm and natural] Jamal had three pizzas and a rule that everyone at the party got half a pizza. How many kids could he feed? He wrote three divided by one half and stopped, because everything he knew said dividing made numbers smaller, and the answer had to be at least three.
[warm and natural] He tried to work it the long way and got one and a half, which meant one and a half kids, which was ridiculous. The pizzas were cooling. The kids were counting.

[warm and natural] So he stopped calculating and looked at the pizzas. Each one held two halves. Three pizzas held six halves. Six kids. Dividing by a half was not making the pizzas smaller; it was counting how many halves fit inside them. And the shortcut said the same thing: flip the half into two over one and multiply. Three times two, six.

[warm and natural] At the end of the party three quarters of a pizza was left, and his mother wanted to know how many eighth-size slices it made. Three quarters divided by one eighth. Flip the eighth and multiply: three quarters times eight is six. Six slices. He checked it backward: six eighths is three quarters.

[warm and natural] Jamal liked the checking best. Division asks how many of one thing fit inside another, and multiplication puts them back together. If the answer multiplies back to where you started, it is right.

[warm] The elevator that counted backward.

[warm] The friend who moved the mean.

[warm] East and north.

[warm] The reason that fell.

[warm] Two rains.

[warm and natural] Inform, persuade or entertain. The shape of the writing tells you which, and the purpose tells you how to read it: check the facts, doubt the pitch, enjoy the story. Ask what the writer wants before you decide what to believe.
[warm] One story against ten thousand.

[warm and natural] Marcus's friend swore a vitamin had cured his colds. Every winter, not one cold. Marcus was ready to spend his allowance on a bottle, because his friend was honest and the story was true.

[warm and natural] Then he found a study of ten thousand people that found the vitamin did not prevent colds. Now he had two true things that disagreed. His friend was not lying. Neither was the study. How could both be true?

[warm and natural] They could, because they were different kinds of evidence. His friend was one story: one person, one winter, no way to check what else changed. The study was many cases from a checkable source, counted and compared. One honest story is a start. Ten thousand counted cases are evidence. He kept his allowance.

[warm and natural] His teacher pointed out what the study had that the story did not: a comparison group. Half the people took the vitamin and half took a look-alike pill with nothing in it, and neither group knew which. Only then could the study tell whether the vitamin, and not something else, made the difference.

[warm and natural] His friend's winter might have gone well for other reasons: fewer sick classmates, more sleep, luck. When two things happen together, one did not necessarily cause the other. Marcus wrote that on a sticky note for his wallet.

[warm and natural] Many cases from a checkable source beat one story or a feeling, however sincere. Weak evidence does not make a claim false, but it does not make it true either. Ask how many, and who counted.
[warm] Slim, thin, skinny.

[warm and natural] Rosa called her friend skinny and her friend went quiet for the rest of the walk home. Rosa had meant it kindly. Skinny meant thin, and thin meant slim, and slim was a compliment. Where had it gone wrong?
[warm and natural] She lined the words up. Slim. Thin. Skinny. On a scale they meant the same thing. She would have sworn they were interchangeable.

[warm and natural] They were not, because words carry more than their meaning. Slim comes with approval. Thin is plain. Skinny carries a little worry, or a little scorn. That extra weight is connotation, the feeling a word carries beyond what it says. Swap a word for a plainer one, and notice what disappears. That is the connotation.

[warm and natural] Her teacher gave the plain meaning a name too, denotation: what a dictionary says. Curious and nosy share a denotation, wanting to know things, but curious sounds like a compliment and nosy like a complaint. House and home name the same building, and only one of them has a family in it.

[warm and natural] Rosa started hearing connotation everywhere. An ad called a small apartment cozy. A coach called a stubborn player determined. Choosing the warm word or the cold one was how writers, and friends, took a side without saying so.

[warm and natural] Connotation is the feeling a word carries beyond its meaning. Writers choose it on purpose, and readers feel it whether they notice or not. Rosa apologized the next day, with a better word.
[warm] What she wanted and what she feared.

[warm and natural] In the novel, the girl lied to her brother about the letter from the bank. Kai stopped reading. She had been honest for two hundred pages. Why now? The author never said, and Kai wanted to close the book.
[warm and natural] His teacher asked him to look not at what the girl said but at what she did under pressure. She hid the letter. She took a second job. She stopped sleeping.

[warm and natural] Kai wrote two columns. What she wanted: her brother's respect. What she feared: losing the house. The lie sat right where those two met. She could not tell him without losing the first, and she could not let him find out without the second coming true. Nobody had told Kai her motive. Her actions had.

[warm and natural] His teacher gave him a name for what the author had done: indirect characterization. The author never wrote she is afraid. She showed it through the girl's actions, her thoughts, what she said and how others reacted to her. Direct characterization just tells you; indirect makes you work it out.

[warm and natural] Near the end the girl told her brother the truth, and he helped her keep the house. She had changed, and a character who changes over a story is called dynamic. The motive had not vanished; she had found a way to satisfy both columns.

[warm and natural] Motive is what a character wants or fears, and it is shown by what they do, especially under pressure. Predict a character by their motive, not by their last line of dialogue, and the book stops surprising you for the wrong reasons.
[warm] The clock that glared.

[warm and natural] The clock glared at me, the story said, and Owen wrote in the margin: clocks cannot glare. He was right, and he was missing the point, and his teacher circled the note with a smile.
[warm and natural] Later in the same chapter, a girl's smile was sunshine. Not like sunshine. Was. Owen underlined that too. The book seemed to be lying on purpose.

[warm and natural] It was, and that was the craft. The glaring clock was personification: a thing given a human act, so the reader feels the pressure of midnight. The smile that was sunshine was a metaphor: one thing said to be another, no like or as. A face as bright as the sun would have been a simile, the gentler cousin with the little word in it.

[warm and natural] His teacher added one more, hyperbole: exaggeration on purpose. I have told you a million times. This backpack weighs a ton. Nobody counts the times or weighs the bag. The size of the exaggeration shows the size of the feeling.
[warm and natural] Then she asked him to write the late night himself without any of them. The clock said 11:58. It was late. He was tired. It was true and dead on the page. He put the glare back.

[warm and natural] Similes compare with like or as, metaphors say one thing is another, personification gives human acts to things, and hyperbole exaggerates on purpose. None of them is meant literally, and all of them make a reader feel what a plain sentence only reports.
[warm] Two rooms.

[warm and natural] Lena read an article about two rival cities and an article about a drought, and she understood the first and got lost in the second. Same magazine, same page size. Why did one feel like a map and the other like fog?
[warm and natural] She went back to the second one and looked for what the first had. The city article kept saying however and similarly. The drought article never did. Did that matter?

[warm and natural] It did. However and similarly were signal words for compare and contrast: two rooms side by side, the reader walking between them. The drought article said the trouble was, and then, one answer: a problem and its solution, one long hallway. The moment she knew each article's shape, she knew where to stand in it.

[warm and natural] Her teacher added the others. First, next and finally mark time order, like a recipe. Because, so and as a result mark cause and effect: the drought began because the rains failed, and as a result the wells ran low. Some articles use more than one shape, so Lena learned to watch for signal words all the way through.

[warm and natural] She drew each shape in her notebook: a timeline, two rooms side by side, a knot and scissors, a row of falling dominoes. When she read, she pictured the shape and filled it in, and the fog lifted.

[warm and natural] A text has a structure, and its signal words tell you which one: time order, comparison, problem and solution, cause and effect. Find the signal words in the first paragraph, and the rest of the piece has a floor plan.
[warm] The mystery of the missing bicycle.

[warm and natural] The novel was a mystery about a stolen bicycle, and the class read it the way detectives read a room. The first question was why the author had written it: not to inform, not to persuade, but to entertain, and knowing that told them to expect a trick. Mysteries hide the truth in plain sight, and the fun is finding it before the last page.

[warm and natural] The second question was evidence. When a character said everyone knew the neighbor was a thief, the class wrote one story in the margin. When the police log said the bicycle was seen at the station at nine, they wrote evidence. One was a feeling said loudly; the other could be checked.

[warm and natural] The words themselves were doing work. The neighbor was described as thin in one chapter and skinny in another, and the class caught the change: same size, different feeling. The author had turned the reader against him with a single word.

[warm and natural] Then there was the motive. The girl who took the bicycle wanted to reach her grandmother's house before dark, and she feared being late more than being caught. The author had shown both without ever saying them: she checked the sky, she skipped supper, she lied to her brother.

[warm and natural] The author had tricks with language too. The rain spat at the girl as she rode; the streetlights watched her pass. Personification, said a boy in the back, and the whole class felt the town turn against her. It was a figure of speech, not a fact, and a good reader enjoys the one without mistaking it for the other.

[warm and natural] The structure helped the detectives most. The chapters about the neighbor used however and on the other hand; the chapters about the girl went first, next, then. One side was a comparison; the other was a timeline, and the timeline led to the station at nine.

[warm and natural] The bicycle turned up in the last chapter where the strongest evidence had pointed all along. The girl brought it back herself, soaked, and told the truth. The police had never had to look far; the station clock and the log had told them where she went.

[warm and natural] Half the class had suspected the neighbor anyway, on the strength of one story and one skinny. That, the teacher said, was the lesson, and it was not about bicycles. Evidence can be checked. A feeling said loudly cannot, however many people repeat it.
[warm] The city inside.
[warm and natural] Jamal bit into an apple and thought nothing of it. His science teacher asked him to think of everything. What had to happen for one bite to become part of his body?
[warm and natural] He said, you swallow it. She waited. He said, then it goes to your stomach. She was still waiting, and Jamal realized he did not actually know what happened next.

[warm and natural] Think of a city. The stomach and intestines are the kitchen, breaking the bite into pieces the body can use. The heart and blood vessels are the roads and trucks, carrying those pieces to every building. The lungs are the air supply. The brain and nerves are the phone lines running it all. Every system is a team of organs with one main job, and one bite needs all of them.

[warm and natural] The kitchen does more than chop. The stomach churns the bite with acid, and the small intestine, a tube longer than Jamal is tall, pulls the sugars and other nutrients into the blood. Then the nutrients and the oxygen carried by red blood cells from the lungs ride the roads together to every muscle.

[warm and natural] The city also keeps itself steady. When Jamal ran at recess and got hot, his skin sweated to cool him and his heart sped up to deliver more oxygen. The body is always adjusting to stay balanced, and scientists call that homeostasis.

[warm and natural] Each body system is a team of organs with one job, and the systems depend on each other. One bite of an apple is a delivery to a whole city, and the city works only because no system works alone.
[warm] The flower in the basement.

[warm and natural] Silas won the flower at the county fair, a prize-winning orange lily, and he wanted to keep it safe. So he put it in the basement, where it was cool and nothing could knock it over.
[warm and natural] He gave it the best soil in town. He watered it every morning. Within a week the leaves turned pale, then yellow, and drooped like they were tired.
[warm and natural] More water did nothing. Better soil did nothing. The flower was fed and watered and dying, and Silas could not see why.

[warm and natural] Then his neighbor asked a strange question: "What is it eating?" Not drinking. Eating. Plants do not eat soil. They eat light. Inside every green leaf are chloroplasts, tiny solar panels that take carbon dioxide from the air, water from the roots, and the energy of sunlight, and build sugar out of them. No light, no sugar. No sugar, no lily. Without light, a plant also stops making the green chlorophyll that catches it, which is why the leaves had faded.
[warm and natural] Silas carried it up to the window. In a few days the leaves began to green again, and within a week the whole plant had turned itself to face the glass.

[warm and natural] The leaves gave something back, too. Building sugar splits water and lets oxygen out into the air, the same oxygen Silas breathed. And at night, with no light, the lily used some of the sugar it had made, the way he used his breakfast.
[warm and natural] Every forest you have ever seen is made mostly of air and light, woven together by leaves.
[warm] The slope of the air.

[warm and natural] From the hilltop Priya watched a line of clouds come across the valley, and felt the wind pick up before they arrived. Her uncle said the wind was blowing toward the storm. That seemed backward. Should the storm not push the wind ahead of it?
[warm and natural] She could not see air, so she could not see what was pushing what. All she had was the feeling on her face and a line of clouds getting closer.

[warm and natural] Her uncle told her to think of air as water on a slope. Cool air is heavy and piles up: high pressure. Warm air is light and rises: low pressure. The heavy air slides toward the light, and that sliding is wind. The storm was a place where warm air was rising, so the wind ran toward it. And the line of clouds was a front, where two air masses met and one shoved the other up.

[warm and natural] The sun sets it all going. It heats the ground unevenly, land faster than water, dark fields faster than pale sand, so some air warms and rises while other air stays cool. On a summer afternoon near a lake, the breeze blows in off the cool water toward the warm land.

[warm and natural] Fronts come in kinds. A cold front, cold air pushing under warm air like a shovel, brings tall clouds and short, hard storms, with cooler air behind them. A warm front, warm air sliding up over cold air, brings long, gentle rain. Priya's line of tall clouds was a cold front.

[warm and natural] Warm air rises and cool air sinks; wind blows from high pressure to low. A front is where two air masses meet, and that is where the weather happens. Feel the wind on a hill and you can read the sky.
[warm] The moths.

[warm and natural] Theo read that the moths near an old factory town had turned dark over a hundred years, and he pictured moths going darker the way skin tans. His teacher said no moth had ever changed color in its life. Theo said then how did they turn dark?
[warm and natural] She showed him a photo of a tree trunk gone black with soot, and a pale moth sitting on it like a light on a hill. Birds eat moths. Which one would a bird see first?

[warm and natural] The pale one. On sooty trees, pale moths were easy to see and got eaten. Dark moths hid and lived, and they had dark children, because color is inherited. Year after year, more dark moths, fewer pale. Nobody changed. The group changed, because the ones who fit the place had the most children.

[warm and natural] Then the air was cleaned up. After laws cut the soot in the second half of the twentieth century, the trunks grew pale with lichen again, the pale moths came back, and the dark ones became rare. The same rule ran in reverse.

[warm and natural] The same thing happens in hospitals. When a medicine kills most of a germ, the few germs that happen to survive it multiply, and soon the medicine works less well. Nobody taught the germs anything. The medicine chose which ones would have children.

[warm and natural] Natural selection needs three things: variation, survival and inheritance. Helpful differences get passed on more, and over generations the group shifts to fit its place. No moth turned dark. The forest chose which moths would have children.
[warm] The kittens that did not match.
[warm and natural] Two black barn cats had four kittens. Three were black. One was gray, soft as smoke, and nobody could say where it came from.
[warm and natural] The farmer checked the barn for strays. There were none. Both parents were black, plain as night. How do two black cats make a gray kitten?

[warm and natural] Each kitten gets two copies of a coat gene, one from each parent. The black copy is dominant: one black copy and the kitten shows black. The gray copy is recessive: it shows only when a kitten gets two gray copies. Both parents were carrying a hidden gray copy behind their black one. Three kittens got at least one black copy. One kitten drew gray from both, and the hidden trait finally showed.

[warm and natural] The farmer's daughter drew it as a square. Each parent had one black copy and one gray copy. Four boxes: black-black, black-gray, gray-black and gray-gray. Only one box in four was gray-gray, so each kitten had a one-in-four chance of gray. Four kittens, one gray: the square came true this time, though it does not always.
[warm and natural] Those copies live in DNA, a long code curled up inside the cells, and a gene is one stretch of it. The kitten carries the same code in its paws, its whiskers and its tail.
[warm and natural] The farmer kept the gray kitten. It never had to wonder where it came from. It had always been there, in both parents, waiting.
[warm and natural] A trait can skip a generation without leaving. Recessive does not mean weak. It means quiet.
[warm] The pyramid.

[warm and natural] Maya wondered why the field had thousands of blades of grass, hundreds of grasshoppers, a few dozen birds and one hawk. If hawks were the strongest, why were there not more of them?

[warm and natural] She counted energy instead of animals. Say the grass held a thousand units of energy from the sun. How much reached the grasshoppers that ate it? She assumed most of it. That turned out to be the mistake.

[warm and natural] Only about a tenth. A grasshopper spends most of what it eats on moving, breathing and staying warm, and only a tenth becomes grasshopper. A thousand units of grass make a hundred units of grasshopper, ten of bird, one of hawk. The energy leaks away at every step, so each level has to be much bigger than the one above it.

[warm and natural] Maya asked where the lost energy went. Most of it left as heat, from every animal breathing, moving and keeping warm. Heat does not come back to the grass. That is why the field needs new sunlight every day.

[warm and natural] The matter is different. When the hawk dies, decomposers break its body down, and the carbon and nitrogen in it return to the soil to build new grass. Matter goes around in a circle. Energy flows through in a line, from the sun to heat.

[warm and natural] Only about a tenth of the energy passes to the next level of a food chain. That is why there is much more grass than there are hawks, and why the pyramid of life is always wide at the bottom.
[warm] The crumpled bag.

[warm and natural] Kai lived on a street with a storm drain and a creek at the bottom of the hill, and he had never once wondered where the creek came from. Then his teacher handed him a crumpled paper bag and a cup of water.

[warm and natural] He poured a little water on the top of the bag. It ran along the creases, joined other trickles, and gathered in one low corner. He poured on the other side. Different creases, same corner. He could not make the water go anywhere else.

[warm and natural] The creases were ridges. The folds between them were creeks. Every drop that fell on the bag ran downhill to the same river, and all the land that drained to that corner was its watershed. His street, his storm drain, the creek: one bag, one corner.

[warm and natural] His teacher showed a real map. In Austin, Texas, creeks such as Shoal Creek and Barton Creek run into the Colorado River, which widens into Lady Bird Lake downtown and flows on to the Gulf of Mexico. Every creek on the map had its own little watershed inside the big one.

[warm and natural] That is why oil dripped in a driveway or fertilizer washed off a lawn matters. Rain carries it down the creases too, into the storm drain and the creek, and what happens on the hill shows up in the river.

[warm and natural] A watershed is all the land that drains to one river, and upstream becomes downstream. What you pour on the top of the bag ends up in the corner, which is why a town cares what happens on the hill above it.
[warm] The garden that taught everything.

[warm and natural] The school garden started as a rectangle of dirt in March. The first lesson was the body. The students who dug it went home tired and hungry, and the teacher drew a city on the board: roads for blood, a kitchen for the stomach, phone lines for the nerves. The heart sped up while they dug and slowed when they rested, keeping the city steady.

[warm and natural] The second lesson was the leaves that came up in April: photosynthesis, light and water and carbon dioxide from the air turned into sugar, and oxygen given away. A pot of beans left in the shed came up pale and spindly, reaching for a light that was not there, and the class kept it as proof.

[warm and natural] In May the weather turned. High pressure brought cool, sinking air and still mornings; then a low came through with a cold front, and a hard wind flattened half the beans. The class had watched the barometer drop the night before.

[warm and natural] The beans with the thickest stems stayed standing and set seed; the thin-stemmed ones snapped. If stem thickness runs in bean families, that is natural selection in one bed, said the teacher: the wind had chosen which plants would leave seeds.

[warm and natural] The tomatoes came up red and yellow from the same packet. Red is dominant in tomatoes and yellow recessive, so the class drew Punnett squares. Two red plants, each carrying a hidden yellow copy, would give about one yellow plant in four. They counted three yellow in fourteen, close enough to make them grin.

[warm and natural] By June the garden was feeding grasshoppers, which were feeding a pair of birds, which were feeding a hawk that came once a week. Only about a tenth of the energy passed up each step, and everyone could see why there was one hawk and a thousand grasshoppers.

[warm and natural] The last lesson was the hose. The water came from the river the whole town drank, which came from the creeks in the hills, which is where the rain went. A watershed, ending in a school bean. When a parent spilled fertilizer by the storm drain, the class knew exactly where it was headed.

[warm and natural] In August they pulled the plants and turned the soil, and the teacher asked what they had grown. Beans, said one student. A body, a leaf, a storm, a family tree, a food chain and a river, said another. Both were right. The bean seeds went into envelopes for next year.
[warm] The summary that gave nothing away.

[warm and natural] Diego's summary of the article was one sentence long and it was mostly his opinion. The article says cities should plant more trees, which is obviously right. His teacher crossed out the last four words and wrote: not yet.
[warm and natural] Not yet? Diego thought summarizing was about what he thought of the thing. Otherwise what was the point of reading it?

[warm and natural] The point came in two parts. First, the summary: the article says cities should plant more trees, for shade and cleaner air, and it gives three cities as examples. Nothing about what Diego thought. A reader could not guess his opinion, and that was the test. Then the response, where he finally got to say obviously right, and why.

[warm and natural] His teacher gave him the rules for the first job. Name the author and the title. Give the main idea and the key details in your own words. Keep it much shorter than the original, and leave yourself out.

[warm and natural] The response had choices. Diego could agree and add a reason of his own, or disagree and say why. He could also connect the article to something he had seen, like the treeless parking lot by his school that baked every afternoon. He did all three in one paragraph.

[warm and natural] Summarize fairly first, then respond. Keep your opinion out of the summary so a reader can trust it, and then spend the response on what you think and what you would push back on. Two jobs, two paragraphs.
[warm] The objection said out loud.

[warm and natural] Priya was arguing for a later school start, and she knew exactly what the coach would say: it would cut practice time. She planned to leave that out and hope nobody thought of it. Her teacher read the draft and asked where the coach was.
[warm and natural] Priya said she had left him out on purpose. If she brought up the objection, would she not be arguing against herself?

[warm and natural] The opposite. She wrote it in: some say a later start would cut practice time. True, up front. Then she answered it: practice could shift later, and rested players play better than tired ones. When the coach stood up at the meeting to object, half the room said, she already covered that. Her argument looked stronger for having met him first.

[warm and natural] Her teacher warned her about one trap. It is easy to answer a weak objection that nobody really holds. That is called a straw man, and audiences can smell it. Priya had chosen the objection the coach would actually make, which is why answering it worked.

[warm and natural] She also learned the sentences that carry it. While it is true that practice would move, rested players play better. Some say the buses cannot change; in fact, other districts have changed theirs. Each sentence gives the other side its due, then turns.

[warm and natural] Name the best objection and answer it. A fair counterclaim makes your argument stronger, not weaker, because it shows you have looked at the other side and still stand where you stand.
[warm] Starting where the reader is.

[warm and natural] Sam had to explain how a board game worked to someone who had never played, and his first draft began with the scoring. His grandmother read it and asked what a piece was. Sam had been playing since he was six and had forgotten anyone could not know.
[warm and natural] He started again, from the top, and got lost in a different way: every sentence had three new words in it. His grandmother read it kindly and asked what a turn was.

[warm and natural] The third draft started where she was. A board, a die, a piece. Then one rule, roll the die and move that many spaces, and then the next rule. Each new word got its meaning the moment it appeared, and each rule got an example she could picture. By the end she was beating him.

[warm and natural] His teacher showed him what held the third draft together: transitions. First, then, after that, finally. Each one told his grandmother where she was in the explanation, the way signs tell you where you are in a building.

[warm and natural] He added one small drawing, the board with an arrow showing which way to move, and a heading over the part about winning. A picture and a heading did in one glance what a paragraph had struggled to do.

[warm and natural] An explanatory essay starts where the reader is and adds one idea at a time. Define a new word when it appears, and give an example for every rule. If your grandmother can follow it, anyone can.
[warm] Chloe and the counterclaim.

[warm and natural] Chloe was twelve when the school cut the art budget, and she wrote to the board. Her first job was a fair summary of their reasons, with none of her opinion in it: reading scores were down, and the money had to come from somewhere.

[warm and natural] Only then came her response. Summarize fairly first; then say what you think. She quoted their own words where she could, so no one could say she had bent them. The board member who read it said it was the first letter that had understood them.

[warm and natural] Her argument named the best objection before anyone else could: some say art is a luxury when reading scores are down. True, she wrote, and then the answer: the students who took art had raised their reading scores that year, and here were the numbers. She checked them twice with the school secretary before she mailed a single page.

[warm and natural] She was careful with those numbers. Scores rising in the same year did not prove art had caused it, she added, but they did show art had not cost the students their reading. A board member underlined that sentence.

[warm and natural] A fair counterclaim wins trust, and trust was what she needed. She did not answer a straw man, the weakest objection nobody held; she answered the one the board actually believed. She practiced reading it aloud to her grandmother, who asked the hardest question she heard all spring: what would you cut instead? She answered that too: the new scoreboard could wait a year.

[warm and natural] The explanatory essay was for the board members who had never taken art. It started where they were, one idea at a time: what a color wheel is, then what value means, then what a child learns by mixing green. Each new word got its meaning the moment it appeared.

[warm and natural] She used transitions like signposts, first, then, finally, and one small drawing of the color wheel, which did in a glance what a paragraph could not. She read the essay aloud once more and cut every sentence that explained what the drawing already showed.

[warm and natural] The budget came back in the spring, smaller than before but back. Chloe kept the letter. Her handwriting had gotten neater in the middle of it, where she had stopped arguing with the board and started explaining to it. The next fall, two other students wrote letters of their own about the library hours, and they asked Chloe to read their drafts first.
[warm] Four regions.

[warm and natural] Kai's family drove across Texas in one long day, and Kai noticed the land keep changing outside the window. Flat and wet and green. Then rolling hills. Then high and dry and endless. Then mountains. He asked if they had left the state. They had not.

[warm and natural] His mother said the peoples who lived here first would have felt those changes more than he did, because the land decided what they ate. Kai did not see how land could decide anything.

[warm and natural] It decided everything. Along the wet Gulf Coast, the Karankawa fished and gathered in the bays. In the piney woods of East Texas, still part of the Gulf Coastal Plains, the Caddo farmed corn, beans and squash in villages. On the rolling North Central Plains, the Wichita farmed along the rivers and hunted buffalo. On the high, dry Great Plains, the Comanche followed the buffalo on horseback. In the Mountains and Basins of the far west, the Jumano farmed beside the rare rivers.

[warm and natural] The land even decided their houses. The Caddo built tall, round houses of grass over wooden frames. The Comanche carried tipis they could take down and move with the herds. The Karankawa paddled dugout canoes through the shallow bays, and the Jumano along the western rivers lived in adobe villages.

[warm and natural] Kai started reading the land from the car. Where it rained, people farmed. Where it was dry and open, people followed the animals. Where the bays were shallow and full of fish, people fished.

[warm and natural] Texas has four natural regions: the Gulf Coastal Plains, the North Central Plains, the Great Plains, and the Mountains and Basins. Each shaped how its first peoples lived, and you can still see the borders from a car window.
[warm] Three centuries and a door.

[warm and natural] Maya's history book said Spain owned Texas for three hundred years, and she pictured three hundred years of Spanish towns. Then she looked at the map from 1800. San Antonio. A few missions. And a great deal of nothing.
[warm and natural] Three centuries and almost no one? How could a country claim a place that size and hardly live in it? Maya thought the map must be missing something.

[warm and natural] It was not. Spain claimed Texas from the 1500s and settled little of it beyond San Antonio, founded in 1718, and a string of missions from the 1690s. The land was far from Mexico City and hard to hold. In 1821 Mexico won its independence, inherited the empty claim, and opened the door to American settlers to fill it. They came faster than anyone in Mexico City expected.

[warm and natural] Her teacher explained why the missions were built at all. In 1685 a French explorer, La Salle, landed on the Texas coast and built a fort. Spain, alarmed, sent priests and soldiers to build missions in the east to hold its claim. Fear of France did more to settle early Texas than any plan.

[warm and natural] Mexico's door had a name: the empresario system. Stephen F. Austin brought the first three hundred families, and many more followed. By the early 1830s settlers from the United States far outnumbered the Mexican Texans, called Tejanos, and quarrels over laws, slavery and self-rule began to grow.

[warm and natural] Spain claimed Texas for three centuries and settled little of it. Mexico won independence in 1821 and invited settlers, who soon outnumbered everyone else. A claim on a map is not the same as a people on the land, and that gap is the next chapter.
[warm] From a cannon to eighteen minutes.

[warm] Five folds.

No liked, no hated, no unfortunately. Watch for the single words that let an opinion back in: sadly, of course, so-called, only. [warm and natural] Verbs can lean too. The article argues, states or reports. It does not rant, admit or whine. Rosa had once written that an author admitted something, and her teacher asked whether the author had confessed or simply said it.

[warm and natural] Her teacher gave her a test for fairness. Would the person who wrote the article agree that her summary said what they meant? And would someone who disagreed with it agree too? [warm and natural] An objective summary says what the text says in neutral words and leaves your opinion out. The dangerous words are the small ones. A mirror does not sigh.
[warm] Outside the frame.
[warm and natural] A pamphlet came through Theo's door: vote for her. Should, must, best, on every line. Theo could tell it wanted him to do something. His mother asked what it wanted him not to see.
[warm and natural] Not to see? It was a page of words. Everything on it was there to read. Theo read it twice and found no lie on it anywhere.

[warm and natural] The lean was not in what the page said. It was in what it left out. Should and must told him the purpose: to persuade. Then he drew a frame around the pamphlet and asked what lived outside it. The costs. Not one number, anywhere on the page. Bias is the shape of the frame.

[warm and natural] His mother pointed to the small print at the bottom: paid for by the campaign. A text that comes from the side it praises has a reason to lean. That does not make it false. It makes it worth checking.

[warm and natural] So Theo found the city's voter guide, which listed the plan and its costs side by side, and a newspaper story that quoted both candidates. The costs were there after all: a new park, paid for over ten years. The pamphlet had told the truth, and only half of it.

[warm and natural] Every text has a purpose: to inform, to persuade or to entertain. A bias is a lean you can see in what a text leaves out and in who is speaking. Read the page, then read the empty space around it, then read another source.
[warm] One tune, two songs.

[warm and natural] Lena read a long novel about two brothers and, the same week, a one-page fable about two foxes. Her teacher asked what they had in common. Nothing, Lena said. One had cars and a hospital. The other had a hen.

[warm and natural] Then she thought about how each ended. The brother who told the truth lost a friend and kept his brother. The fox who told the truth lost the hen and kept the den. Different stories. Same shape at the end.

[warm and natural] A theme is not a topic. It is a sentence about what a story says. Both stories said that honesty costs something and is worth it. The novel showed it over three hundred pages. The fable said it outright in a moral at the bottom. Two songs, one tune.

[warm and natural] Her teacher warned her about one-word answers. Honesty is a topic, not a theme. A theme is a whole sentence someone could agree with or argue against: honesty costs something and is worth it.

[warm and natural] Then Lena backed it up the way a lawyer would, with one piece of evidence from each text: the brother who kept his brother, the fox who kept the den. A theme you can prove from two very different stories is one worth believing.

[warm and natural] A theme is a sentence about what a story says about life, and very different texts can share one. A fable states its theme as a moral; a novel makes you find it. Look at what each character paid, and what they kept.
[warm] The fire station that burned down.

[warm] The balloon on the wall.

[warm and natural] Savanah left the farm a few years later for the city. She still moves heavy things the same way: one steady force, and let the motion do the rest.

[warm] Boxes inside boxes.

[warm and natural] Moon, planet, solar system, galaxy, universe: each is inside the next. Distances are measured in light-years, because kilometers run out of zeros. The marble is small, and it is home.
[warm] The walk on a graph.

[warm] The laundry pile.

[warm and natural] Layers pile up over time, so deeper is older, unless the Earth has folded or overturned them. Fossils and the layers around them tell what a place was like and when. A cliff is a laundry pile that took a million years.

[warm] A fight worth picking.

[warm and natural] A thesis that everyone agrees with is a topic wearing a thesis costume. There was nothing to prove and nowhere for the essay to go.

[warm and natural] He tried again. Dogs make better pets than cats for busy families. Now someone would argue. His cousin would argue right now. And once he had a claim someone could fight, the reasons lined up under it on their own: dogs get you outside, dogs fit a schedule, dogs guard the house. The outline wrote itself.

[warm and natural] His teacher pushed once more: a strong thesis also says why. Dogs make better pets than cats for busy families because they build a routine. Now the because pointed at the reasons before he had even listed them.

[warm and natural] Under each reason in the outline went a piece of evidence and a note about the other side: cats are cheaper, some would say. He gave that a line too, and planned his answer. The outline now held the whole essay on one page. When he sat down to write, every paragraph already knew its job.
[warm and natural] Write the thesis first, then list the reasons under it. A good thesis is one someone could disagree with, because an essay is a fight worth picking, and a fight needs another side.
[warm] The missing sentence.

[warm and natural] Ana wrote to the city. Claim: the town needs a safer crossing at Oak and Third. Evidence: twelve near-misses this year, counted by the crossing guard. She was proud of the number. The city wrote back and asked what the number had to do with a crossing.
[warm and natural] Ana was furious. The connection was obvious. Twelve near-misses meant danger, and a crossing fixed danger. But she had not written that sentence. She had assumed it.

[warm and natural] That sentence has a name: the warrant. It says why the evidence counts for the claim. Twelve near-misses mean that twelve times someone was nearly hurt, and a crossing that makes drivers stop would cut that number. Claim, evidence, warrant.

[warm and natural] The warrant also told her what to ask for. On a busy road, a traffic engineer told her, plain painted stripes alone do little; flashing lights that drivers can see make them far more likely to stop. Ana changed her claim to match her warrant.

[warm and natural] Her teacher added one more habit: pick evidence a stranger can check. The crossing guard's count was good. A photo of the corner at rush hour was better still. She sent it all again, and the city sent a crew to put up a crossing with flashing lights.

[warm and natural] A paragraph that proves something has three parts: the claim, the evidence, and the warrant that says why the evidence counts. The warrant is the sentence most often missing, because the writer already believes it.
[warm] Body first.

[warm and natural] Diego stared at a blank page for twenty minutes trying to write his introduction. He could not introduce an essay he had not written. Every opening sentence promised something he did not have yet, and he deleted each one.
[warm and natural] His teacher told him to skip it. Write the body first. Diego thought that was cheating. Essays started at the top.

The conclusion looked back at the three reasons and said the thesis again in fresh words. Five paragraphs, one skeleton.

[warm and natural] Between the body paragraphs he added transitions, first, also, most of all, so a reader could feel the reasons stacking up. Then he read the whole essay aloud and fixed every sentence he tripped over. His ears caught mistakes his eyes had skipped.

[warm and natural] A five-paragraph essay is an introduction with the thesis, three body paragraphs and a conclusion that looks back. Write the body first, then the introduction that fits it. Nobody builds a house starting with the roof.
[warm] Frederick builds the essay.

[warm and natural] Frederick was thirteen and had a jar of pond water on his desk and a thesis nobody could ignore: the pond behind the school was healthier than the county said. Evidence: fourteen kinds of insect larvae in one jar, counted under the microscope his dad had finally let him use alone, including mayflies, stoneflies and caddisflies. He counted twice, and his dad counted once more to be sure.

[warm and natural] Warrant: mayflies, stoneflies and caddisflies are sensitive to pollution and are among the first to disappear from dirty water. So finding all three, among so many kinds, is a sign the water is clean. The evidence counted because the warrant said why.

[warm and natural] He named the other side too. Some would say one jar is one sample, and it was. So his conclusion asked the county to test the pond properly, at several spots and in more than one season, instead of claiming more than a jar could prove.

[warm and natural] He built the body first, three paragraphs with one reason each, and then the introduction that fit it. For the hook he used a question from his little sister: why do the bugs in our pond have tails? The thesis came at the end of that first paragraph, where a reader expected it.

[warm and natural] The five-paragraph essay went to the county office with a photograph of the jar. The conclusion said the thesis again in the light of what was shown. He read it aloud to his dad twice and cut every sentence that made him stumble.

[warm and natural] The county sent someone to look. Frederick was there, in a lab coat two sizes too big, and the someone was impressed. [warm] Why, how, and what may not.

[warm and natural] The Declaration says why, the Constitution says how, and the Bill of Rights says what may never be done. Three questions, three answers, and a country runs on all of them at once.
[warm] Learning to drive.

[warm] The coin toss.

[warm] Three promises.

[warm] Two sides of the bed.
